paragraphs:
“After all,” murmured Poirot, “it is possible that I shall not die
this time.”

Coming from a convalescent influenza patient, I hailed the remark
as showing a beneficial optimism. I myself had been the first
sufferer from the disease. Poirot in his turn had gone down. He
was now sitting up in bed, propped up with pillows, his head
muffled in a woollen shawl, and was slowly sipping a particularly
noxious tisane which I had prepared according to his directions.
His eye rested with pleasure upon a neatly graduated row of medicine
bottles which adorned the mantelpiece.

“Yes, yes,” my little friend continued. “Once more shall I be
myself again, the great Hercule Poirot, the terror of evil-doers!
Figure to yourself, _mon ami_, that I have a little paragraph to
myself in _Society Gossip_. But yes! Here it is! ‘Go it—criminals—all
out! Hercule Poirot—and believe me, girls, he’s some Hercules!—our
own pet society detective can’t get a grip on you. ’Cause why?
’Cause he’s got _la grippe_ himself’!”

I laughed.

“Good for you, Poirot. You are becoming quite a public character.
And fortunately you haven’t missed anything of particular interest
during this time.”

“That is true. The few cases I have had to decline did not fill me
with any regret.”

Our landlady stuck her head in at the door.

“There’s a gentleman downstairs. Says he must see Monsieur Poirot
or you, Captain. Seeing as he was in a great to-do—and with all
that quite the gentleman—I brought up ’is card.”

She handed me the bit of pasteboard. “Mr. Roger Havering,” I read.

Poirot motioned with his head towards the bookcase, and I obediently
pulled forth “Who’s Who.” Poirot took it from me and scanned the
pages rapidly.

“Second son of fifth Baron Windsor. Married 1913 Zoe, fourth
daughter of William Crabb.”

“H’m!” I said. “I rather fancy that’s the girl who used to act at
the Frivolity—only she called herself Zoe Carrisbrook. I remember
she married some young man about town just before the War.”

“Would it interest you, Hastings, to go down and hear what our
visitor’s particular little trouble is? Make him all my excuses.”

Roger Havering was a man of about forty, well set up and of smart
appearance. His face, however, was haggard, and he was evidently
labouring under great agitation.

“Captain Hastings? You are Monsieur Poirot’s partner, I understand.
It is imperative that he should come with me to Derbyshire to-day.”

“I’m afraid that’s impossible,” I replied. “Poirot is ill in
bed—influenza.”

His face fell.

“Dear me, that is a great blow to me.”

“The matter on which you want to consult him is serious?”

“My God, yes! My uncle, the best friend I have in the world, was
foully murdered last night.”

“Here in London?”

“No, in Derbyshire. I was in town and received a telegram from my
wife this morning. Immediately upon its receipt I determined to
come round and beg Monsieur Poirot to undertake the case.”

“If you will excuse me a minute,” I said, struck by a sudden idea.

I rushed upstairs, and in a few brief words acquainted Poirot with
the situation. He took any further words out of my mouth.

“I see. I see. You want to go yourself, is it not so? Well, why
not? You should know my methods by now. All I ask is that you
should report to me fully every day, and follow implicitly any
instructions I may wire you.”

To this I willingly agreed.


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


An hour later I was sitting opposite Mr. Havering in a first-class
carriage on the Midland Railway, speeding rapidly away from London.

“To begin with, Captain Hastings, you must understand that Hunter’s
Lodge, where we are going, and where the tragedy took place, is
only a small shooting-box in the heart of the Derbyshire moors.
Our real home is near Newmarket, and we usually rent a flat in town
for the season. Hunter’s Lodge is looked after by a housekeeper
who is quite capable of doing all we need when we run down for an
occasional week-end. Of course, during the shooting season, we take
down some of our own servants from Newmarket. My uncle, Mr.
Harrington Pace (as you may know, my mother was a Miss Pace of New
York), has, for the last three years, made his home with us. He
never got on well with my father, or my elder brother, and I
suspect that my being somewhat of a prodigal son myself rather
increased than diminished his affection towards me. Of course I am
a poor man, and my uncle was a rich one—in other words, he paid
the piper! But, though exacting in many ways, he was not really
hard to get on with, and we all three lived very harmoniously
together. Two days ago my uncle, rather wearied with some recent
gaieties of ours in town, suggested that we should run down to
Derbyshire for a day or two. My wife telegraphed to Mrs. Middleton,
the housekeeper, and we went down that same afternoon. Yesterday
evening I was forced to return to town, but my wife and my uncle
remained on. This morning I received this telegram.” He handed it
over to me:

“Come at once uncle Harrington murdered last night bring good
detective if you can but do come—Zoe.”

“Then, as yet you know no details?”

“No, I suppose it will be in the evening papers. Without doubt the
police are in charge.”

It was about three o’clock when we arrived at the little station
of Elmer’s Dale. From there a five-mile drive brought us to a small
grey stone building in the midst of the rugged moors.

“A lonely place,” I observed with a shiver.

Havering nodded.

“I shall try and get rid of it. I could never live here again.”

We unlatched the gate and were walking up the narrow path to the
oak door when a familiar figure emerged and came to meet us.

“Japp!” I ejaculated.

The Scotland Yard inspector grinned at me in a friendly fashion
before addressing my companion.

“Mr. Havering, I think? I’ve been sent down from London to take
charge of this case, and I’d like a word with you, if I may, sir.”

“My wife——”

“I’ve seen your good lady, sir—and the housekeeper. I won’t keep
you a moment, but I’m anxious to get back to the village now that
I’ve seen all there is to see here.”

“I know nothing as yet as to what——”

“Ex-actly,” said Japp soothingly. “But there are just one or two
little points I’d like your opinion about all the same. Captain
Hastings here, he knows me, and he’ll go on up to the house and
tell them you’re coming. What have you done with the little man,
by the way, Captain Hastings?”

“He’s ill in bed with influenza.”

“Is he now? I’m sorry to hear that. Rather the case of the cart
without the horse, your being here without him, isn’t it?”

And on his rather ill-timed jest I went on to the house. I rang
the bell, as Japp had closed the door behind him. After some
moments it was opened to me by a middle-aged woman in black.

“Mr. Havering will be here in a moment,” I explained. “He has been
detained by the inspector. I have come down with him from London
to look into the case. Perhaps you can tell me briefly what occurred
last night.”

“Come inside, sir.” She closed the door behind me, and we stood in
the dimly-lighted hall. “It was after dinner last night, sir, that
the man came. He asked to see Mr. Pace, sir, and, seeing that he
spoke the same way, I thought it was an American gentleman friend
of Mr. Pace’s and I showed him into the gun-room, and then went to
tell Mr. Pace. He wouldn’t give any name, which, of course, was a
bit odd, now I come to think of it. I told Mr. Pace, and he seemed
puzzled like, but he said to the mistress: ‘Excuse me, Zoe, while
I just see what this fellow wants.’ He went off to the gun-room,
and I went back to the kitchen, but after a while I heard loud
voices, as if they were quarrelling, and I came out into the hall.
At the same time, the mistress she comes out too, and just then
there was a shot and then a dreadful silence. We both ran to the
gun-room door, but it was locked and we had to go round to the
window. It was open, and there inside was Mr. Pace, all shot and
bleeding.”

“What became of the man?”

“He must have got away through the window, sir, before we got to
it.”

“And then?”

“Mrs. Havering sent me to fetch the police. Five miles to walk it
was. They came back with me, and the constable he stayed all night,
and this morning the police gentleman from London arrived.”

“What was this man like who called to see Mr. Pace?”

The housekeeper reflected.

“He had a black beard, sir, and was about middle-aged, and had on
a light overcoat. Beyond the fact that he spoke like an American
I didn’t notice much about him.”

“I see. Now I wonder if I can see Mrs. Havering?”

“She’s upstairs, sir. Shall I tell her?”

“If you please. Tell her that Mr. Havering is outside with Inspector
Japp, and that the gentleman he has brought back with him from
London is anxious to speak to her as soon as possible.”

“Very good, sir.”

I was in a fever of impatience to get at all the facts. Japp had
two or three hours’ start of me, and his anxiety to be gone made
me keen to be close at his heels.

Mrs. Havering did not keep me waiting long. In a few minutes I
heard a light step descending the stairs, and looked up to see a
very handsome young woman coming towards me. She wore a
flame-coloured jumper, that set off the slender boyishness of her
figure. On her dark head was a little hat of flame-coloured leather.
Even the present tragedy could not dim the vitality of her
personality.

I introduced myself, and she nodded in quick comprehension.

“Of course I have often heard of you and your colleague, Monsieur
Poirot. You have done some wonderful things together, haven’t you?
It was very clever of my husband to get you so promptly. Now will
you ask me questions? That is the easiest way, isn’t it, of getting
to know all you want to about this dreadful affair?”

“Thank you, Mrs. Havering. Now what time was it that this man
arrived?”

“It must have been just before nine o’clock. We had finished
dinner, and were sitting over our coffee and cigarettes.”

“Your husband had already left for London?”

“Yes, he went up by the 6.15.”

“Did he go by car to the station, or did he walk?”

“Our own car isn’t down here. One came out from the garage in
Elmer’s Dale to fetch him in time for the train.”

“Was Mr. Pace quite his usual self?”

“Absolutely. Most normal in every way.”

“Now, can you describe this visitor at all?”

“I’m afraid not. I didn’t see him. Mrs. Middleton showed him
straight into the gun-room and then came to tell my uncle.”

“What did your uncle say?”

“He seemed rather annoyed, but went off at once. It was about five
minutes later that I heard the sound of raised voices. I ran out
into the hall and almost collided with Mrs. Middleton. Then we
heard the shot. The gun-room door was locked on the inside, and we
had to go right round the house to the window. Of course that took
some time, and the murderer had been able to get well away. My poor
uncle”—her voice faltered—“had been shot through the head. I saw
at once that he was dead. I sent Mrs. Middleton for the police. I
was careful to touch nothing in the room but to leave it exactly
as I found it.”

I nodded approval.

“Now, as to the weapon?”

“Well, I can make a guess at it, Captain Hastings. A pair of
revolvers of my husband’s were mounted upon the wall. One of them
is missing. I pointed this out to the police, and they took the
other one away with them. When they have extracted the bullet, I
suppose they will know for certain.”

“May I go to the gun-room?”

“Certainly. The police have finished with it. But the body has been
removed.”

She accompanied me to the scene of the crime. At that moment Havering
entered the hall, and with a quick apology his wife ran to him. I
was left to undertake my investigations alone.

I may as well confess at once that they were rather disappointing.
In detective novels clues abound, but here I could find nothing
that struck me as out of the ordinary except a large bloodstain on
the carpet where I judged the dead man had fallen. I examined
everything with painstaking care and took a couple of pictures of
the room with my little camera which I had brought with me. I also
examined the ground outside the window, but it appeared to have
been so heavily trampled underfoot that I judged it was useless to
waste time over it. No, I had seen all that Hunter’s Lodge had to
show me. I must go back to Elmer’s Dale and get into touch with
Japp. Accordingly I took leave of the Haverings, and was driven
off in the car that had brought us up from the station.

I found Japp at the Matlock Arms and he took me forthwith to see
the body. Harrington Pace was a small, spare clean-shaven man,
typically American in appearance. He had been shot through the back
of the head, and the revolver had been discharged at close quarters.

“Turned away for a moment,” remarked Japp, “and the other fellow
snatched up a revolver and shot him. The one Mrs. Havering handed
over to us was fully loaded and I suppose the other one was also.
Curious what darn fool things people do. Fancy keeping two loaded
revolvers hanging up on your wall.”

“What do you think of the case?” I asked, as we left the gruesome
chamber behind us.

“Well, I’d got my eye on Havering to begin with. Oh, yes!” noting
my exclamation of astonishment. “Havering has one or two shady
incidents in his past. When he was a boy at Oxford there was some
funny business about the signature on one of his father’s cheques.
All hushed up of course. Then, he’s pretty heavily in debt now,
and they’re the kind of debts he wouldn’t like to go to his uncle
about, whereas you may be sure the uncle’s will would be in his
favour. Yes, I’d got my eye on him, and that’s why I wanted to
speak to him before he saw his wife, but their statements dovetail
all right, and I’ve been to the station and there’s no doubt
whatever that he left by the 6.15. That gets up to London about
10.30. He went straight to his club, he says, and if that’s
confirmed all right—why, he couldn’t have been shooting his uncle
here at nine o’clock in a black beard!”

“Ah, yes, I was going to ask you what you thought about that
beard?”

Japp winked.

“I think it grew pretty fast—grew in the five miles from Elmer’s
Dale to Hunter’s Lodge. Americans that I’ve met are mostly
clean-shaven. Yes, it’s amongst Mr. Pace’s American associates that
we’ll have to look for the murderer. I questioned the housekeeper
first, and then her mistress, and their stories agree all right,
but I’m sorry Mrs. Havering didn’t get a look at the fellow. She’s
a smart woman, and she might have noticed something that would set
us on the track.”

I sat down and wrote a minute and lengthy account to Poirot. I was
able to add various further items of information before I posted
the letter.

The bullet had been extracted and was proved to have been fired
from a revolver identical with the one held by the police.
Furthermore, Mr. Havering’s movements on the night in question had
been checked and verified, and it was proved beyond doubt that he
had actually arrived in London by the train in question. And,
thirdly, a sensational development had occurred. A city gentleman,
living at Ealing, on crossing Haven Green to get to the District
Railway Station that morning, had observed a brown-paper parcel
stuck between the railings. Opening it, he found that it contained
a revolver. He handed the parcel over to the local police station,
and before night it was proved to be the one we were in search of,
the fellow to that given us by Mrs. Havering. One bullet had been
fired from it.

All this I added to my report. A wire from Poirot arrived whilst
I was at breakfast the following morning:

“Of course black bearded man was not Havering only you or Japp
would have such an idea wire me description of housekeeper and what
clothes she wore this morning same of Mrs. Havering do not waste
time taking photographs of interiors they are underexposed and not
in the least artistic.”

It seemed to me that Poirot’s style was unnecessarily facetious.
I also fancied he was a shade jealous of my position on the spot
with full facilities for handling the case. His request for a
description of the clothes worn by the two women appeared to me to
be simply ridiculous, but I complied as well as I, a mere man, was
able to.

At eleven a reply wire came from Poirot:

“Advise Japp arrest housekeeper before it is too late.”

Dumbfounded, I took the wire to Japp. He swore softly under his
breath.

“He’s the goods, Monsieur Poirot! If he says so, there’s something
in it. And I hardly noticed the woman. I don’t know that I can go
so far as arresting her, but I’ll have her watched. We’ll go up
right away, and take another look at her.”

But it was too late. Mrs. Middleton, that quiet middle-aged woman,
who had appeared so normal and respectable, had vanished into thin
air. Her box had been left behind. It contained only ordinary
wearing apparel. There was no clue in it to her identity, or as to
her whereabouts.

From Mrs. Havering we elicited all the facts we could:

“I engaged her about three weeks ago when Mrs. Emery, our former
housekeeper, left. She came to me from Mrs. Selbourne’s Agency in
Mount Street—a very well-known place. I get all my servants from
there. They sent several women to see me, but this Mrs. Middleton
seemed much the nicest, and had splendid references. I engaged her
on the spot, and notified the Agency of the fact. I can’t believe
that there was anything wrong with her. She was such a nice quiet
woman.”

The thing was certainly a mystery. Whilst it was clear that the
woman herself could not have committed the crime, since at the
moment the shot was fired Mrs. Havering was with her in the hall,
nevertheless she must have some connection with the murder, or why
should she suddenly take to her heels and bolt?

I wired the latest development to Poirot and suggested returning
to London and making inquiries at Selbourne’s Agency.

Poirot’s reply was prompt:

“Useless to inquire at agency they will never have heard of her
find out what vehicle took her up to hunters lodge when she first
arrived there.”

Though mystified, I was obedient. The means of transport in Elmer’s
Dale were limited. The local garage had two battered Ford cars,
and there were two station flies. None of these had been
requisitioned on the date in question. Questioned, Mrs. Havering
explained that she had given the woman the money for her fare down
to Derbyshire and sufficient to hire a car or fly to take her up
to Hunter’s Lodge. There was usually one of the Fords at the
station on the chance of its being required. Taking into
consideration the further fact that nobody at the station had
noticed the arrival of a stranger, black-bearded or otherwise, on
the fatal evening, everything seemed to point to the conclusion
that the murderer had come to the spot in a car, which had been
waiting near at hand to aid his escape, and that the same car had
brought the mysterious housekeeper to her new post. I may mention
that inquiries at the Agency in London bore out Poirot’s
prognostication. No such woman as “Mrs. Middleton” had ever been
on their books. They had received the Hon. Mrs. Havering’s
application for a housekeeper, and had sent her various applicants
for the post. When she sent them the engagement fee, she omitted
to mention which woman she had selected.

Somewhat crestfallen, I returned to London. I found Poirot
established in an arm-chair by the fire in a garish, silk
dressing-gown. He greeted me with much affection.

“_Mon ami_ Hastings! But how glad I am to see you. Veritably I have
for you a great affection. And you have enjoyed yourself? You have
run to and fro with the good Japp? You have interrogated and
investigated to your heart’s content?”

“Poirot,” I cried, “the thing’s a dark mystery! It will never be
solved.”

“It is true that we are not likely to cover ourselves with glory
over it.”

“No, indeed. It’s a hard nut to crack.”

“Oh, as far as that goes, I am very good at cracking the nuts! A
veritable squirrel! It is not that which embarrasses me. I know
well enough who killed Mr. Harrington Pace.”

“You know? How did you find out?”

“Your illuminating answers to my wires supplied me with the truth.
See here, Hastings, let us examine the facts methodically and in
order. Mr. Harrington Pace is a man with a considerable fortune
which at his death will doubtless pass to his nephew. Point No. 1.
His nephew is known to be desperately hard up. Point No. 2. His
nephew is also known to be—shall we say a man of rather loose
moral fibre? Point No. 3.”

“But Roger Havering is proved to have journeyed straight up to
London.”

“_Précisément_—and therefore, as Mr. Havering left Elmer’s Dale at
6.15, and since Mr. Pace cannot have been killed before he left,
or the doctor would have spotted the time of the crime as being
given wrongly when he examined the body, we conclude quite rightly,
that Mr. Havering did not shoot his uncle. But there is a Mrs.
Havering, Hastings.”

“Impossible! The housekeeper was with her when the shot was fired.”

“Ah, yes, the housekeeper. But she has disappeared.”

“She will be found.”

“I think not. There is something peculiarly elusive about that
housekeeper, don’t you think so, Hastings? It struck me at once.”

“She played her part, I suppose, and then got out in the nick of
time.”

“And what was her part?”

“Well, presumably to admit her confederate, the black-bearded man.”

“Oh, no, that was not her part! Her part was what you have just
mentioned, to provide an alibi for Mrs. Havering at the moment the
shot was fired. And no one will ever find her, _mon ami_, because
she does not exist! ‘There’s no sech person,’ as your so great
Shakespeare says.”

“It was Dickens,” I murmured, unable to suppress a smile. “But what
do you mean, Poirot?”

“I mean that Zoe Havering was an actress before her marriage, that
you and Japp only saw the housekeeper in a dark hall, a dim
middle-aged figure in black with a faint subdued voice, and finally
that neither you nor Japp, nor the local police whom the housekeeper
fetched, ever saw Mrs. Middleton and her mistress at one and the
same time. It was child’s play for that clever and daring woman.
On the pretext of summoning her mistress, she runs upstairs, slips
on a bright jumper and a hat with black curls attached which she
jams down over the grey transformation. A few deft touches, and
the make-up is removed, a slight dusting of rouge, and the brilliant
Zoe Havering comes down with her clear ringing voice. Nobody looks
particularly at the housekeeper. Why should they? There is nothing
to connect her with the crime. She, too, has an alibi.”

“But the revolver that was found at Ealing? Mrs. Havering could
not have placed it there?”

“No, that was Roger Havering’s job—but it was a mistake on their
part. It put me on the right track. A man who has committed a
murder with a revolver which he found on the spot would fling it
away at once, he would not carry it up to London with him. No, the
motive was clear, the criminals wished to focus the interest of
the police on a spot far removed from Derbyshire they were anxious
to get the police away as soon as possible from the vicinity of
Hunter’s Lodge. Of course the revolver found at Ealing was not the
one with which Mr. Pace was shot. Roger Havering discharged one
shot from it, brought it up to London, went straight to his club
to establish his alibi, then went quickly out to Ealing by the
district, a matter of about twenty minutes only, placed the parcel
where it was found and so back to town. That charming creature,
his wife, quietly shoots Mr. Pace after dinner—you remember he was
shot from behind? Another significant point, that!—reloads the
revolver and puts it back in its place, and then starts off with
her desperate little comedy.”

“It’s incredible,” I murmured, fascinated, “and yet——”

“And yet it is true. _Bien sur_, my friend, it is true. But to
bring that precious pair to justice, that is another matter. Well,
Japp must do what he can—I have written him fully—but I very much
fear, Hastings, that we shall be obliged to leave them to Fate, or
_le bon Dieu_, whichever you prefer.”

“The wicked flourish like a green bay tree,” I reminded him.

“But at a price, Hastings, always at a price, _croyez-moi!_”

Poirot’s forebodings were confirmed. Japp, though convinced of the
truth of his theory, was unable to get together the necessary
evidence to ensure a conviction.

Mr. Pace’s huge fortune passed into the hands of his murderers.
Nevertheless, Nemesis did overtake them, and when I read in the
paper that the Hon. Roger and Mrs. Havering were amongst those
killed in the crashing of the Air Mail to Paris I knew that Justice
was satisfied.

first_paras:
Coming from a convalescent influenza patient, I hailed the remark
as showing a beneficial optimism. I myself had been the first
sufferer from the disease. Poirot in his turn had gone down. He
was now sitting up in bed, propped up with pillows, his head
muffled in a woollen shawl, and was slowly sipping a particularly
noxious tisane which I had prepared according to his directions.
His eye rested with pleasure upon a neatly graduated row of medicine
bottles which adorned the mantelpiece.

“I see,” cried Poirot. “The uncle, he is murdered! And you, you would have me fly to Derbyshire? It is impossible! But you, Hastings, you shall go in my place. You shall be my eyes and my ears. You will take the train with Monsieur Havering, you will see the scene of the crime, you will talk to the good Inspector of the police, and then you will return and tell all to me. Is it not so? Quickly then, go and tell Monsieur Havering that you are at his service. I will remain here and think. Already my ‘little grey cells’ are beginning to work. The uncle, who was he? How was he killed? Go, Hastings, go!”

“I see!” cried Poirot, his eyes suddenly sparkling with a renewed light. “The drama, it arrives even to the bed of the invalid! You must go, Hastings. You shall be my eyes and my ears. But first, bring the Monsieur Havering up here. I wish to interrogate him briefly before you depart for the wilds of Derbyshire. One does not solve a murder by staying in bed, it is true, but one can certainly direct the operations from it with the help of the little grey cells! Bring him up, I pray you, and we shall see what we shall see.”

“I see,” said Poirot, a sudden spark of interest lighting up his eyes. “A murder in the country—it is a classic! Since the grippe, she holds me prisoner, you, my dear Hastings, must represent me. You will go to Derbyshire; you will observe, you will report, and you will remember that it is the little things—the trifles—that matter most. Go down and ask him the name of the estate and the details of the household. Who was there? Who discovered the body? I shall be here, surrounded by my medicine bottles, but my mind, it shall be with you at the scene of the crime. Go, and do not lose a moment!”

“I see,” said Poirot, his eyes twinkling with a sudden spark of interest despite his malady. “A murder most foul in the wilds of Derbyshire! Though my body is a prisoner to this wretched _grippe_, my mind remains as agile as ever. You, my friend, shall be my eyes and my ears. You will go to Derbyshire in my place. You will observe, you will report, and you will bring back the truth to this sickroom. Go down at once and tell Mr. Havering that Captain Hastings will accompany him, acting as the representative of Hercule Poirot. And Hastings—bring me my notebook; there is no time to lose!”

“I see!” cried Poirot, his eyes sparking with a sudden return of their old fire. “A murder most foul in the depths of the country! You must go, Hastings. You shall be my eyes and my ears. I, from this bed of suffering, will direct the operations. Tell Mr. Havering that you will accompany him. But first, let us have the facts. The name of the victim, his residence, the manner of his death! Go, my friend, and do not forget to bring back every detail, no matter how insignificant it may seem to the ordinary mind. For to the mind of Hercule Poirot, nothing is insignificant!”

“I see. I see. You want to go yourself, is it not so? Well, why
not? You should know my methods by now. All I ask is that you
should report to me fully every day, and follow implicitly any
instructions I may wire you.”

To this I willingly agreed.


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


An hour later I was sitting opposite Mr. Havering in a first-class
carriage on the Midland Railway, speeding rapidly away from London.

“Exactly, sir,” said Japp. “It’s a plain enough case, though we haven’t laid hands on the man yet. Your uncle was shot in the gun room last night about nine o’clock. A man called to see him, a middle-aged man with a grey beard and spectacles. Mrs. Middleton, the housekeeper, let him in. He asked for Mr. Pace, and she showed him into the gun room. A few minutes later she and Mrs. Havering heard a shot. They ran to the room, but the door was locked. By the time they got in, the window was wide open, the man was gone, and Mr. Pace was dead on the floor, shot through the head with a revolver.”

“I am Mrs. Middleton, the housekeeper,” she replied with a weary sigh, stepping back to let me enter. “A terrible business, sir, quite terrible. It was just after nine o’clock last night. “It was a most terrible thing, sir,” the woman began, her voice steady but her hands trembling slightly against her apron. “About nine o’clock last night, a gentleman called. “It was a nightmare, Captain Hastings,” she began, her voice low but steady. “We were just finishing dinner when this man arrived. She accompanied me to the scene of the crime. At that moment Havering
entered the hall, and with a quick apology his wife ran to him. I
was left to undertake my investigations alone.

I was able to get a bed at the village inn, and there I found Japp,

“Well, what have you found?”

“Wait a bit,” I said. “First tell me how you got on here.”

I went to bed that night with a feeling that I had done a good
day’s work. I had collected a good deal of information, and I felt

opinion on the matter, but I knew that I must act on my own
initiative. Early the next morning I sent him a long telegram,

Japp again. I found him in a state of great excitement.

“We’ve got him!” he cried. “A man answering the description has
been seen in London. He was wearing a light overcoat and had a
black beard. He was seen getting out of a taxi at St. Pancras.”

“That’s great news!” I said. “Have they caught him?”

“Not yet, but they’re on his track. It’s only a matter of time.”

I felt a thrill of excitement. This was real detective work. I
had played my part in bringing a murderer to justice. I spent the
rest of the day wandering about the village, and talking to the
local people. Everyone was full of the murder, and there were
all sorts of rumours and theories. But I kept my own counsel,
and waited for news from London.

That evening I received a telegram from Poirot.

“Return to London immediately. Bring the Haverings and the

He looked at Havering.

“You killed your uncle, Mr. Havering. And your wife helped you to

Havering sank back into his chair, his face grey with despair. Mrs.

“It’s over,” Poirot said. “The police are waiting outside.”

He rang a bell, and Japp entered the room.

“Take them away, Japp,” Poirot said. “They are the murderers of

Japp led them out of the room. I was left alone with Poirot.

“Well, Hastings,” he said. “What do you think of my little

“It was wonderful, Poirot!” I said. “But how did you know about the

“I didn’t,” Poirot said with a smile. “I was—how you say?—bluffing.
But it worked, did it not? The guilty conscience, it is a

“But what about the man with the black beard?”

“Oh, him! He was just a little invention of mine. I thought it

And with a chuckle, Poirot turned back to his tisane.

I found Japp at the local inn, and together we went over the case.
He was very optimistic.

“I’m on the track of the fellow already, Captain Hastings. Got a
regular description of him. Black beard—overcoat—American
accent—he was seen by several people in the village and at the
station. He was noticed particularly, being a stranger in these
parts, and I’m pretty sure I can lay my hands on him before very
long.”

“I’m glad to hear it,” I said. “Now, as to the weapon? I hear one
of the revolvers is missing?”

“That’s it. It’s a pretty sure case, I should say. He must have
come here with the intention of doing for the old man. I suspect
a little bit of blackmail. He’d probably had some dealings with
him in America.”

I could not help thinking that this was very likely. Harrington
Pace’s past life in the States was a bit of a mystery, and it
seemed more than probable that someone should have a grudge against
him. Japp was quite convinced of it.

“Now, what about the will? You’ve found out something about that,
I suppose?”

“He left everything to his nephew, Roger Havering.”

“And what is the amount of the estate?”

“Something like two millions, I believe. He was a very wealthy
man.”

“And Roger Havering and his wife?”

“They’re not at all well off. In fact, they’re in a very bad way.
I’m afraid I can’t tell you much about them, but I believe they’ve
both been pretty extravagant in their time.”

I nodded. It seemed to me that a very clear motive was emerging.
Harrington Pace was a rich man, and his death would mean a great
deal to his nephew. Still, there was no reason to suspect him. He
had been in London at the time of the murder. His wife had been at
Hunter’s Lodge, but she could have had no hand in it. No, the
mystery of the bearded stranger seemed the most likely solution.

I returned to town the following morning and went straight to
Poirot’s bedside. He listened with interest to my account of the
case.

“You have done well, Hastings. You have missed nothing?”

“I think not.”

“And the housekeeper—Mrs. Middleton—what did you think of her?”

“A very ordinary, middle-aged woman. Quite what you would expect.”

“And she had been with the Haverings long?”

“No, only a few weeks. They engaged her through an advertisement.”

“I see. And the wife—Mrs. Havering—she is a very attractive
woman, you say?”

“Very. Quite a beauty in her way.”

“And her husband?”

“A very pleasant fellow. I liked him.”

Poirot lay back and closed his eyes.

“It is a curious case, Hastings. A very curious case. I should like
to think about it a little.”

I left him to his reflections. I felt that I had done my part, and
that it was now up to him to find the solution. Still, I could not
help wondering what he would make of it. The case seemed so simple.
The bearded stranger—the motive—it all seemed to fit in so
perfectly. What could there be to think about?

In the afternoon I went out for a walk, and when I returned I found
a telegram waiting for me. It was from Japp.

“Have arrested man answering description. Found him at Liverpool.
Everything points to him. Coming up to town to-morrow.”

I rushed upstairs to tell Poirot the news. He did not seem as
impressed as I had expected.

“So they have arrested him, have they? Well, we shall see. We shall
see.”

“You don’t think they’ve got the right man?”

“I do not say that, Hastings. But it is possible—it is just
possible—that they have made a mistake.”

I could not understand him. He seemed so certain that there was
something wrong. What could it be? I waited impatiently for the
following day.

Japp arrived at our rooms about eleven o’clock. He looked very
pleased with himself.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, I’ve got him! Caught him just as he was
about to board a boat for New York. He’s the man, right enough.”

“You are sure of that, Japp?”

“Certain. He’s a regular bad lot. Been in trouble before, I believe.
And he had the missing revolver in his possession!”

This seemed conclusive. I looked at Poirot. He was sitting up in
bed, his eyes fixed on Japp.

“And the name of this man?”

“He calls himself James Marsh. But I expect he has half a dozen
aliases.”

“And he admits the murder?”

“No, he denies it, of course. Says he’s never been near Derbyshire
in his life. But we’ve got plenty of witnesses to prove that he
was there.”

“I see. And the will? You have seen that?”

“Yes. Everything goes to Roger Havering. He’s a lucky man.”

Poirot was silent for a moment. Then he turned to me.

“Hastings, I have a little commission for you. I want you to go
back to Hunter’s Lodge.”

“To Hunter’s Lodge? But why?”

“I want you to find out one or two things for me. First of all, I
want to know if Mrs. Middleton is still there.”

“I expect so. Why shouldn’t she be?”

“And then I want you to find out if anyone else saw this James
Marsh in the village.”

“But Japp has already done that.”

“I know. But I want you to do it again. And—one more thing. I
want you to find out if there are any other revolvers in the
house.”

“Any other revolvers? But Mrs. Havering said there were only two.”

“I know. But I want you to make sure. You understand?”

“Yes, I think so. But I don’t see what you’re driving at.”

“Never mind that, Hastings. Just do as I ask you.”

I set off for Derbyshire again that afternoon. I felt that Poirot
was on a wild-goose chase, but I was determined to follow his
instructions to the letter.

When I arrived at Hunter’s Lodge I found that Mrs. Middleton had
left. She had gone away the previous morning, saying that she could
not stay in the house after what had happened. This seemed natural
enough, and I did not think much of it.

I then went into the village and made inquiries about James Marsh.
I found several people who had seen him, and their descriptions
tallied exactly with those I had already received. There could be
no doubt that he had been in the neighborhood at the time of the
murder.

Finally, I returned to the house and made a thorough search for any
other weapons. I found none. The only revolvers in the place were
the two that had been on the wall in the gun-room.

I returned to London the following day and reported my findings to
Poirot. He seemed disappointed.

“So Mrs. Middleton has gone, has she? That is a pity. A great pity.
And you found no other weapons?”

“None.”

“And the village people—they all saw James Marsh?”

“Yes, everyone I spoke to.”

Poirot sighed.

“It is as I feared. We are dealing with a very clever person,
Hastings. A very clever person indeed.”

“But Japp has got his man!” I cried. “What more do you want?”

“I want the truth, Hastings. And I am not sure that we have got it
yet.”

I was beginning to get irritated. Poirot was always so mysterious.
Why couldn’t he say what he thought?

The next few days passed slowly. Japp was busy preparing his case
against James Marsh, and I spent most of my time with him. He was
very confident of success.

“It’s a clear case, Captain Hastings. A very clear case. I don’t
see how he can possibly get off.”

I was beginning to think so too. Everything seemed to point to
James Marsh. And yet, at the back of my mind, I could not help
wondering if Poirot was right. Was there something we had missed?

One afternoon, about a week after the murder, I was sitting with
Poirot in his room. He was much better now, and was able to sit up
in a chair.

“Hastings,” he said suddenly, “I want you to go and see Mr. Roger
Havering.”

“Mr. Havering? Why?”

“I want you to ask him a question. I want to know if he has ever
seen James Marsh before.”

“But he was in London at the time of the murder!”

“I know. But that does not mean he has never seen him. Go and ask
him, Hastings.”

I went to the Haverings’ flat in town. I found Roger Havering alone.
He seemed glad to see me.

“Have you any news, Captain Hastings?”

“No, not exactly. But Monsieur Poirot has asked me to come and see
you. He wants to know if you have ever seen James Marsh before.”

Havering looked surprised.

“James Marsh? No, I don’t think so. Why do you ask?”

“Monsieur Poirot seems to think it might be important.”

“I see. Well, you can tell him from me that I have never heard of
him.”

I returned to Poirot and gave him the message. He nodded slowly.

“I thought as much. And now, Hastings, I want you to do one more
thing for me. I want you to go and see Mrs. Havering.”

“Mrs. Havering? But what for?”

“I want you to ask her the same question.”

I was getting tired of these errands, but I did as I was told. I
found Zoe Havering at home. She was looking as beautiful as ever,
but she seemed a bit nervous.

“Captain Hastings! This is a surprise. What can I do for you?”

“Monsieur Poirot has sent me to ask you a question, Mrs. Havering.
He wants to know if you have ever seen James Marsh before.”

She turned pale.

“James Marsh? No—no, I don’t think so. Why should he think I
had?”

“He didn’t say. He just asked me to find out.”

“I see. Well, you can tell him that I don’t know anyone of that
name.”

I returned to Poirot and told him what she had said. He smiled.

“Very good, Hastings. Very good indeed. And now, I think I can tell
you the truth about this case.”

I leaned forward, my heart beating fast.

“You know who did it?”

“I think so, Hastings. I think so.”

“Who was it? Was it James Marsh?”

“No, Hastings. It was not James Marsh.”

“Then who was it?”

“It was someone much nearer home, Hastings. Someone who had a very
good reason for wanting Harrington Pace out of the way.”

“You don’t mean—Roger Havering?”

“No, Hastings. Not Roger Havering.”

“Then who?”

“Think, Hastings. Think! Who was in the house at the time of the
murder? Who had access to the weapons? Who could have known about
the will?”

I thought for a moment.

“Mrs. Havering? Or Mrs. Middleton?”

“Exactly, Hastings. One of those two.”

“But they were both together when the shot was fired!”

“Were they, Hastings? Are you sure of that?”

“Well, they said they were.”

“Ah! They said they were. But did anyone else see them?”

“No, I don’t think so.”

“Then it is possible that one of them was not telling the truth.”

“But which one?”

“That is what we have to find out, Hastings. That is what we have
to find out.”

He fell silent, and I did not like to disturb him. I was beginning
to see what he meant. If one of them had been lying, then the whole
case would be different. But which one? And why?

The next day Poirot was well enough to go out. He insisted on going
to the police station to see Japp. I went with him.

Japp was in his office, looking very busy.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, what can I do for you? I’m afraid I haven’t
much time. I’m just getting ready for the trial.”

“I will not keep you long, Japp. I only want to ask you one thing.
Have you found any trace of Mrs. Middleton?”

“No, not yet. But I don’t think it matters much. She’s only a
witness, after all.”

“I am not so sure of that, Japp. I think she may be more than a
witness.”

Japp looked at him in surprise.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that I think she may be the key to the whole mystery.”

“Mrs. Middleton? But she’s just an ordinary housekeeper!”

“Is she, Japp? Is she?”

Poirot leaned forward, his eyes gleaming.

“Listen to me, Japp. I have a theory. It is only a theory, mind you,
but I think it is the right one.”

He then proceeded to outline his ideas to Japp. I listened in
amazement. It was a most extraordinary theory, but it seemed to
fit all the facts.

When he had finished, Japp sat back in his chair, looking stunned.

“My God, Monsieur Poirot! Do you really think that’s what happened?”

“I am almost sure of it, Japp. And I think I can prove it.”

“How?”

“By finding Mrs. Middleton.”

“But we don’t know where she is!”

“I think I do, Japp. I think I know exactly where she is.”

“Where?”

“In London, Japp. In a small hotel near the station.”

“How do you know that?”

“Because I have had her followed, Japp. I have had her followed
ever since she left Hunter’s Lodge.”

I stared at him.

“You have had her followed? But when—how?”

“I have my methods, Hastings. I have my methods.”

He turned back to Japp.

“If you will come with me, Japp, I think we can find her now.”

We set off at once. Poirot led us to a small, dingy hotel in a back
street. He spoke to the manager for a few minutes, and then we went
upstairs to a room on the second floor.

Poirot knocked on the door. There was no answer. He knocked again.
Still no answer.

“We must break it open, Japp!” he cried.

Japp put his shoulder to the door and burst it open. We rushed into
the room.

It was empty.

But on the table there was a note, addressed to Monsieur Poirot.

He tore it open and read it aloud.

“Dear Monsieur Poirot,

You are very clever. Too clever for me, I’m afraid. By the time you
find this, I shall be far away. Do not try to find me. It will be
useless.

Yours truly,

Mrs. Middleton.”

Poirot looked at us, a grim expression on his face.

“She has escaped us, Japp. She has escaped us.”

“But we can still catch her!” Japp cried. “She can’t have gone far!”

“I am not so sure, Japp. I am not so sure.”

He turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all now?”

“I don’t know what to think, Poirot. It’s all so confusing.”

“It is not confusing, Hastings. It is very simple. But we must be
patient. We must be patient.”

We returned to our rooms, and Poirot spent the rest of the day in
thought. I did not like to disturb him. I knew that he was working
on the problem, and that sooner or later he would find the answer.

The next morning he was his usual self again.

“Well, Hastings, I think I have it! I think I have it at last!”

“You know who did it?”

“Yes, Hastings. I know who did it.”

“Who?”

“It was Mrs. Havering, Hastings. Mrs. Havering and Mrs. Middleton.”

“But I thought you said Mrs. Middleton had escaped!”

“She has, Hastings. But that does not mean she was not involved.”

“But how did they do it?”

“It was very simple, Hastings. Mrs. Middleton was not a real
housekeeper at all. She was an accomplice. She was the one who
let the murderer into the house.”

“But who was the murderer?”

“James Marsh, of course. But he was not acting alone. He was acting
on the instructions of Mrs. Havering.”

“But why should she want to kill her uncle?”

“For the money, Hastings. For the money. She knew that he had left
everything to her husband, and she wanted it for herself.”

“But her husband was in London!”

“I know. But she was not. She was at Hunter’s Lodge. And she had
everything planned. She had even arranged for James Marsh to be
seen in the village, so that the police would suspect him.”

“But what about the shot?”

“That was the cleverest part of it all, Hastings. There was no
shot.”

“No shot? But everyone heard it!”

“No, Hastings. They only thought they heard it. It was a clever
trick, performed with the help of a gramophone record.”

I stared at him in amazement.

“A gramophone record? But how?”

“It is very simple, Hastings. Mrs. Havering had a record of a
gunshot, and she played it at the right moment. Everyone thought
they heard a shot, but it was only a recording.”

“But what about the body?”

“The body was already there, Hastings. Harrington Pace had been
killed some time before. Mrs. Havering had killed him herself,
using one of her husband’s revolvers.”

“But why did she need James Marsh?”

“To act as a scapegoat, Hastings. To take the blame for the murder.”

“I see. And Mrs. Middleton?”

“She was there to witness the ‘murder’ and to provide an alibi for
Mrs. Havering. She was a very clever actress, Hastings. A very
clever actress indeed.”

I was stunned. It was a most extraordinary story. And yet, it
seemed to fit all the facts.

“But how did you find out, Poirot?”

“I suspected from the first, Hastings. There were several things
that didn’t seem right. The description of the murderer—the
missing revolver—the fact that Mrs. Middleton had only been with
the Haverings for a few weeks. It all pointed to a carefully
planned crime.”

“And James Marsh?”

“He was just a common criminal, Hastings. A man with a record.
Mrs. Havering had found him and offered him money to play his
part. He didn’t know what he was getting into, but he was willing
to take the risk.”

“And now?”

“Now, Hastings, we must find Mrs. Havering. We must bring her to
justice.”

We went to the Haverings’ flat, but they were not there. They had
left town that morning, and no one knew where they had gone.

“We must find them, Japp!” Poirot cried. “We must find them before
it is too late!”

We spent the next few days searching for them, but it was no use.
They had vanished into thin air.

And then, one morning, we received a letter. It was from Roger
Havering.

“Dear Monsieur Poirot,

I am writing to tell you the truth about my uncle’s death. It was
not my wife who killed him. It was me.

I was in debt, and I needed money. I knew that my uncle had left
everything to me, and I decided to kill him. I planned everything
carefully, and I used James Marsh to help me.

My wife knew nothing about it. She is innocent.

I am sorry for what I have done, and I am prepared to take the
consequences.

Yours truly,

Roger Havering.”

Poirot read the letter in silence. Then he looked at us.

“So, it was the husband after all. I should have known. I should
have known.”

“But what about the gramophone record?” I asked. “And Mrs.
Middleton?”

“They were all part of his plan, Hastings. He was a very clever man.
A very clever man indeed.”

“And now?”

“Now, Hastings, he will have to pay for his crime. He will have to
pay.”

And that was the end of the mystery of Hunter’s Lodge. Roger
Havering was arrested and brought to trial. He was found guilty
of murder and sentenced to death.

His wife, Zoe Havering, was acquitted of all charges. She
disappeared soon after the trial, and was never heard from again.

As for James Marsh, he was also found guilty of complicity in the
murder and sentenced to a long term of imprisonment.

And so, once again, Hercule Poirot had triumphed. He had found the
truth, and justice had been done.

“But Poirot,” I said, as we sat in our rooms a few days later,
“how did you know it was Roger Havering? You seemed so sure it was
his wife.”

Poirot smiled.

“I did not know, Hastings. I only suspected. But when I saw that
letter, I knew I was right.”

“But why did he write it?”

“Because he loved his wife, Hastings. He loved her more than
anything else in the world. And he could not bear to see her
suffer for a crime she did not commit.”

“I see. So it was love that finally tripped him up.”

“Yes, Hastings. Love. It is a very powerful thing. A very powerful
thing indeed.”

And with that, the great detective returned to his books, and I
to my reflections. It had been a strange and tragic case, but in
the end, the truth had prevailed. And that, after all, was what
mattered most.

I found Japp at the local inn, and together we went over the case.
He was very pleased with himself.

“I’ve got my man, Captain Hastings! It’s only a question of hours.”

“A black beard, middle-aged, and an American accent?”

“Well, it’s not exactly that, but I’ve got his description, and
I’ve got his name. It’s a man named James, an old servant of Mr.
Pace’s. He was dismissed for some trifle or other, and he’s been
heard to make many threats against him. He was seen in the
neighbourhood on the day of the crime. I’ve no doubt we’ll have
him in no time.”

“But the black beard?”

“I don’t know about that. But he’s a man of about fifty, and he
was seen wearing a light overcoat.”

“Mrs. Middleton said he had a black beard.”

“Well, you know what these women are! They’re never very accurate
when it comes to descriptions. I expect he had a bit of a growth.”

I was not satisfied. There was something that didn’t quite fit.
I felt that Japp was being a bit too optimistic.

“Wait till I get back to town and see Poirot,” I said. “He’ll find
something that we’ve all missed.”

Japp laughed.

“Oh, Poirot! He’s a bit of a back number, isn’t he? If it hadn’t
been for the influenza, he’d have been here himself, and then I
suppose he’d have seen through the whole thing in a minute!”

I was slightly annoyed.

“At any rate,” I said, “I’ll send him a wire and tell him how things
stand.”

I did so, and also wrote a long letter, giving every detail that
I could think of. I also sent him the two photographs I had taken,
one of the gun-room and one of the ground outside the window.

The following morning I received a telegram:

“Wire me description of housekeeper also length of her service—Poirot.”

I was rather puzzled. What could the housekeeper have to do with
it? However, I made the necessary inquiries and wired the result
to Poirot.

“Middle-aged, tall, thin, dark hair, slightly grey. Has been with
the Haverings for five years.”

An hour later I received another telegram:

“Return to London immediately—Poirot.”

I was extremely disappointed. I had hoped to see the end of the
case. But I knew that Poirot’s orders must be obeyed. I took the
afternoon train to town.

“Well, Japp, you haven’t lost much time, have you?” I said, as I
walked into the little inn at Elmer’s Dale.

“No, I haven’t. I don’t mind telling you I’m pretty pleased with
myself. I’ve been busy since I saw you last.”

“You think you’ve got your man?”

“I don’t think. I know. We’re in for a big thing here, Hastings.
We’re going to have an arrest before many hours have passed.”

“Well, you haven’t let the grass grow under your feet,” I answered.
“Let’s hear the details.”

“Not now. I’ve a lot of things to attend to. There’s the revolver.”
He produced it from his pocket and laid it on the table. “And
there’s the bullet.”

“Where did you find the revolver?”

“It was hidden in a hollow tree about a hundred yards from the
house.”

“And you think the man who used it was the one who called last
night?”

“The American with the black beard? Yes, that’s him.”

“Have you caught him?”

“Not yet, but I soon shall. I’ve been making inquiries. A man
answering to that description was seen on the road that leads from
Hunter’s Lodge to the main road. He was seen about half-past nine,
and he was walking towards the railway station.”

“Did he go there?”

“No. He must have struck across the fields or something. Anyway,
we’ll get him soon enough.”

I was rather crestfallen. My own part in the affair seemed to be
so very small. I had hoped to do something that would reflect
credit upon Poirot’s methods, and here was Japp with his case
practically complete. However, there was one thing I could do, and
that was to send a full report to my friend. I spent the next hour
in doing so, and then strolled out into the village. I met Japp
outside the post-office.

“I’m going back to London to-night,” he told me. “I’ve done all
that can be done here. I’m going to have a talk with the people
at the station before I go.”

I decided to go with him. We found the station-master and several
of the porters on the platform. Japp was soon in conversation with
them.

“Now, about this man with the black beard,” he began. “Did any of
you see him last night?”

The station-master shook his head.

“No, sir, I can’t say as I did.”

“Nor you?” Japp turned to a porter.

“No, sir.”

“That’s strange. He must have passed this way.”

“Wait a bit, sir,” said one of the men. “I did see a gentleman
with a black beard last night. He came by the 8.15 from London.”

“The 8.15? That would get here about eleven o’clock. No, that’s
too late. The murder was committed at nine.”

“Well, this gentleman had a black beard, anyway.”

“Did he leave by a later train?”

“No, sir. He went away in a car that was waiting for him.”

“A car? Whose car?”

“I couldn’t say, sir. It was a big dark car.”

“Did you see the number?”

“No, sir.”

Japp turned away, looking rather disgruntled.

“That doesn’t seem to lead anywhere,” he remarked. “I think I’ll
be getting back now.”

I saw him off by the evening train, and then returned to the inn.
I felt that I had not much to report to Poirot, but I was determined
to do my best. I had my photos to develop, and that would take me
some time. I also had to think over all the facts of the case and
see if I could find any clue that Japp had missed.

I spent the next morning in developing my photos. They were not
very good, but they gave a very fair idea of the gun-room. One of
them showed the bloodstain on the carpet, and the other showed the
wall where the revolvers had been hanging. I also had a photo of
the window.

I was just finishing when a telegram was brought to me. It was
from Poirot.

“Report received. Excellent. Please send me description of
housekeeper at once. Also find out if any of the servants at
Newmarket have recently been dismissed. Wait for further
instructions.—Poirot.”

I was rather puzzled by this. What could the housekeeper have to
do with the case? And why the servants at Newmarket? However, I
had promised to follow Poirot’s instructions, and I set about
carrying them out. I went up to Hunter’s Lodge and saw Mrs.
Middleton. She was a quiet, middle-aged woman, with grey hair and
spectacles. She had been with the Haverings for about three years,
and seemed to be a very reliable person. I also found out that
none of the servants at Newmarket had been dismissed recently.

I sent this information to Poirot and then waited. I was beginning
to feel rather bored. Japp had gone back to London, and there
seemed to be nothing more for me to do. I spent the afternoon
wandering about the moors, and then returned to the inn for dinner.

I was just finishing when another telegram arrived.

“Return to London at once. Bring Mrs. Middleton with you if
possible. If not, come alone. Important developments.—Poirot.”

I was more puzzled than ever. What could Poirot want with the
housekeeper? And what were the “important developments”? However,
there was nothing for it but to obey. I went up to Hunter’s Lodge
and saw Mrs. Havering. I told her that Poirot wanted to see Mrs.
Middleton.

“But why?” she asked. “What can she have to tell him?”

“I don’t know,” I replied. “But he is very insistent.”

“Well, I suppose she must go, then. But it’s very inconvenient. I
don’t know how I shall manage without her.”

“I’m sorry, but Poirot’s orders are very strict.”

In the end it was arranged that Mrs. Middleton should go with me
to London the next morning. We arrived at Marylebone about midday,
and I took her straight to Poirot’s rooms.

He was sitting up in bed, looking much better. He greeted us with
his usual courtesy.

“Ah, Captain Hastings! And this is Mrs. Middleton? I am very glad
to see you, madame. Please be seated.”

He then proceeded to question her closely about the events of the
night of the murder. She told her story clearly and concisely,
and Poirot seemed satisfied.

“Thank you, madame. That will be all for the present. Perhaps you
would be so good as to wait in the next room for a few minutes?”

When she had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?”

“I don’t know what to think,” I replied. “Japp seems to have the
case well in hand.”

“Japp is a very good fellow,” said Poirot. “But he has a tendency
to jump to conclusions. Now, tell me, Hastings, what did you think
of Mrs. Middleton?”

“She seemed a very decent, reliable woman,” I said.

“And Mrs. Havering?”

“She is a very handsome and charming woman.”

“And Mr. Havering?”

“He seemed very much upset by his uncle’s death.”

“I see. Now, Hastings, I want you to do something for me. I want
you to go to the British Museum and look up the files of the New
York papers for the last few years. I want you to find out all you
can about Mr. Harrington Pace.”

“But why?” I asked.

“Because, my friend, I have a little idea. A very little idea, but
one that may be important. Now go, and do not fail me.”

I spent the rest of the afternoon at the British Museum. I found
that Mr. Harrington Pace had been a very wealthy man, but that he
had had a somewhat checkered career. He had been involved in
several shady financial deals, and had once been narrowly escaped
being prosecuted for fraud. He had also had a number of
disagreements with his family, and had finally left America to
live in England.

I returned to Poirot’s rooms and gave him this information. He
listened with great interest.

“Ah! It is as I thought. Now, Hastings, I want you to do one more
thing for me. I want you to go to the office of the Midland Railway
and find out all you can about the trains from Elmer’s Dale to
London on the night of the murder.”

I did as I was told, and found that there was only one train from
Elmer’s Dale to London after nine o’clock. This was the 10.20,
which reached Marylebone at 3.30 the next morning.

I gave this information to Poirot, and he seemed very pleased.

“Excellent! Now, Hastings, I think I have all the facts I need.
To-morrow we shall have the answer to the mystery.”

The next morning Poirot was up and dressed. He seemed to be quite
himself again.

“Now, Hastings, we must go to the Haverings’ flat in town. I have
asked them to meet us there.”

When we arrived at the flat, we found Mr. and Mrs. Havering
waiting for us. Japp was also there.

“Well, Poirot,” said Japp. “Have you found the murderer yet?”

“I think so, Japp,” said Poirot. “But first, I should like to ask
Mr. Havering a few questions.”

“Certainly,” said Havering. “What do you want to know?”

“Mr. Havering, when you left Hunter’s Lodge on the night of the
murder, what time did you arrive in London?”

“I arrived at Marylebone at 10.30,” said Havering.

“And where did you go then?”

“I went straight to my club.”

“And you stayed there all night?”

“Yes.”

“I see. Now, Mrs. Havering, when did you last see Mrs. Middleton?”

“I saw her this morning, before she left with Captain Hastings.”

“And you have not seen her since?”

“No.”

“That is strange,” said Poirot. “Because Mrs. Middleton has
disappeared.”

“Disappeared!” cried Mrs. Havering. “But where could she have
gone?”

“That is what I should like to know,” said Poirot. “She left my
rooms yesterday afternoon, saying that she was going back to the
flat, but she never arrived.”

“This is very extraordinary,” said Havering. “What do you think it
means, Poirot?”

“I think it means, Mr. Havering, that Mrs. Middleton was not a
housekeeper at all.”

“Not a housekeeper? Then who was she?”

“She was an accomplice,” said Poirot.

“An accomplice? To whom?”

“To the murderer,” said Poirot.

“But who was the murderer?” asked Japp.

“The murderer,” said Poirot, “was Mr. Harrington Pace himself.”

“Mr. Harrington Pace!” we all cried in amazement.

“But he’s dead!” said Japp.

“No, Japp,” said Poirot. “He is not dead. The man who was murdered
at Hunter’s Lodge was not Mr. Harrington Pace. It was someone else.”

“Someone else? But who?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to tell you.”

He then proceeded to explain his theory. He believed that Mr.
Harrington Pace had been involved in a fraudulent scheme in
America, and that he had come to England to escape prosecution.
He had then decided to disappear altogether, and had staged his
own murder. He had found a man who resembled him, and had killed
him in the gun-room at Hunter’s Lodge. He had then escaped
through the window, leaving behind the revolver and the bullet.
Mrs. Middleton had been his accomplice, and had helped him to
carry out his plan.

“But what about the black beard?” asked Japp.

“The black beard was a disguise,” said Poirot. “Mr. Harrington
Pace had a black beard when he lived in America, but he had
shaved it off when he came to England. He simply put it on again
for the murder.”

“And where is Mr. Harrington Pace now?” asked Havering.

“He is probably on his way to South America,” said Poirot. “But
I have already notified the police, and he will be arrested when
he arrives.”

“Well, Poirot,” said Japp. “I must say you’ve done it again. I
never would have thought of that.”

“It was simple, my friend,” said Poirot. “Once I had found out
about Mr. Harrington Pace’s past, it was all very clear.”

And so the mystery of Hunter’s Lodge was solved. Poirot had once
more proved his genius, and I was left to marvel at his
extraordinary powers of deduction.

I found Japp at the local inn, and together we went over the
details of the case. He was very busy and had many things to attend
to, so I felt that the best thing I could do was to put myself at
his service.

“You’ve seen the gun-room, Captain? Did you see anything that might
be a clue?”

“Nothing. But I’ve taken a few photographs. They might come in
useful later on.”

“Good idea. Now I suppose you’ll be wanting to see the housekeeper.
I have her downstairs.”

“Not now. I’ve already seen her and she’s told me her story. I want
to know about the man with the black beard.”

“Well, we’ve got his description. A light overcoat, black beard,
middle-aged. That shouldn’t be too difficult to trace. He must
have come from Elmer’s Dale, or have been seen at the station.
I’m going to make a few enquiries.”

“I’ll come with you, Japp.”

“If you like, Captain.”

We spent the rest of the day in making enquiries at the village
and the station, but without result. No one seemed to have seen
the mysterious stranger. It was as if he had dropped from the
clouds and vanished into thin air.

I was beginning to feel a little discouraged. I had hoped for
something more tangible. However, I was not going to give up yet.
I would wait and see what Poirot had to say.

I sent him a long telegram that evening, giving him all the
information I had been able to gather. I also mentioned the fact
that I had taken some photographs.

I spent a restless night, and was up early the next morning. I
was anxious to hear from Poirot.

It was about ten o’clock when his reply arrived. I tore it open
eagerly.

“Congratulations on your zeal. Photographs most important. Please
send them to me at once. Also find out if Mrs. Middleton has any
relations in the neighbourhood. Keep a sharp eye on Roger Havering.
Follow your instructions implicitly. Poirot.”

I was a little puzzled by his instructions. Why should he be so
interested in Mrs. Middleton’s relations? And why should I keep
a sharp eye on Roger Havering? He had seemed so genuine in his
grief. Still, I knew better than to question Poirot’s orders.

I spent the morning in making further enquiries. I found out that
Mrs. Middleton had no relations in the neighbourhood. She had come
to Hunter’s Lodge about three years ago, and had lived there ever
since. She was a quiet, respectable woman, and was well liked by
everyone.

As for Roger Havering, I saw him several times during the morning.
He seemed very busy with his own affairs, and I did not see anything
suspicious in his behaviour.

In the afternoon I went to the station to meet the London train.
I was hoping that Japp might have some news.

He was waiting for me on the platform.

“Well, Captain, any luck?”

“None. I’ve been making enquiries all morning, but haven’t found
out anything new. What about you?”

“I’ve had a bit of luck. I’ve found a man who saw the stranger
yesterday evening. He was walking along the road to Hunter’s Lodge
about half-past eight.”

“What did he look like?”

“Just as the housekeeper described him. Black beard, light
overcoat, middle-aged. He seemed to be in a hurry.”

“That’s something, anyway. Did he see where he went?”

“No, he lost sight of him after a bit. But it confirms the
housekeeper’s story.”

I felt a little more hopeful after hearing this. At least we knew
that the man really existed.

I spent the rest of the day in further enquiries, but without
result. It was as if the earth had swallowed him up.

In the evening I received another telegram from Poirot.

“Important you should find out if any of the servants at Hunter’s
Lodge have seen the stranger before. Also find out if any of them
have any reason to dislike Mr. Pace. Report to me to-morrow.
Poirot.”

I spent the next morning in carrying out Poirot’s instructions.
I spoke to all the servants, but none of them had ever seen the
stranger before. As for Mr. Pace, they all seemed to have liked
him well enough. He was a bit eccentric, perhaps, but he was always
kind and generous.

I was beginning to feel that I was getting nowhere. Every clue
seemed to lead to a dead end.

I was just about to give up for the day when I remembered something.
The housekeeper had mentioned that the stranger spoke with an
American accent. Perhaps I should make some enquiries among the
American community in London.

I mentioned this to Japp when I saw him later that afternoon.

“Not a bad idea, Captain. I’ll see what I can find out. In the
meantime, I’ve got some news for you. The bullet has been
extracted from Mr. Pace’s head. It was fired from a .38 revolver.”

“The same as the one that’s missing from Hunter’s Lodge?”

“Exactly. It looks as if the murderer used Mr. Havering’s own gun.”

This was a significant piece of information. It suggested that the
murderer was someone who knew the house well.

I spent the rest of the day in thinking over the case. I was
convinced that there was something I had missed, something that
would reveal the truth.

The next morning I received another telegram from Poirot.

“Come back to London at once. Bring the photographs with you.
Everything is clear to me now. Poirot.”

I was amazed. How could he have solved the mystery without even
leaving his bed? But I knew that Poirot was never wrong.

I packed my bags and caught the first train to London. I was
anxious to hear what he had to say.

When I arrived at his rooms, I found him sitting up in bed, looking
much better than when I had left him.

“Ah, Hastings! You are back. And the photographs? Did you bring
them?”

“Yes, here they are.”

I handed them to him, and he scanned them eagerly.

“Excellent! Excellent! Just as I thought.”

“What is it, Poirot? What have you found out?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything. But first, let us have some
tea. I am feeling much better now, and I think I can face a little
excitement.”

I rang for the tea, and while we waited, Poirot began to explain.

“You see, Hastings, the key to the mystery lies in the description
of the stranger. A black beard, a light overcoat, an American
accent. It is all so simple.”

“Simple? I don’t see anything simple about it.”

“That is because you are looking at it from the wrong perspective.
You are looking for a man who matches that description. But what
if there is no such man?”

“No such man? But the housekeeper saw him! And the man Japp found
saw him too!”

“Ah, but did they? Think, Hastings. Think.”

I thought for a moment, but I was still puzzled.

“I don’t understand, Poirot. What are you getting at?”

“I am getting at the fact that the stranger was a myth, a creation
of the murderer’s imagination. He was invented to divert suspicion
from the real culprit.”

“But the description? The black beard, the light overcoat?”

“All part of the disguise, my friend. All part of the disguise.”

“But who would want to kill Mr. Pace? And why?”

“That is the question, isn’t it? And the answer is quite simple.
Mr. Pace was a very wealthy man. He had no children, and his only
heirs were his nephew, Roger Havering, and his niece, Zoe Havering.
If he were to die, they would inherit everything.”

“But Roger Havering was in London when the murder took place! He
has an alibi!”

“An alibi? Are you sure about that, Hastings?”

“Well, he said he was in London. And his wife confirmed it.”

“Ah, but did anyone else see him? Did anyone else confirm his
story?”

I thought for a moment.

“No, I suppose not. But why would he kill his uncle? He said they
were the best of friends.”

“Money, my friend. Money. It is the root of all evil, as they say.
Roger Havering was a poor man, and his uncle was a rich one. He
needed money, and he needed it badly.”

“But how did he do it? How did he get to Hunter’s Lodge and back
to London without being seen?”

“That is where the cleverness of his plan comes in. He didn’t go
to Hunter’s Lodge. He was already there.”

“Already there? But his wife said he left for London at 6.15!”

“Exactly. And that is where she lied. She was in on the plot from
the beginning. They planned it together, the two of them.”

“But what about the housekeeper? She saw the stranger!”

“Ah, the housekeeper! That is the most clever part of all. You see,
Hastings, there was no housekeeper.”

“No housekeeper? But I saw her! I talked to her!”

“Did you, Hastings? Did you really?”

I was beginning to feel a little confused.

“Yes, of course I did! She was a middle-aged woman in black.”

“And did you see her face? Did you see her clearly?”

“Well, it was a bit dark in the hall. And she was wearing a cap
and apron.”

“Exactly. And that is why you didn’t recognise her. Because she
wasn’t a housekeeper at all. She was Zoe Havering in disguise!”

I was stunned. I couldn’t believe it.

“Zoe Havering? But she was upstairs when I arrived! And she came
down a few minutes later!”

“A few minutes later, Hastings. Just enough time for her to change
her clothes and remove her disguise. It was a very clever trick,
and it almost worked.”

“But the stranger? The man with the black beard?”

“That was Roger Havering, of course. He didn't go to London at all.
He stayed at Hunter's Lodge, and at the appointed time, he put on
his disguise and went to the gun-room to kill his uncle. Then he
slipped out through the window and disappeared into the night.
Later, he took the train to London and appeared at our rooms the
next morning, the picture of grief and despair.”

“But what about the man Japp found? The one who saw the stranger?”

“A plant, my friend. A plant. He was paid to say he saw the
stranger, to give the story more credibility. It was all part of
the plan.”

I was silent for a moment, taking it all in. It was a brilliant
plot, and it had almost succeeded. If it hadn't been for Poirot's
keen mind, they might have gotten away with it.

“But what about the photographs, Poirot? Why were they so
important?”

“Ah, the photographs! They were the final piece of the puzzle.
You see, Hastings, when I looked at the photographs, I noticed
something very interesting. In one of them, there was a small
object on the floor, near the bloodstain. It was a piece of black
hair.”

“A piece of black hair? From the stranger's beard?”

“Exactly. But it wasn't real hair, Hastings. It was crepe hair,
the kind used by actors and actresses. And that's when I knew for
certain that the stranger was a fake.”

I was amazed at Poirot's attention to detail. He had seen something
that I had completely missed.

“So, what happens now, Poirot? Will they be arrested?”

“Oh, yes, Hastings. I have already informed Japp, and he is on
his way to Hunter’s Lodge now. They will be behind bars before the
day is out.”

I felt a sense of satisfaction. Justice had been served, and the
guilty parties would pay for their crime.

“Well, Poirot, you’ve done it again. You’re a genius.”

“Thank you, Hastings. But it was nothing, really. Just a matter
of using one's little grey cells. And now, I think I will have
another cup of tea.”

I smiled as I poured him another cup. It was good to have the old
Poirot back.

The end.

I found Japp at the Matlock Arms and he took me forthwith to see
the body. Harrington Pace was a small, spare clean-shaven man,
typically American in appearance. He had been shot through the back
of the head, and the revolver had been discharged at close quarters.

“Well, I think we shall be able to identify our man as soon as we
get a few more details. For one thing, there’s no doubt that he
must have been an American, from the housekeeper’s description.”

“You mean that he was probably an old friend or acquaintance of
Pace’s?”

“Shouldn’t be at all surprised. If he was, and had a grudge against
the old gentleman, it would explain his coming down and asking for
him. But what we’re going on now is that he must have been stayin’
in the neighbourhood. We’ve already found a man who remembers
seeing a middle-aged man in a light overcoat walking along the road
towards Hunter’s Lodge about eight o’clock last night. He says the
fellow had a black beard. He was also seen at the station this
morning—taken the early train to London. If we get on to him we’re
as good as sure of him.”

“What about the weapon?”

“One of the pair. The missing one. If we can find it it will be a
clue. We’ve been looking for it everywhere, but without success.
If our man took it away with him it should be easy enough to trace.
I’m sending up to London to see what they can find out there.
I’ve got the number of the revolver. It’s an unusual one, and
ought to be easy to identify.”

I nodded.

“And what about the motive? That’s the most important thing of all.”

“Well, you know, these old millionaires are always makin’ enemies.
They’re hard as nails, and they generally leave a good many people
vowin’ vengeance behind ’em. Harrington Pace was no exception to
the rule.”

“Is there anyone who would benefit by his death?”

“His nephew, Roger Havering, of course. He comes in for a good bit,
I’m told. But he was in London at the time, and his wife’s been
livin’ with the old man for the last three years. She’d have no
reason to kill the goose that laid the golden eggs. No, it’s some
old enemy of his, I expect. We’ll find him all right.”

I was not so sure. It seemed to me that Japp was taking things a
little too much for granted. However, I said nothing, but went
back to my hotel and wrote a long and detailed account of the case
to Poirot. Then I went to bed and slept soundly.

“Well, it’s early to say yet. I’ve seen some of these cases before.
The fellow with the black beard—I shouldn’t be surprised if he’s
in custody by to-morrow.”

I described the appearance of the man from what Mrs. Middleton
had told me, but Japp only shook his head.

“I’m going to have a talk with her myself,” he said. “I’m not so
sure she wasn’t the one who did it.”

I was about to protest when he interrupted me.

“Yes, I know what you’re going to say—the motive! Well, Pace was
a rich man, and Mrs. Middleton is his housekeeper. It’s possible
that she was in his will, isn’t it?”

“But Mrs. Havering—she saw her in the hall, didn’t she?”

“That’s what she says! But they may be in it together.”

“Japp, you’re always so suspicious.”

“It’s my job, you know. Anyhow, I’ll have another go at Mrs.
Middleton. I’m going back to Hunter’s Lodge now.”

I had the same idea myself, so we drove back together. This time,
however, it was Mrs. Middleton alone who received us. Mrs. Havering,
she told us, was lying down with a bad headache.

“I’m sorry to trouble you again,” began Japp, “but there are just
one or two little things I’d like to make sure about.”

He then proceeded to question the woman very closely. She adhered
to her former story, however, and after about half-an-hour’s
cross-examination he was no further than when he began.

“I’m going to have a look round,” he announced. “I suppose you’ve
no objection, Mrs. Middleton?”

“Not at all, sir. What is it you want to see?”

“Everything! Every room in the house!”

I stayed below and waited for him. When he came down again, he
looked disappointed.

“Nothing!” he said. “Not a thing!”

“What were you looking for?” I asked.

“Evidence, of course! A blood-stained garment, or something of
that kind. But there’s absolutely nothing.”

“I’ll tell you what I’m going to do,” I said. “I’m going to
telegraph to Poirot and tell him all the facts. He’ll be able to
tell me what to do next.”

“A very good idea,” agreed Japp. “And I’ll go and have another
talk with the Haverings.”

I drove back to Elmer’s Dale and dispatched my telegram. In about
two hours’ time I received the following reply:

“Wait for my letter—Poirot.”

“I should say it was a pretty clear case, Hastings. Pace was a
man of considerable property, and Havering is his next of kin.
There may have been some quarrel between them, but the boy had his
own way of getting out of it. He must have got some one to do the
dirty work for him, though I’m blowed if I can see how. But wait
till we find the second revolver. It may be a matter of some time,
