but we’ll have it all right.”

“But Havering was in London last night,” I reminded him.

“Yes, we’ve found that out for certain. He was seen at his club at
half-past ten, and stayed there for some time.”

“Then it must have been the American visitor who did it?”

“Yes, but where did he come from, and where did he go to? No one
saw him either before or after the murder. No one in Elmer’s Dale
knows anything about him.”

“What about the weapon?”

“We’ve found that. It was lying in some bushes at the side of the
road about half a mile from the house.”

“Any finger-prints?”

“Not a sign of them. He must have worn gloves.”

“Well, Japp, I’m going to telegraph to Poirot and see if he has
any suggestions to make.”

“Quite so. You do that. I’m just going to have a final look at the
gun-room.”

I followed him out, and having despatched my telegram, I returned
to the Matlock Arms. In about an hour’s time I received Poirot’s
reply.

“Requesting you to return immediately. Bring Mrs. Middleton with
you.”

I stared at the slip of paper in amazement. Mrs. Middleton! What
on earth did he want with her? I went back to Hunter’s Lodge and
acquainted the Haverings with my instructions. They were as
astonished as I was.

“But what can Monsieur Poirot want with her?” asked Zoe Havering.
“She can tell him no more than she has told us. It seems so very
extraordinary.”

“I’m afraid I can’t tell you,” I replied. “But Poirot is a law
unto himself. I must obey his orders.”

Mrs. Middleton appeared to be even more surprised than her mistress.
However, she made no objection, and about an hour later we were
on our way back to London.

When we arrived at our rooms in St. James’s Street, Poirot was
sitting up in bed, his head still muffled in its woollen shawl.
He received us with his usual politeness.

“Ah, Mrs. Middleton, it is very good of you to come. I have a few
questions I should like to ask you.”

The housekeeper took the chair I placed for her, and waited
expectantly.

“Now, Mrs. Middleton, will you tell me once more exactly what
happened on the night of the murder?”

Mrs. Middleton repeated her story with the utmost composure. Poirot
listened with the greatest attention. When she had finished he
thanked her and told her she might go.

“Well, Poirot?” I asked, when the door had closed behind her. “What
do you think of it all?”

Poirot did not answer for a moment. He was staring at the wall
opposite him with a very strange expression on his face.

“Hastings,” he said at last, “I think we have been very blind.”

“Blind? What do you mean?”

“I mean that the solution of this case is very simple—too simple,
perhaps, for us to see it.”

“You mean that you know who killed Mr. Pace?”

“I think so, Hastings. I think so.”

“Then who was it?”

“Wait a moment. I have one more question to ask. Mrs. Middleton!”

The housekeeper reappeared at the door.

“Yes, sir?”

“I forgot to ask you one thing. Did you notice if the American
gentleman had a motor-car?”

“No, sir. I didn’t see any.”

“Thank you. That is all.”

When she had gone, Poirot turned to me again.

“Now, Hastings, I will tell you what I think. But first I must
ask you a question. What did you think of Mrs. Havering?”

“I thought she was a very charming and attractive woman,” I
replied.

“And Mrs. Middleton?”

“A very ordinary middle-aged woman. Why do you ask?”

“Because, Hastings, I think that Mrs. Havering and Mrs. Middleton
are one and the same person!”

I stared at him in blank amazement.

“One and the same person? But, Poirot, that’s impossible! I saw
them both at Hunter’s Lodge.”

“Did you see them both together?”

I thought for a moment.

“No—I don’t think I did. Mrs. Middleton opened the door to me,
and then went to fetch Mrs. Havering. And when Mrs. Havering came
down, Mrs. Middleton had disappeared.”

“Exactly. And when you went back to fetch Mrs. Middleton to bring
her to London, did you see Mrs. Havering then?”

“No—she was in her room, I believe.”

“Precisely. It was a very clever piece of acting, Hastings. Mrs.
Havering is, as you know, an actress. She found it easy enough to
play the two parts.”

“But why? What was the object of it?”

“The object was to provide herself with an alibi. If she could
prove that she was in the hall with the housekeeper when the shot
was fired, she would be safe from suspicion.”

“But who fired the shot, then?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I can guess.
Hastings, I want you to go back to Derbyshire at once. I want you
to find out if anyone saw a man with a black beard in the
neighbourhood of Hunter’s Lodge on the night of the murder. And I
want you to find out if anyone saw a motor-car waiting anywhere
near.”

“But, Poirot, if Mrs. Havering is the murderer——”

“I did not say she was the murderer, Hastings. I said she had
provided herself with an alibi. Now go, my friend, and do as I ask.”

I was back in Derbyshire the next morning. I spent the whole day
making inquiries, but with no result. No one had seen a man with
a black beard, and no one had seen a motor-car. I returned to
London feeling very discouraged.

“Well, Hastings?” Poirot asked, when I told him the result of my
investigations.

“Nothing, Poirot. Absolutely nothing.”

Poirot smiled.

“On the contrary, Hastings, you have found out a great deal. If
no one saw the man with the black beard, and no one saw the
motor-car, it is because they did not exist!”

“Then who killed Mr. Pace?”

“I think, Hastings, that we had better pay another visit to
Hunter’s Lodge.”

We arrived at Elmer’s Dale late that afternoon. Japp was there to
meet us.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’m glad to see you’re better.
Have you come to show us how to do our work?”

“Perhaps, Inspector, perhaps,” Poirot replied with a smile. “Now,
if you please, we will go to Hunter’s Lodge.”

When we arrived, we were met by Roger Havering. He seemed very
surprised to see us.

“Monsieur Poirot! This is an unexpected pleasure. I thought you
were too ill to travel.”

“I am much better, thank you, Mr. Havering. I have come to see if
I can help you to find the murderer of your uncle.”

“That is very good of you. But I’m afraid the police are doing
all they can.”

“No doubt, no doubt. But sometimes a fresh eye—is it not so?”

We went into the house. Mrs. Havering was in the drawing-room. She
seemed even more surprised than her husband to see us.

“Monsieur Poirot! I had no idea you were coming.”

“I felt that I must, Madame. The case is so interesting.”

“Interesting? It is a tragedy!”

“Precisely. A tragedy. Now, Mr. Havering, I should like to ask
you a few questions.”

“Certainly, Monsieur Poirot. Anything I can do to help.”

“Now, Mr. Havering, what time did you leave for London on the
night of the murder?”

“By the 6.15 train. I have already told the inspector so.”

“And you were seen at your club at half-past ten?”

“Yes.”

“And you stayed there for some time?”

“Until about midnight.”

“I see. Now, Mr. Havering, did you see your uncle before you
left?”

“Yes, I said goodbye to him in the gun-room.”

“And he was then quite well?”

“Yes, absolutely.”

“Thank you. Now, Mrs. Havering, I have a question for you. Where
is Mrs. Middleton?”

Zoe Havering started.

“Mrs. Middleton? She—she has left us.”

“Left you? When?”

“The day after she went to London with Captain Hastings. She said
she couldn’t stay in a house where there had been a murder.”

“I see. And where has she gone?”

“I—I don’t know. She didn’t leave an address.”

Poirot looked at her for a moment with a very strange expression.

“That is very unfortunate,” he said at last. “Because I wanted to
ask her another question.”

“What was it?”

“I wanted to ask her if she had ever seen this before.”

He took a small object from his pocket and held it out. It was a
button—a small, black button.

“I found it in the gun-room, Mrs. Havering. It is a button from a
woman’s dress.”

Zoe Havering turned very pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” she stammered.

“I think you do, Madame. I think you know very well what I mean.”

He turned to Roger Havering.

“And now, Mr. Havering, I have one more question for you. Where
is the other revolver?”

“The other revolver? The police have it.”

“No, Mr. Havering. The police have the revolver that was found in
the bushes. But there was another revolver—the one that was used
to kill Mr. Pace.”

“But I tell you, the police have it!”

“No, Mr. Havering. That revolver was never found.”

“Then where is it?”

“I think, Mr. Havering, that it is in this room.”

He walked over to a large bureau that stood in the corner.

“Monsieur Poirot!” Roger Havering cried, starting forward. “What
are you doing?”

“I am looking for the revolver, Mr. Havering.”

He opened the lid of the bureau and began to search through the
drawers. Suddenly he gave a cry of triumph.

“Ah! Here it is!”

He held up a small revolver.

“And here,” he continued, “is something else.”

He held up a small, black beard.

“Monsieur Poirot!” Zoe Havering cried, falling on her knees. “It
wasn’t Roger! It was me! I did it!”

“No, Zoe!” Roger Havering cried, rushing to her side. “It was me!
I killed him!”

Poirot looked from one to the other.

“I think,” he said quietly, “that you both did it. It was a very
clever plot, but you made one mistake.”

“What was it?” Roger Havering asked hoarsely.

“You forgot that Hercule Poirot is not easily deceived. You thought
that by creating the character of Mrs. Middleton, you could provide
Mrs. Havering with an alibi. But you forgot that Mrs. Middleton
would have to be seen by someone other than yourselves. And as no
one else ever saw her, I knew that she did not exist.”

“But I saw her!” I cried.

“Yes, Hastings, you saw her. But you are very easily deceived.”

He turned to Japp.

“Inspector, I think you have your prisoners.”

Japp stepped forward.

“Roger Havering, Zoe Havering, I arrest you for the murder of
Harrington Pace.”

As they were being led away, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my little case?”

“I think you are the most wonderful man in the world, Poirot!”

Poirot smiled.

“Perhaps, Hastings, perhaps. But now, if you please, we will go
back to London. I think I have had enough of the country for one
day.”

“Well, it’s early to say, of course. I’m inclined to think it’s
one of those professional jobs that go wrong. Someone has been
watching for some time, and seen the master go away. Then he’s
nipped in, and found himself caught in the act. The description of
the man is a bit vague, but we’re on his track. We’ve found a car
that’s been seen in the neighbourhood, and we’re following it up.
I expect we shall have him before the evening’s out.”

“I’m glad to hear it,” I said heartily. “Now, Japp, if I might
have a word with you——”

And I detailed to him all that I had seen and heard at Hunter’s
Lodge.

“Well, it’s very interesting, Captain Hastings,” said Japp when I
had finished. “It’s a bit unusual, to my mind, his having been shot
from behind. Usually these fellows make more of a fight of it. And
what about the revolver? If it’s one of Havering’s, it’s a bit of
luck for him to have it ready to his hand. Seems almost as if he’d
planned it beforehand.”

“You mean the man who killed him?”

“Exactly. It’s almost as if he knew the house.”

“He might have been an old servant, or something of that sort,”
I suggested.

“Maybe, though I don’t quite see why he should have come in and
asked for Mr. Pace. It’s a bit too daring, isn’t it?”

“Yes, it is. But, then, why did he do it?”

“Well, we shall know more about that when we catch him.”

“If you do catch him!”

“Oh, we’ll catch him all right. We’ve got a clue already. Someone
saw a man answering to the description in a car on the road to
Derby. I’m off now, and I’ll let you know as soon as we have any
news.”

With that Japp took himself off, and I was left to my own devices.
I had not much to do, and I spent the rest of the day in making
investigations on my own account. I interviewed the garage keeper
at Elmer’s Dale, and found that he had indeed sent a car to
Hunter’s Lodge on the evening in question. The driver, a lad of
nineteen or twenty, had seen Mr. Havering into the train, and had
then driven back to the garage. He had noticed nothing out of the
way. I also interviewed one or two of the villagers, but with no
better success. No one had seen anyone answering to the description
of the mysterious visitor. It was after seven o’clock when I
returned to the Matlock Arms. I found a telegram from Poirot
awaiting me.

“Report fully,” it ran.

I sat down and wrote a long and detailed account of all that I had
discovered. I posted it, and then, after a solitary meal, I went
to bed. I was tired out with my day’s work, and was soon fast asleep.

“Well, of course, there’s no doubt that this American fellow killed
him. But who was he? That’s the question. I’ve already sent out
the description of him and I hope he’ll be arrested before he can
get clear away. Mrs. Middleton said he spoke with an American
accent. If we can get him, we should find out the motive for the
crime.”

“I’m with you there, Japp. It was a cold-blooded affair. But I
shouldn’t wonder if there was more behind it than meets the eye.
You’re going to search for him, I suppose?”

“Naturally. But I’m going to stay here and see what I can find
out in the way of clues. I don’t believe in leaving anything to
chance.”

“Well, I’m going back to town,” I replied. “I’ve seen all there is
to see and Poirot will be anxious for my report.”

“Poor old Poirot! He’ll be sorry to have missed it. Tell him I’m
all for a little help, and if he’s anything to suggest I’ll be
glad to hear it. Only don’t let him send me any of those little
bits of advice of his. He’s a bit too fond of them, isn’t he?”

I could not help a smile. Japp’s professional jealousy was always
peeping out.

“Well, good-bye, Japp. Good luck to you.”

“Good-bye, Captain. Same to you.”

I returned to town that evening and was with Poirot early the next
morning. He was still in bed, and looked, I thought, even more
muffled and wrapped up than before. He listened with interest to
my story, and then asked me several questions. I told him all that
I had seen and what Japp had said. He seemed particularly interested
in the description of the mysterious visitor.

“A black beard, you say, and a light overcoat? And he spoke with
an American accent? That is interesting, Hastings. Very
interesting.”

“I thought so too,” I replied. “It’s a pity we haven’t any more
clues to go upon.”

“But we have, Hastings. We have the two revolvers.”

“The two revolvers?”

“Yes. One of them is missing, and the other one was loaded.”

“Well, what of it?”

“A great deal, Hastings. A great deal. If the murderer used one
of the revolvers, why did he not use the other one? And why did
he leave the other one behind?”

“I suppose he only needed one,” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But it is curious, is it not?”

“I don’t see anything very curious about it,” I replied. “The
man probably saw the revolvers hanging on the wall and snatched
up one of them.”

“But why did he leave the other one? It would have been much
safer to take both of them.”

“I don’t see that. One was enough for his purpose.”

“Perhaps. But it is a point to remember, Hastings.”

He was silent for a few moments, and then he asked:

“And what about the housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton? What did you
think of her?”

“She seemed a very capable woman,” I replied. “A bit old-fashioned,
perhaps, but quite reliable.”

“And Mrs. Havering? What did you think of her?”

“She is a very handsome woman,” I said. “And very energetic. I
should say she was the sort of person who would be very helpful
in an emergency.”

“I see. And Mr. Havering?”

“He seemed very much upset by his uncle’s death. He was evidently
very fond of him.”

“I see. Well, Hastings, I think I have all the facts now. I shall
have to think the matter over.”

He closed his eyes and I left him. I felt that I had done all that
I could, and that it was now up to Poirot to find the murderer.

The next few days passed without any further news of the case.
Japp was still busy in Derbyshire, but he had not yet succeeded in
tracing the mysterious visitor. Poirot remained in bed, but he
seemed to be recovering from his influenza. He spent most of his
time thinking, and he did not seem to be in any hurry to take
active steps.

On the fourth day, however, he sent for me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have been thinking about this case. I
believe I know who the murderer is.”

“You do?” I cried. “Who is it?”

“I will tell you later,” he replied. “But first I want you to go
down to Derbyshire again. I have a little task for you.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“I want you to go to Hunter’s Lodge and see if you can find anything
that we have missed. I have a feeling that there is something there
that will give us the clue we need.”

“But Japp has already searched the place,” I protested. “He would
have found anything there was to find.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But Japp is a very good policeman, but
he does not always see what is before his eyes. I want you to look
for something in particular.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to look for a piece of paper, Hastings. A piece of
paper that has been torn up.”

“A piece of paper?” I repeated. “But what kind of paper?”

“Any kind of paper, Hastings. But it must be torn up. And it must
be in the gun-room.”

“I’ll do my best,” I said. “But I don’t think I’ll find anything.”

“We shall see, Hastings. We shall see.”

I went down to Derbyshire that afternoon. I found Hunter’s Lodge
much as I had left it. The Haverings were still there, but they
seemed very quiet and subdued. I told them that I had come to have
another look at the gun-room, and they made no objection.

I spent several hours searching the room, but I could find nothing.
I looked under the carpet, in the drawers of the desk, and even
in the chimney, but there was no sign of any torn-up paper. I was
just about to give up when I noticed a small scrap of paper lying
in the corner of the room. It was very small, and it had evidently
been overlooked by the police.

I picked it up and examined it. It was a piece of white paper,
and it had been torn into several small pieces. I carefully
collected all the pieces I could find and put them in an envelope.

I returned to London the next morning and went straight to Poirot’s
rooms. He was sitting up in bed, and he looked much better than
he had done the day before.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “did you find anything?”

“I found this,” I said, handing him the envelope.

He opened it and spread the pieces of paper out on the bed. He
spent some time fitting them together, and then he looked up at me
with a smile.

“Well done, Hastings,” he said. “Well done. This is exactly what
I wanted.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a telegram, Hastings. A telegram from Mr. Havering to his
wife.”

“A telegram?” I repeated. “But what does it say?”

Poirot read it out to me:

“‘Everything all right. Uncle Harrington dead. Will be home
to-morrow. Roger.’”

I stared at him in amazement.

“But what does it mean?” I asked. “If Mr. Havering sent that
telegram, he must have known his uncle was dead before he left
London.”

“Precisely, Hastings. Precisely. And that means that he must have
been the one who killed him.”

“But he was in London!” I protested. “He went up by the 6.15
train.”

“Did he, Hastings? Did he? We only have his word for that. And
the word of his wife.”

“But the housekeeper saw him go!”

“Did she, Hastings? Did she? She saw a man in a light overcoat
and a black beard. But was it Mr. Havering?”

“But he didn’t have a black beard!”

“No, Hastings. But he could have worn one. And he could have
worn a light overcoat.”

“But why would he do it?” I asked. “He was his uncle’s favourite.
He would have inherited his money anyway.”

“Perhaps, Hastings. But perhaps he couldn’t wait. Perhaps he
needed the money now. And perhaps there was something else.
Something that we don’t know about.”

“But how did he get back to London so quickly?” I asked.

“He didn’t, Hastings. He didn’t go to London at all. He stayed in
Derbyshire and killed his uncle, and then he went to London and
sent the telegram.”

“But how did he get to London?”

“He could have taken a car, Hastings. Or he could have taken a
train from another station.”

“I see. But what about the housekeeper? She said she saw the man.”

“Yes, Hastings. But she didn't see his face. She only saw his
beard and his overcoat. And she said he spoke with an American
accent. But anyone can imitate an American accent, Hastings.
Anyone.”

“I see. So you think it was Mr. Havering?”

“I am sure of it, Hastings. I am sure of it.”

“But what are you going to do?” I asked.

“I am going to send for Japp,” he replied. “I think he will be
interested in what we have found.”

Japp arrived a few hours later, and Poirot showed him the telegram.
Japp was very impressed.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “you’ve done it again. I don’t
know how you do it, but you always seem to find the one thing we’ve
missed.”

“It was nothing, Japp. Nothing. It was just a matter of using the
little grey cells.”

“Well, I’ll get onto it right away,” said Japp. “I’ll have Mr.
Havering arrested before the day is out.”

“Wait, Japp,” said Poirot. “There is one more thing.”

“What is it?” asked Japp.

“I want you to check on the housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton.”

“The housekeeper?” repeated Japp. “But why?”

“Because I have a feeling that she knows more than she is telling
us.”

“I’ll do that, Monsieur Poirot. I’ll do that.”

Japp left, and Poirot and I were left alone.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of that?”

“I think it’s wonderful, Poirot. Just wonderful.”

“It is simple, Hastings. Simple. But it is always the simple
things that are the most difficult to see.”

He closed his eyes and I left him. I felt that I had learned a
great deal from him that day.

The next morning, I was surprised to see Japp enter our rooms. He
looked very dejected.

“Well, Japp,” I said, “have you arrested Mr. Havering?”

“No, Captain,” he replied. “I haven’t.”

“Why not?” I asked.

“Because he’s disappeared,” said Japp. “He and his wife. They’re
both gone.”

“Gone?” I repeated. “But where?”

“We don’t know,” said Japp. “They must have got wind of what we
were up to and cleared out.”

“And the housekeeper?” I asked.

“She’s gone too,” said Japp. “They all disappeared together.”

“I see. So they’ve got away.”

“It looks like it, Captain. It looks like it.”

Poirot, who had been listening to our conversation, suddenly
spoke up.

“Do not be discouraged, Japp,” he said. “They cannot have gone
far. They will be caught, I am sure of it.”

“I hope so, Monsieur Poirot,” said Japp. “I hope so.”

He left, and Poirot and I were once again alone.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “it looks like you were right about Mr.
Havering.”

“Yes, Hastings. I was right. But there is one thing that bothers
me.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“The housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton. Why did she go with them?”

“I suppose she was in on it,” I suggested.

“Perhaps, Hastings. Perhaps. But it is curious, is it not?”

“I don’t see anything very curious about it,” I replied. “If she
was their accomplice, it would make sense for her to go with them.”

“Perhaps, Hastings. Perhaps. But I have a feeling that there is
something more to it than that.”

He was silent for a few moments, and then he looked up at me with
a smile.

“Well, Hastings, we shall see. We shall see.”

And so the case of the Hunter’s Lodge murder remained unsolved.
The Haverings and Mrs. Middleton were never found, and the mystery
of Harrington Pace’s death was never fully cleared up. But I always
felt that Poirot knew more than he was telling me, and that one
day he would reveal the truth about what had happened that night
in Derbyshire.

“Well, I’d got my eye on Havering to begin with. Oh, yes!” noting
my exclamation of astonishment. “Havering has one or two shady
incidents in his past. When he was a boy at Oxford there was some
funny business about the signature on one of his father’s cheques.
All hushed up of course. Then, he’s pretty heavily in debt now,
and they’re the kind of debts he wouldn’t like to go to his uncle
about, whereas you may be sure the uncle’s will would be in his
favour. Yes, I’d got my eye on him, and that’s why I wanted to
speak to him before he saw his wife, but their statements dovetail
all right, and I’ve been to the station and there’s no doubt
whatever that he left by the 6.15. That gets up to London about
10.30. He went straight to his club, he says, and if that’s
confirmed all right—why, he couldn’t have been shooting his uncle
here at nine o’clock in a black beard!”

“Ah, yes, I was going to ask you what you thought about that
beard?”

Japp winked.

The following morning I had another talk with Japp.

“I’m off to London,” he said, “there’s nothing more for me to do
here. I shall start on the American end of it. By the way, there’s
one thing I’d like you to tell me, Captain Hastings, when you write
to Monsieur Poirot—how’s the little man? Tell him he can leave
this to me and go on with his tisane.”

I chuckled.

“I think he will be quite happy if I can tell him I have found a
clue he has overlooked.”

“And have you?”

“Well, not exactly, but I have a little theory of my own.”

Japp laughed.

“Well, good-luck to you, Captain. I shall have to go and see this
Mrs. Middleton, the housekeeper, again. There’s something about
her I don’t quite like. She seems to have had a lot of places. I’ll
look up her references when I get back to town.”

I did not see Japp again before his train left. In the afternoon
I went back to Hunter’s Lodge. Mrs. Havering had gone to the
inquest, but the housekeeper was at home. I was curious about this
woman. She had seemed so very ordinary, and yet Japp had been
distrustful.

She was a tall, thin woman, with a somewhat sallow skin and a
certain air of refinement.

“I suppose you’ll be staying here for the present, Mrs. Middleton?”

“I really don’t know, sir. It’s for Mrs. Havering to say.”

“You are a Londoner, aren’t you?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Have you been with Mrs. Havering long?”

“I have only been here for the last three weeks, sir.”

“And before that?”

“I was with a lady in Kensington—Mrs. Harrison. Her husband’s in
the War Office.”

“I see. Now about this man who came the other night. You didn’t
see what he was like?”

“No, sir, not really. I only just saw him for a moment in the
hall.”

“But you’re sure he had a black beard?”

“Oh, yes, sir.”

“And a light overcoat?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And he spoke like an American?”

“Yes, sir.”

I felt I was getting no further. I went back to Elmer’s Dale and
telegraphed my progress to Poirot.

The answer came back promptly:

“_Search for Middleton and her references immediately._”

Now this was exactly what Japp was doing. I felt a little piqued
that Poirot should have hit upon the same idea. However, I went
to work at once. I had already got the address of Mrs. Harrison,
the lady in Kensington. I wired to her, and also to the firm of
domestic agents through whom Mrs. Middleton had been engaged.

The replies were most unexpected. Mrs. Harrison had never heard
of a Mrs. Middleton. The agents also had no record of such a
person.

I was thunderstruck. This Mrs. Middleton then was a complete
impostor! What could be her motive for being at Hunter’s Lodge at
all? I felt I was on the brink of a great discovery.

I went back to the house, but only to find that Mrs. Middleton had
vanished! No one knew where she had gone. She had simply walked
out of the house and disappeared.

I returned to London in a state of great excitement. I found Poirot
much better. He was sitting up in an armchair, and his first words
to me were:

“Well, Hastings, and what have you discovered?”

I told him all my news.

“But this is wonderful!” he cried. “This Mrs. Middleton—she is the
key to the whole mystery!”

“I agree with you,” I said. “She was undoubtedly an accomplice of
the murderer. But how are we to find her?”

“That should not be difficult. But first, tell me, Hastings, did
you see Mrs. Havering’s flame-coloured jumper?”

I stared at him.

“Yes, I did. But what has that to do with it?”

“A great deal. And the little leather hat?”

“Yes, that too.”

“And you are sure that it was Mrs. Havering who wore them?”

“Of course I am! I saw her!”

Poirot smiled.

“And you say she was a very handsome woman?”

“She certainly was.”

“And Mrs. Middleton?”

“Oh, she was quite different—a thin, middle-aged woman, with a
sallow skin.”

“I see. Now, Hastings, I want you to go to the Frivolity Theatre
and see if you can find out anything about Zoe Carrisbrook’s
understudy.”

“Her understudy? But she has left the stage for years!”

“Never mind. Do as I ask.”

I went, and came back with the information that Zoe Carrisbrook’s
understudy had been a girl called Mary Price, and that she had
afterwards married a man called Middleton.

Poirot nodded.

“I thought as much. Now, Hastings, I want you to go back to
Derbyshire and find out if any one else saw the man with the black
beard.”

“But the housekeeper saw him!”

“I said _any one else_, Hastings.”

I went back, and after a good deal of trouble I found a boy who
had been passing the gate of Hunter’s Lodge at about nine o’clock.
He had seen a man in a light overcoat, but he had not noticed any
beard.

I returned to London with this news.

“Excellent!” said Poirot. “Now we have all the pieces of the
puzzle.”

“You mean you know who the murderer is?”

“I do.”

“Then who is it?”

“Wait a little. First I must see Inspector Japp.”

Japp came round that evening. He looked a little crestfallen.

“I’ve had no luck with those American associates of Pace’s,” he
said. “And as for that Mrs. Middleton, she seems to have vanished
into thin air.”

“That is not surprising,” said Poirot, “seeing that she never
existed.”

“Never existed? But Hastings saw her!”

“He saw a woman who called herself Mrs. Middleton. But there was
no such person. Mrs. Middleton was Mrs. Havering!”

“Mrs. Havering!” we both ejaculated.

“But I saw them both!” I cried. “I saw Mrs. Middleton when I first
went to the house, and I saw Mrs. Havering a few minutes
afterwards!”

“You saw two women, Hastings. One was Mrs. Havering in a
flame-coloured jumper and a little leather hat, and the other was
Mrs. Havering in a black dress and a sallow make-up. It is an old
theatrical trick, my friend. A change of dress and a little
theatrical grease-paint, and the thing is done. Remember that Zoe
Carrisbrook was an actress.”

“But the voices?”

“She was an actress, I tell you! And as for the American
visitor—there was no American visitor! It was Mr. Havering who
murdered his uncle!”

“But he was in the train to London!”

“He was in the train to London, yes. But he did not stay in it.
He got out at the first station, where he was not known, and came
back to Hunter’s Lodge in a car he had previously hidden. He
entered the house, shot his uncle, and then went back to the
station in time to catch a later train to London. His wife,
meanwhile, was playing the part of the housekeeper to provide him
with an alibi. It was she who showed the mythical American visitor
into the gun-room, and it was she who later appeared as herself to
discover the body.”

“But the man the boy saw?”

“That was Havering himself, before he had put on his black beard.
He was a little careless there, you see.”

“And the missing revolver?”

“He took it with him and threw it away. The one they found was the
one he had used, which he had carefully cleaned and replaced.”

“But why did they do it?”

“Money, my friend, money! Havering was in debt, and his uncle was
a rich man. It is the old story.”

“And Mrs. Middleton’s references?”

“They were a part of the plot. They knew that if the police
investigated them, they would find they were false, and that would
lead them to suspect the housekeeper—who had already disappeared!”

“It was a clever plot,” I said.

“Yes,” said Poirot, “but not quite clever enough for Hercule
Poirot!”

And he sipped his tisane with an air of great satisfaction.

THE END

“About the will?” I had asked Japp.

“Oh, that’s quite simple. He’s left everything to Havering. He
was a rich man, but his money was mostly in American securities.”

The next morning I received a wire from Poirot.

“Wait where you are. Am coming down to Elmer’s Dale to-morrow.
Send car to meet me.”

I was delighted. It was so like Poirot! No doubt he had seen some
point that I had overlooked, and was coming to see for himself.
He arrived at two o’clock, still very much muffled up and looking
the picture of misery.

“_Ah, quel froid!_” he groaned. “And this tisane, it is cold also!”

I made him as comfortable as possible in the little inn sitting-room,
and he listened with the closest attention to all I had to tell
him.

“But this is interesting, is it not?” he remarked. “The
housekeeper, she says she did not see the man?”

“No, she saw him.”

“_Parfaitement!_ But Mrs. Havering—she did not see him?”

“No.”

“And yet it was she who was the first to run into the hall?”

“Yes.”

“And the housekeeper, she came out of the kitchen?”

“Yes.”

“Which is at the back of the house?”

“Yes.”

“And the gun-room is at the front?”

“Yes.”

“So that the housekeeper had further to go than Mrs. Havering?”

“Yes, I suppose so.”

“Yet they met in the hall?”

“Yes, they almost collided.”

“And it was then they heard the shot?”

“Yes.”

“_Tiens!_ That is very interesting.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he asked:

“This housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton—what is she like?”

“A middle-aged, respectable-looking woman.”

“How long has she been with the Haverings?”

“Only a short time, I believe. They only go to Hunter’s Lodge
occasionally, as you know.”

“And where did she come from?”

“I don’t know. I can find out if you like.”

“It does not matter. And she was alone in the house?”

“Yes, except for Mr. Pace and Mrs. Havering.”

“I see. Now, Hastings, I should like to see this gun-room. Can
you arrange it?”

“Certainly. I will go and see the Haverings at once.”

I returned in about an hour’s time.

“It is all right. They will be delighted to see you. They are
most anxious to have the matter cleared up.”

We drove up to Hunter’s Lodge in the car I had seen before. Mrs.
Havering received us, and she and Poirot were soon deep in
conversation. I left them and went in search of the housekeeper.
I found her in the kitchen, and she repeated her story to me
without any variation.

“And you are sure the man had a black beard?” I asked.

“Oh, yes, sir. A great thick black beard it was.”

“And a light overcoat?”

“Yes, sir, a kind of fawn colour.”

“I see. Thank you, Mrs. Middleton.”

I went back to the gun-room. Poirot was standing by the window,
looking out.

“A lonely spot, Hastings,” he remarked.

“It is indeed.”

“And the window was open, you say?”

“Yes.”

“And the door was locked?”

“Yes.”

“By whom?”

“By the murderer, I suppose.”

“But how could he lock it from the outside?”

“He didn’t. He locked it from the inside, and then escaped through
the window.”

“_Precisely._ And the key?”

“It was in the lock.”

“On the inside?”

“Yes.”

“_Tiens!_ That is very interesting.”

He turned to Mrs. Havering.

“And you, madame, you heard the shot?”

“Yes, Monsieur Poirot. I was in the hall, and I heard it quite
plainly.”

“And you, too, Mrs. Middleton?”

The housekeeper had entered the room.

“Yes, sir. I was just coming out of the kitchen.”

“And you both ran to the gun-room door?”

“Yes.”

“And it was locked?”

“Yes.”

“So you went round to the window?”

“Yes.”

“And you found Mr. Pace dead?”

“Yes.”

“And the murderer—he had disappeared?”

“Yes.”

“And the revolver?”

“It was lying on the floor.”

“I see. I see. It is all very clear. Now, I should like to see
the other revolver—the one that was not used.”

Mrs. Havering brought it to him. He examined it closely.

“A very fine weapon,” he remarked. “And you say there were two
of them?”

“Yes. They were a pair.”

“And the other one is with the police?”

“Yes.”

“I see. I see. Well, I do not think there is anything more I want
to know.”

He took his leave of Mrs. Havering, and we drove back to the inn.
Poirot was very silent during the drive, and I did not like to
disturb him. When we reached our room, he sat down in a chair and
closed his eyes. I thought he was asleep, but after a while he
spoke.

“Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of Mrs. Middleton?”

“She seems a very decent, respectable woman,” I replied.

“And Mrs. Havering?”

“A very charming and clever woman.”

“Yes, she is clever—very clever. And her husband?”

“He seems a very pleasant fellow.”

“Yes, a very pleasant fellow. And Harrington Pace?”

“He was a very rich man, and he has left all his money to his
nephew.”

“Yes, that is very interesting, is it not? And the man with the
black beard?”

“He is the mystery.”

“He is indeed. A very great mystery. Tell me, Hastings, what did
you think of the bloodstain on the carpet?”

“It was very large.”

“Yes, it was very large. And the revolver—it was lying on the
floor?”

“Yes.”

“And the window—it was open?”

“Yes.”

“And the door—it was locked?”

“Yes.”

“On the inside?”

“Yes.”

“_Tiens!_ It is all very interesting.”

He was silent again for a long time. Then he suddenly sat up and
looked at me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have it!”

“You have what?” I asked in surprise.

“The solution! It is all quite simple. I see it all now.”

“But how? What do you mean?”

“I will tell you. But first we must go back to Hunter’s Lodge.”

“Now? But it is nearly dinner-time.”

“No matter. We must go at once. There is no time to lose.”

He hurried me out of the room and into the car. When we reached
Hunter’s Lodge, he asked to see Mrs. Havering. She came to us in
the hall, looking somewhat surprised.

“Monsieur Poirot! You have come back?”

“Yes, madame. I have come back because I have something to tell
you.”

“To tell me? What is it?”

“I have found the murderer of Mr. Harrington Pace.”

Mrs. Havering gasped.

“You have found him? Who is it?”

“It is a very simple story, madame. A very simple story indeed.
Shall we go into the gun-room?”

She led the way in silence. Poirot went straight to the window
and looked out.

“The murderer came in by this window, madame. He was a man with
a black beard and a light overcoat. He spoke like an American.
He was shown into this room by Mrs. Middleton. He had a quarrel
with Mr. Pace. He snatched up a revolver and shot him. Then he
locked the door from the inside and escaped through the window.
Is that not so?”

“Yes, yes, that is what happened.”

“But there is one thing that you have forgotten, madame.”

“What is that?”

“The key of the door. You said it was in the lock—on the inside.”

“Yes, it was.”

“But how could the murderer lock the door from the inside and
then escape through the window, leaving the key in the lock?”

Mrs. Havering stared at him.

“I—I don’t know. I suppose he must have done it somehow.”

“No, madame, he could not have done it. It is impossible. There
is only one way in which that door could have been locked from
the inside, and that is by someone who was inside the room.”

“But there was no one in the room but my uncle!”

“Precisely. And your uncle did not lock the door and then shoot
himself in the back of the head. No, madame, the door was locked
from the inside by someone who was in the room after your uncle
was dead.”

“But who could it have been? Mrs. Middleton and I were in the
hall.”

“Were you, madame? Were you both in the hall?”

“Yes, of course we were.”

“I think not. I think one of you was in this room.”

Mrs. Havering’s face turned very pale.

“What do you mean?” she whispered.

“I mean, madame, that there was no man with a black beard. There
was no American visitor. It was all a clever plot to murder Mr.
Pace and to make it look like the work of an outsider.”

“But the housekeeper saw him!”

“Did she, madame? Or did she only say she saw him? You see, it is
very simple. You and your husband were in great need of money.
Your uncle was a rich man. If he died, your husband would inherit
everything. So you planned to murder him. Your husband went to
London to establish an alibi. You stayed here. You were the man
with the black beard, madame!”

“I? But that is ridiculous!”

“Is it? You are a clever actress, Mrs. Havering. You have often
played male parts on the stage. It was easy for you to put on a
black beard and a light overcoat and to pretend to be an American
visitor. You let yourself in at the front door, and then you went
into the gun-room. You had already hidden the housekeeper——”

“But where is she? Where is Mrs. Middleton?”

“There is no Mrs. Middleton, madame. She was only another of your
clever disguises. You played both parts—the housekeeper and the
mistress. It was easy enough. You only had to change your clothes
 and put on a wig. When the police came, you were Mrs. Havering.
When Captain Hastings came, you were Mrs. Havering. But when the
man with the black beard was supposed to be here, you were Mrs.
Middleton.”

Mrs. Havering began to laugh. It was a high-pitched, hysterical
laugh.

“You are mad, Monsieur Poirot! Quite mad! How could I be in two
places at once? How could I be the housekeeper and the mistress
at the same time?”

“It was very simple, madame. You only had to make sure that no
one saw you both together. And you did that very cleverly. You
told Captain Hastings that the housekeeper was in the kitchen,
and you told the police that she was in her room. You even made
up a story about her going to fetch the police, so that she would
be out of the way for a few hours. It was a very clever plot,
madame, but you made one mistake.”

“And what was 그 mistake?”

“The bloodstain on the carpet. It was much too large. It showed
that the body had been lying there for a long time—much longer
than a few minutes. It showed that Mr. Pace had been dead for
several hours before you and the housekeeper—or rather, you and
yourself—pretended to hear the shot.”

Mrs. Havering’s laughter stopped suddenly. She looked at Poirot
with eyes of hatred.

“You think you are very clever, don’t you?” she hissed. “But you
can’t prove anything. You have no evidence!”

“I think I have, madame. You see, I have been talking to the
people at the garage in Elmer’s Dale. They tell me that they did
not send a car to fetch Mr. Havering to the station. He walked.
And they also tell me that a lady in a flame-coloured jumper and
a flame-coloured hat was seen walking towards the station about
the same time. That lady was you, madame. You went to the station
to meet your husband, and then the two of you came back here
together. It was your husband who played the part of the man with
the black beard, and it was you who played the part of the
housekeeper. You murdered your uncle between you, and then you
made up this clever story to cover your tracks.”

Mrs. Havering did not answer. She stood staring at Poirot, her
face a mask of fury.

“And there is one more thing,” Poirot continued. “The second
revolver. You thought you had hidden it safely, but I found it.
It was hidden in the chimney of the housekeeper’s room. And it
has been fired, madame. It has been fired once.”

With a cry of rage, Mrs. Havering turned and ran from the room.
But she did not get far. Inspector Japp was waiting for her in
the hall.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we drove back to London the next day,
“that was a very clever piece of work. I must admit, I was
completely fooled by that housekeeper business.”

“It was a very clever plot, Hastings,” Poirot replied. “The
Haverings are a very clever couple. It was only by looking at the
little things—the bloodstain, the key in the lock, the
flame-coloured jumper—that I was able to see the truth. It is
always the little things that give the criminal away.”

“And what about the man with the black beard?”

“He was Mr. Havering, of course. He didn’t go to London at all.
He stayed here and helped his wife with the murder. Then he went
to London later and made sure he was seen at his club. It was a
very good alibi, but it wasn’t good enough for Hercule Poirot!”

And with a little smile of satisfaction, my friend leaned back
in his seat and closed his eyes.

“After all,” he murmured, “it is possible that I shall not die
this time.”

In the first place, the stationmaster at Elmer’s Dale had seen a
tall man in a light overcoat and a black beard arrive by the 8.35
train from Manchester. He had got out and asked the way to Hunter’s
Lodge. In the second place, a woman at a cottage on the road to
Hunter’s Lodge had seen him pass her window about 8.50. This man
appeared to be the one seen by Mrs. Middleton. The murder must have
taken place between 9.0 and 9.15, and the man must have made his
way across the moors to a small station called Blackman’s Heath,
where he had caught the 10.15 for Manchester.

This seemed to me a very important discovery. Japp was also of this
opinion, and we spent the following day in Manchester making
fruitless inquiries at all the hotels. No such person as we
described had been seen. On my return to Elmer’s Dale I found a
telegram from Poirot:

“Send me a description of the housekeeper.”

I replied:

“Middle-aged, respectable, hair slightly grey, speaks with a North
Country accent.”

A second telegram from Poirot followed:

“Is she a woman of some education?”

I was a little puzzled.

“Middle-class, I should say. Why?”

The answer came:

“I have my reasons. Wire me if you can find out how long she has
been in the Haverings’ service.”

I found that she had been with them for about a year.

I thought I had done rather well, and I was disappointed when I
got a letter from Poirot which seemed to me to be absolutely
beside the point.

“My dear Hastings,” he wrote. “I am disappointed in you. You have
the eyes, but you do not use them. You have seen, but you have not
observed. You tell me of the bloodstain on the carpet, but you do
not tell me if it was dry or wet. You tell me that the ground
outside the window was trampled, but you do not tell me what kind
of footsteps they were. You tell me of the two revolvers on the
wall, but you do not tell me if they were of the same make. You
tell me of the man with the black beard, but you do not tell me
if his beard was real or false. You tell me of the woman at the
cottage, but you do not tell me if she had a clock in her house.
No, no, my friend, you are not a detective. You are a very
charming young man, but you have not the ‘little grey cells.’
I am better, but I am still very weak. I shall be with you
to-morrow. In the meantime, do nothing. Do not even think.
It is dangerous.”

I was a little hurt, but I realized that Poirot was still
suffering from the effects of his illness. I met him at the station
the following day, and we drove together to the Matlock Arms.
Poirot was still muffled in his woollen shawl, and he looked very
frail and old. He would not hear of going to Hunter’s Lodge that
evening, but insisted on going to bed at once. He had a long talk
with Japp, however, and I noticed that he seemed particularly
interested in the description of the man with the black beard.

The next morning Poirot was much better. He insisted on a large
breakfast, and then we set off for Hunter’s Lodge. We were met by
Mr. Havering, who seemed more than ever haggard and anxious.

“I am glad you have come, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “The police
seem to be making no progress at all.”

Poirot nodded.

“It is a difficult case, Mr. Havering. A very difficult case. Now,
if I might see the room where the tragedy took place?”

We went into the gun-room. Poirot looked round him with interest.
He examined the bloodstain on the carpet, and then he went to the
window and looked out.

“The ground is very much trampled, as you said, Hastings,” he
remarked. “It is a pity. It is a great pity.”

He turned back into the room.

“Now, these revolvers. They were both of the same make, I
understand?”

“Yes,” said Havering. “They were a pair.”

Poirot took the one that was remaining on the wall and examined it
carefully.

“A very pretty weapon,” he murmured. “And it was fully loaded, you
say, Japp?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And the other one—the one that was used—was also fully loaded?”

“So Mrs. Havering says.”

Poirot nodded.

“Now, I should like to see the housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton.”

Mrs. Middleton was summoned. She looked at Poirot with a certain
amount of suspicion.

“You were the one who saw the man with the black beard, Mrs.
Middleton?” Poirot asked.

“Yes, sir.”

“And he was a tall man?”

“Yes, sir. Tall and middle-aged.”

“And he had a light overcoat?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And a black beard?”

“Yes, sir.”

“A very black beard?”

“Yes, sir. Very black.”

“And he spoke with an American accent?”

“Yes, sir. Just like Mr. Pace.”

“I see. I see. And he went into the gun-room?”

“Yes, sir. I showed him in myself.”

“And then you went back to the kitchen?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And it was from there that you heard the voices?”

“Yes, sir. Loud voices, as if they were quarrelling.”

“And then the shot?”

“Yes, sir. And then I ran out into the hall, and the mistress she
came out too.”

“I see. I see. Thank you, Mrs. Middleton. That will be all for the
present.”

The housekeeper left the room. Poirot turned to Havering.

“I should like to see your wife, Mr. Havering.”

Mrs. Havering came in a few minutes later. She was dressed in black
now, and she looked very pale and tired.

“Monsieur Poirot?” she said. “I have heard so much of you. I hope
you will be able to find out who killed my poor uncle.”

“I will do my best, Madame,” Poirot replied. “Now, I want you to
tell me exactly what happened that night. You were sitting in the
drawing-room, I understand, when the man arrived?”

“Yes. We had just finished dinner.”

“And your husband had already left?”

“Yes. He went by the 6.15.”

“And you heard the man arrive?”

“I heard the bell ring, and then I heard Mrs. Middleton speaking to
someone in the hall. A few minutes later she came in and told my
uncle that a gentleman wanted to see him.”

“And your uncle went at once?”

“Yes. He seemed a little surprised, but he went at once.”

“And then you heard the voices?”

“Yes. They seemed to be quarrelling. I was just going to see what
was the matter when I heard the shot.”

“And then you and Mrs. Middleton went to the gun-room?”

“Yes. But the door was locked, and we had to go round to the
window.”

“I see. I see. Thank you, Madame.”

Poirot fell into a fit of abstraction. For some minutes he sat with
his eyes closed, his head leaning back against the chair. Then he
suddenly sat up.

“Japp,” he said. “I should like to see that woman at the cottage.”

We drove to the cottage. The woman was a simple, country soul. She
confirmed her previous statement. She had seen the man with the
black beard pass her window at about 8.50.

“And did you notice the time particularly?” Poirot asked.

“Yes, sir. I’d just looked at the clock. It was exactly ten minutes
to nine.”

“And was your clock right?”

“Yes, sir. It’s never a minute out.”

“I see. I see. Thank you.”

As we drove back to the Matlock Arms, Poirot seemed very thoughtful.

“Well, Poirot,” I said. “What do you think of it?”

“It is a very interesting case, Hastings. A very interesting case
indeed.”

“Do you think the man with the black beard is the murderer?”

“I think, Hastings, that the man with the black beard is the key
to the whole mystery.”

“But who is he?”

“Ah! That is the question. Who is he?”

Japp was waiting for us at the hotel.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “Have you found out anything?”

“I have found out several things, Japp. In the first place, I have
found out that Mrs. Middleton is a very remarkable woman.”

“In what way?”

“In many ways. But I will tell you more about that later. In the
meantime, I want you to find out for me if any of Mr. Pace’s
American friends are in England at the present moment.”

“I’ve already done that, sir. There’s a Mr. Cyrus Hammer who’s
staying at the Savoy. He’s a big steel man, and he was a great
friend of Mr. Pace’s.”

“Cyrus Hammer? I have heard the name. And has he a black beard,
this Mr. Hammer?”

“No, sir. He’s clean-shaven.”

“Ah! Clean-shaven. That is interesting. Very interesting.”

The next day Poirot was again in a state of great activity. He sent
several telegrams, and he spent a long time in consultation with
Japp. In the afternoon we went again to Hunter’s Lodge.

“I want to see Mrs. Middleton again,” Poirot said.

But Mrs. Middleton was not to be found. She had gone out, the other
servant said, and she had not yet returned.

“Gone out?” Poirot said. “That is strange. Very strange.”

He turned to Mr. Havering.

“Mr. Havering, I want you to tell me exactly how you engaged Mrs.
Middleton.”

“I engaged her through an advertisement in the _Morning Post_,”
Havering replied. “I interviewed her in London, and she seemed
just the sort of person we wanted.”

“And did you see her references?”

“Yes. They were very good ones.”

“And have you got them still?”

“I’m afraid not. I think my wife destroyed them.”

“I see. I see. And you have no idea where she has gone to-day?”

“None at all.”

Poirot turned to Japp.

“Japp, I want you to find that woman. It is very important.”

“I’ll do my best, sir. But she’s got a good start of us.”

“She must be found, Japp. She must be found.”

We returned to the Matlock Arms. Poirot was very silent during the
drive. When we arrived, he went straight to his room.

An hour later he sent for me.

“Hastings,” he said. “I have it.”

“You have what, Poirot?”

“The solution to the mystery.”

“You know who killed Harrington Pace?”

“I do.”

“Was it the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with a black beard, Hastings.”

“But the stationmaster saw him! And the woman at the cottage saw
him! And Mrs. Middleton saw him!”

“They saw a man with a black beard, yes. But he was not a real man.
He was a character in a play.”

“A character in a play?”

“Precisely. Now, Hastings, I want you to think. What was the most
remarkable thing about this case?”

“The man with the black beard, I suppose.”

“No, no. That was the most obvious thing. The most remarkable thing
was the fact that Mrs. Middleton was engaged by Mr. Havering in
London through an advertisement.”

“I don’t see anything very remarkable in that.”

“Don’t you? Think, Hastings. A housekeeper is usually engaged
through a registry office. Or she is recommended by a friend. To
engage a housekeeper through an advertisement in a newspaper is, to
say the least of it, unusual.”

“But it does happen sometimes.”

“Yes, it happens. But in this case it was very convenient. It meant
that no one in the neighbourhood knew Mrs. Middleton. No one had
ever seen her before she arrived at Hunter’s Lodge.”

“But what has that to do with the murder?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything. Now, tell me, Hastings, what
was Mrs. Havering’s profession before she married?”

“She was an actress. I told you that.”

“Exactly. She was an actress. And a very good one, I have no doubt.
Now, suppose that Mrs. Middleton and Mrs. Havering were one and the
same person?”

“Poirot! What an extraordinary idea!”

“Is it so extraordinary? Think. Mrs. Middleton was never seen by
the other servant. She only arrived at Hunter’s Lodge when the
Haverings went there for the week-end. She was always in the
kitchen when Mrs. Havering was in the drawing-room. And when the
man with the black beard arrived, she showed him into the
gun-room and then went to tell her mistress. But no one saw them
together. No one ever saw Mrs. Middleton and Mrs. Havering at the
same time.”

“But the shot! They both heard the shot!”

“Did they? Mrs. Middleton said they did. But who saw her? No one.
She said she ran out into the hall and met her mistress. But there
was no one else there to see them.”

“But the man with the black beard? The stationmaster saw him! And
the woman at the cottage!”

“They saw a man with a black beard, yes. But who was that man? It
was Mr. Havering, Hastings! Mr. Havering, who had supposedly left
for London by the 6.15!”

“But the stationmaster saw him go!”

“He saw a man go. But was it Mr. Havering? It was a man in Mr.
Havering’s clothes, no doubt. But his face was hidden by his hat
and his collar. It would be easy enough for someone else to take
his place. Someone like—shall we say—Mrs. Havering?”

“Mrs. Havering? But she was at the house!”

“Was she? Think, Hastings. The 6.15 from Elmer’s Dale is a slow
train. It stops at several stations. It would be easy for someone
to get out at the first stop and walk back to Hunter’s Lodge. It
is only five miles, you say. A good walker could do it in an
hour.”

“But then who was the man with the black beard?”

“It was Mr. Havering. He did not go to London at all. He got off
the train, put on a false beard and a light overcoat, and walked
back to the house. He arrived there at nine o’clock, was shown
into the gun-room by his ‘housekeeper’—his wife in disguise—and
then he shot his uncle.”

“But the woman at the cottage? She saw him at 8.50!”

“Exactly. He made sure that she would see him. He even asked her
the way, I have no doubt, to make sure that she would notice him.
It was all part of the plan.”

“And then?”

“Then he threw away the beard and the overcoat, and walked to
Blackman’s Heath, where he caught the 10.15 for Manchester. From
Manchester he could easily get to London in time to be seen at his
club the next morning.”

“But why Manchester?”

“Because it is a large city. It would be easy to disappear there.
And it would also suggest that the murderer was someone from
outside—someone who had come from a distance.”

“It’s incredible, Poirot! Absolutely incredible!”

“Is it? It is the only explanation that fits all the facts. And
there is one more thing, Hastings. The revolvers. You remember I
asked if they were of the same make?”

“Yes.”

“They were a pair. But one of them was missing. The one that was
used to kill Mr. Pace. Now, why should a murderer take the weapon
away with him? It is a very dangerous thing to do. If he were
caught with it in his possession, it would be certain death. No,
the reason he took it was because he could not leave it behind.
And why could he not leave it behind? Because it was not his! It
was the other revolver of the pair—the one that had been hanging
on the wall!”

“But Mrs. Havering said it was missing!”

“Exactly. She said it was missing. But she had it all the time.
She used it to kill her uncle, and then she gave it to her husband
to dispose of.”

“But you said Havering killed him!”

“No, no, Hastings. I said he was the man with the black beard.
But it was Mrs. Havering who fired the shot. Think. She was the
one who was in the house. She was the one who had the opportunity.
Havering was only there to provide the ‘witnesses’ with a
description of the murderer.”

“But the voices? The quarrelling?”

“All part of the acting, my friend. Mrs. Havering is a very good
actress, as I said. She played two parts—the housekeeper and the
mistress. And she played them both to perfection.”

“It’s amazing, Poirot. Simply amazing.”

“It was a clever plan, Hastings. Very clever. But they made one
mistake.”

“What was that?”

“They forgot that Hercule Poirot has the ‘little grey cells.’ And
now, Japp, I think you have heard enough. You can go and arrest Mr.
and Mrs. Havering.”

Japp, who had been listening from behind the door, stepped into the
room.

“I’ll do that, sir. And thank you. It’s a very neat piece of work.”

As Japp left the room, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“And now, Hastings, I think I should like another of your
excellent tisanes. This detective business is very exhausting.”

The following morning, I received a telegram from Poirot which ran as follows: “Inquire if any person in the village saw the American. Also, find out how long Mrs. Middleton has been in the service of the Haverings and who recommended her.” I spent the morning in Elmer's Dale, but my inquiries were singularly unproductive. No one had seen a man with a black beard, nor indeed any stranger at all, arrive by the evening trains or pass through the village. Returning to the Lodge, I found Mrs. Havering alone, her husband having gone into Matlock. She told me that Mrs. Middleton had been engaged about three weeks ago through an advertisement, and that she had come to them with excellent written references from a Mrs. Selbourne of Plymouth.

The evening papers gave a full account of the tragedy. They added
to what I already knew that Harrington Pace had been a great
collector of old English furniture. He was also a widower. His
fortune was estimated at about half a million, and he had no
near relatives besides his nephew, Roger Havering.

On the following day, about mid-day, I received a wire from
Poirot:

“Wire names of servants in the house. Is Mrs. Middleton middle-aged?
Has she a slight limp?”

I went to the post-office and wired back:

“Middleton middle-aged, no limp. Other servants, two maids, cook,
gardener, and chauffeur have not yet arrived from Newmarket.”

The same afternoon a second wire reached me.

“Return to London immediately. Bring Mrs. Middleton with you.”

I was much surprised by these instructions, but I did not hesitate
to carry them out. It was no easy task to persuade Mrs. Middleton
to accompany me, but at last she consented.

“My word, sir,” she said, when we were safely in the train. “I
don’t know what I’m doing. It’s a queer world and no mistake. To
think of me going to see a famous detective!”

I took her straight to our rooms. Poirot was sitting up in bed
and the row of medicine bottles on the mantelpiece had if anything
increased. He greeted us with a smile.

“Ah, Mrs. Middleton, it was good of you to come. Will you sit
down?”

She did so, and Poirot looked at her with interest.

“You have been in the service of Mr. Havering for some time?”

“About a month, sir.”

“How did you hear of the situation?”

“Through an advertisement in the _Morning Post_.”

“And your references?”

“They were all right, sir. I’ve always been in the best houses.”

“I’m sure of it. Now about the night of the murder. You showed this
man into the gun-room?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And you are quite sure he had a black beard?”

“Oh, yes, sir.”

“You did not see him leave?”

“No, sir.”

“Now, Mrs. Middleton, I am going to ask you a very important
question. You say you were in the kitchen when you heard the sound
of the shot. How long was it after that that you and Mrs. Havering
arrived at the gun-room door?”

“It couldn’t have been more than a minute, sir.”

“And the door was locked?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And then you went round to the window?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And you found Mr. Pace lying on the floor?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And the murderer had disappeared?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And you did not see him?”

“No, sir.”

“Thank you, Mrs. Middleton. That will do.”

I showed her out, and she went off, still in a state of great
bewilderment.

“Well, Poirot?” I asked.

“Well, Hastings? What do you think of it?”

“I don’t know what to think. He must be a very clever fellow,
this American. He seems to have vanished into thin air.”

“That is just it. It is too simple. Why a black beard? It is so
uncommon, so easily seen. And then, why didn’t Mrs. Middleton
see him leave? She was in the kitchen, but she must have heard
him go out by the front door.”

“He went out by the window.”

“And yet it was Mrs. Havering who suggested that.”

“What do you mean, Poirot?”

“I mean, Hastings, that I am beginning to have a very good idea
of who killed Mr. Harrington Pace.”

“You don’t mean—not Roger Havering?”

“Roger Havering was in the train to London.”

“His wife then?”

“She was in the hall with Mrs. Middleton.”

“Then who was it?”

“That is what I am going to find out. I want you to go down to
Hunter’s Lodge again, Hastings. I have a little commission for you.”

He whispered in my ear.

“But Poirot,” I protested.

“Do as I tell you, Hastings. It is very important.”

I was back at Hunter’s Lodge by the evening. I found the Haverings
at dinner. They were both very much surprised to see me.

“I have come back,” I explained, “on a little matter of business
for Monsieur Poirot.”

I looked at Mrs. Havering. She was as beautiful as ever, but she
seemed to me to be a little pale.

“I want to see the gun-room again,” I said.

Roger Havering rose and led the way.

“I’m afraid you won’t find anything more,” he said. “The police
have been over it with a fine-tooth comb.”

I did not answer him, but began to look about me. I moved a large
satinwood bureau, and as I did so, I heard a little exclamation
from Mrs. Havering who had followed us into the room.

“What is it?” I asked.

“Nothing,” she said, but her face was ashy white.

I continued my search, but I found nothing.

“I’m afraid I’ve had my journey for nothing,” I said.

“I’m sorry,” said Roger Havering. “But I told you I didn’t think
you’d find anything.”

I stayed at the village inn that night, and the next morning I
returned to London.

“Well, Hastings?” Poirot asked, as I entered his room.

“I’ve found nothing, Poirot. I moved the bureau as you told me,
but there was nothing there.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes sparkled. “And did Mrs. Havering say anything?”

“She seemed very much upset when I moved it.”

“I thought so. Now, Hastings, I am going to tell you who killed
Mr. Harrington Pace.”

“Who was it?”

“It was Mrs. Havering.”

“Mrs. Havering! But she was in the hall with the housekeeper!”

“Was she? That is just the point. We have only her word for it—and
the word of the housekeeper.”

“But the housekeeper saw her!”

“Did she? Think, Hastings. It was dark in the hall. They both
heard the shot. They both ran to the gun-room door. But who says
the door was locked? Mrs. Havering! Who says they had to go round
to the window? Mrs. Havering! Mrs. Middleton only followed her.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with a black beard. It was Mrs. Havering herself!”

“Mrs. Havering! But she’s a woman!”

“A very clever woman, Hastings. She is an actress, remember. It
would be a simple matter for her to put on a light overcoat and
a black beard. She shows herself to the housekeeper, who has only
been in the house a month and doesn’t know her mistress very well.
Then she goes into the gun-room, and a few minutes later she fires
the shot. She then throws off the coat and the beard, and runs
out into the hall, meeting the housekeeper. She tells her the
door is locked, and they go round to the window. It is all so
simple!”

“But what about the beard and the coat?”

“She hid them, Hastings. Behind that large satinwood bureau that
you moved!”

“But I didn’t find them!”

“No, because she had already removed them. But her face when you
moved the bureau told me all I wanted to know.”

“But why did she do it?”

“For money, Hastings. Roger Havering is the heir to his uncle’s
fortune. And he was in debt. They were both in it together, no
doubt, but it was she who did the actual deed.”

“It’s incredible!” I said.

“Not at all. It is very simple. But there is one thing that I do
not understand. Why did she send for me? That was a very foolish
thing to do.”

“Perhaps she thought it would make her look more innocent,” I
suggested.

“Perhaps. But she is a very clever woman, Hastings. A very clever
woman indeed.”

And Poirot fell back on his pillows, and began to sip his tisane
once more.

The bullet had been extracted and was proved to have been fired
from a revolver identical with the one held by the police.
Furthermore, Mr. Havering’s movements on the night in question had
been checked and verified, and it was proved beyond doubt that he
had actually arrived in London by the train in question. And,
thirdly, a sensational development had occurred. A city gentleman,
living at Ealing, on crossing Haven Green to get to the District
Railway Station that morning, had observed a brown-paper parcel
stuck between the railings. Opening it, he found that it contained
a revolver. He handed the parcel over to the local police station,
and before night it was proved to be the one we were in search of,
the fellow to that given us by Mrs. Havering. One bullet had been
fired from it.

All this I added to my report. A wire from Poirot arrived whilst
I was at breakfast the following morning:

“Communicate with registry office regarding Middleton. How long in
their service? Had she references? Wire answer immediately.—Poirot.”
“REPLY IMMEDIATELY WAS MRS. MIDDLETON ENGAGED THROUGH AN AGENCY. IF SO WHICH. IF NOT HOW DID SHE COME TO THE HAVERINGS. SEND ALSO FULL DESCRIPTION HER PERSONAL APPEARANCE. POIROT.”

“Return at once and bring the housekeeper with you—Poirot.”

“Bring the housekeeper!” I ejaculated.

“He means Mrs. Middleton, I suppose?” said Japp. “Now why on earth
does he want her? I’ve been over her story with her twice and she
has nothing to add to it. She hasn’t even a change of clothes
except what she stands up in. But I suppose we’d better take her.
The little man’s usually got something up his sleeve.”

“And what about the Haverings?”

“They’re going up to London to-day, and I’m going with them. It’s
all in our way. I suppose I can tell Mrs. Middleton that she’s
wanted?”

The housekeeper was quite willing to come, and though somewhat
astonished, I think she was rather pleased at the idea of seeing
London. We all travelled up together. Japp and the Haverings went
straight to the Yard, and I took Mrs. Middleton in a taxi to our
lodgings.

“I am glad to see you, Hastings,” said Poirot, looking up from
his bed. “And this is the good Mrs. Middleton? Please sit down,
madame. I will not keep you long. I want to ask you just one or
two questions.”

He then proceeded to put the housekeeper through a most searching
examination. At the end of it he seemed satisfied.

“That will do, Mrs. Middleton. I will not detain you any longer.”

As soon as she had left the room, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“I don’t know. I’m quite in the dark. I suppose the American with
the black beard exists, but where is he?”

“I don’t think he exists at all,” said Poirot.

“What! Then you think——”

“I think it was a very clever piece of work. A very clever piece
of work indeed.”

“But the Haverings? They were both together when the shot was
fired.”

“Were they? Are you sure of that?”

“Well, the housekeeper says so.”

“Ah, the housekeeper! Do you know what she is like, Hastings?”

“Well, I’ve seen her.”

“Describe her to me.”

“She’s a middle-aged woman, dressed in black, with grey hair and
spectacles.”

“Exactly. A very good description. And Mrs. Havering? Describe
her.”

“She’s a young woman, very dark, and rather handsome.”

“And you saw them both together? No, you didn’t. You only saw them
separately. And when you saw Mrs. Havering she was wearing a
flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured hat.”

“Yes.”

“And yet, Hastings, it is my belief that Mrs. Havering and Mrs.
Middleton are one and the same person!”

“Poirot! It’s impossible!”

“Is it? Think it over. Who saw them both together? No one. The
constable? No, he only saw Mrs. Havering. The housekeeper, he was
told, was in the kitchen. When you went to the house, you saw the
housekeeper. Then she went upstairs to call her mistress, and
presently Mrs. Havering came down. A change of dress, a wig, and
a pair of spectacles, and the thing is done. It was Mrs. Havering
who showed the mysterious American into the gun-room. It was Mrs.
Havering who, after a few minutes, fired the shot, and it was Mrs.
Havering who then locked the gun-room door from the outside, ran
round the house, and broke the window. Then she had only to wait
until the arrival of the police. As for the revolver, she
doubtless gave it to her husband when he left for London, and he
disposed of it as he did. A very pretty little plot.”

“But the motive?”

“Money, my friend, money! Harrington Pace was a very wealthy man,
and Roger Havering was his heir. With Pace out of the way, the
Havering fortunes would be at a very different level. And then
there’s another thing. Pace was a man of very strict ideas. If
he had found out certain things about his nephew’s past—things
that Japp hinted at—it is more than likely he would have
disinherited him.”

“It’s a very clever theory,” I said, “but there’s one thing you’ve
forgotten. What about the housekeeper we’ve just brought up from
Derbyshire?”

“Exactly,” said Poirot, with a smile. “What about her? I should
like to know where she is at this moment.”

“She’s downstairs, of course. I’ll go and fetch her.”

But when I got downstairs, I found that Mrs. Middleton had
vanished! No one had seen her go, but she was certainly not in the
house. I rushed back to Poirot with the news.

“You see?” he said. “I was right. She has disappeared—as I knew
she would.”

“But how did she get away?”

“That is simple enough. She just walked out of the front door. No
one was watching her. She had done her part, and there was no
further need for her presence.”

“Then you think the Haverings are the murderers?”

“I am sure of it. But we shall never be able to prove it. They have
been too clever for us. That is the worst of these people who
commit a crime for money—they are always so very careful.”

“But what about the housekeeper?” I persisted. “If she wasn’t Mrs.
Havering, who was she?”

“She was a woman they had hired for the purpose—some actress,
perhaps, who was out of a job. They would pay her well, of course,
and she would have no idea that she was being used as an
accomplice in a murder. She would just think it was some
mysterious joke.”

“It’s a wonderful theory, Poirot,” I said, “but I can’t help
feeling there’s a flaw in it somewhere.”

“There is no flaw, Hastings. I am sure of it. And now, if you will
be so good, I should like another cup of that excellent tisane.”

I looked at him in some doubt, but he seemed so sure of himself
that I could only suppose he was right. And yet, I could not help
wondering...

The Haverings were never brought to justice. There was no evidence
against them, and they inherited the whole of Harrington Pace’s
vast fortune. They are now one of the most popular couples in
society, and no one would ever dream of suspecting them of such a
dastardly crime.

But sometimes, when I see Mrs. Havering’s beautiful face, I cannot
help thinking of that lonely shooting-box on the Derbyshire moors,
and of the man who was so foully murdered there. And I wonder...

Is it possible that Poirot was right? Or was there some other
explanation—some explanation that we have never even dreamed of?

I suppose we shall never know. The secret of Hunter’s Lodge is
likely to remain a secret until the end of time.

“PLEASE WIRE ME AT ONCE FULL DESCRIPTION OF HOUSEKEEPER STOP ALSO
DATE SHE ENTERED SERVICE AND IF ENGAGED THROUGH AN AGENCY STOP
POIROT.”

“TELL ME IF MRS. MIDDLETON IS STILL AT HUNTER’S LODGE STOP IF NOT WHERE IS SHE STOP DESCRIBE HER PERSON MINUTELY STOP ALSO THE CLOTHES OF THE AMERICAN VISITOR STOP POIROT.” I was somewhat puzzled by this communication, but I lost no time in carrying out my friend’s instructions. I drove out to Hunter’s Lodge once more, only to find the household in some slight confusion. Mrs. Havering met me in the hall, looking somewhat harassed. She informed me that Mrs. Middleton had left her service that very morning, having received a telegram stating that her mother was dangerously ill. Mrs. Havering had been unable to find any fault with the woman’s story, though she was naturally annoyed at being left without a servant at such a time. I noted this down, together with the fact that Mrs. Middleton had been engaged through an agency in London, and then proceeded to ask for a description of the housekeeper’s appearance. Mrs. Havering described her as a woman of about forty, with greyish hair, wearing glasses, and always very neat in her black dress. As for the American visitor, both she and the late Mr. Pace’s valet (who had been in London at the time of the murder) confirmed the description of the light overcoat and the black beard.

“Of course black bearded man was not Havering only you or Japp
would have such an idea wire me description of housekeeper and what
clothes she wore this morning same of Mrs. Havering do not waste
time taking photographs of interiors they are underexposed and not
in the least artistic.”

I was a little annoyed at Poirot’s disparaging remarks about my snapshots, for I had rather prided myself on them. However, I lost no time in complying with his request. Mrs. Middleton, the housekeeper, was a woman of about forty-five, tall and somewhat angular, with a remarkably silent tread. She wore a black dress of some woollen material, with a white apron and turn-over collar and cuffs of stiff starch. Her hair was dark, touched with grey, and she wore it in a very plain fashion. As for Mrs. Havering, when I had seen her on the previous day, she had been wearing the flame-coloured jumper and leather hat I have already mentioned, but this morning she was in a simple suit of grey tweed with a small felt hat to match. I dispatched these details to Poirot by wire, wondering what on earth he wanted them for, and spent the rest of the morning with Japp, who was beginning to feel that the trail of the mysterious American was growing cold.

I was, I must admit, a little hurt by Poirot’s disparaging remarks concerning my photography. I have always considered myself to have a very fair eye for a picture. However, I knew his moods, and I hastened to comply with his request. Mrs. Middleton was a tall, gaunt woman of middle age, with grey hair smoothed back from her forehead; she wore a black dress of some heavy material and a white apron. Mrs. Havering, when I saw her at breakfast, was still wearing the flame-coloured jumper and the little leather hat of the same shade. I dispatched the required information by wire and waited with some impatience for Poirot’s next move.

I was slightly piqued by Poirot’s disparagement of my photography, but I set about obtaining the information he required. Mrs. Middleton, I noted, was a woman of perhaps forty-five, with a quiet, efficient manner; she wore a plain black dress of some heavy material, with the customary white apron and cap. Mrs. Havering, when I saw her that morning, had exchanged her flame-coloured jumper for a smart, well-cut suit of grey frieze, with a small felt hat to match. I despatched these particulars to London by wire, wondering privately what on earth the ladies’ wardrobe could have to do with the mysterious man in the black beard.

I was somewhat taken aback by Poirot’s request. What could the ladies’ attire
possibly have to do with the identification of a mysterious bearded
stranger? However, I knew from experience that it was better to
comply. I returned to Hunter’s Lodge and noted that Mrs. Middleton
was wearing a plain black dress of some woollen material, with a
white starch collar and cuffs, and a large silk apron. Mrs. Havering,
whom I encountered in the garden, had replaced her vivid
flame-coloured outfit of the previous day with a quiet, well-cut suit
of grey frieze.

I was, I must admit, a little huffed by Poirot’s disparaging
remarks about my snapshots. He has no appreciation of the
difficulties of indoor photography. However, I complied with his
request and sent him a full description of the two women as I had
seen them that morning. Mrs. Middleton was a tall, gaunt woman of
about forty, dressed in a neat black gown with a white apron and
cap. Mrs. Havering, when I saw her that morning, was wearing a
stunningly simple suit of grey tweed which suited her dark beauty
to perfection. I added that both women seemed remarkably composed
under the circumstances, though Mrs. Havering’s eyes were
red-rimmed as if from a sleepless night.

It seemed to me that Poirot’s style was unnecessarily facetious.
