I also fancied he was a shade jealous of my position on the spot
with full facilities for handling the case. His request for a
description of the clothes worn by the two women appeared to me to
be simply ridiculous, but I complied as well as I, a mere man, was
able to.

At eleven a reply wire came from Poirot:

“Advise Japp arrest housekeeper before it is too late.”

Dumbfounded, I took the wire to Japp. He swore softly under his
breath.

“What’s the little man up to? Arrest her! On what charge? She’s
the only witness we’ve got!”

“I’ll tell you what,” I suggested. “Let’s go up there and see what
she’s like.”

“Well, we may as well. I’ve nothing else to do.”

The five-mile drive was soon over, and we were once more at
Hunter’s Lodge.

“Well, Mrs. Middleton,” Japp began, as the housekeeper opened the
door to us, “I’m sorry to have to trouble you again, but there are
one or two more questions I’d like to ask you.”

The woman looked at him with an air of mild surprise.

“Certainly, sir. Will you come into the dining-room?”

She led the way, and Japp followed her. I remained behind for a
moment in the hall.

“Mrs. Havering is at home, I suppose?” I asked.

“She’s upstairs, sir. Shall I tell her you’re here?”

“No, don’t trouble. I’ll go up myself.”

I ran up the stairs and knocked at the door of Mrs. Havering’s
room.

“Come in,” she said, and I entered.

She was sitting in front of her dressing-table, a little tray by
her side.

“Oh, it’s you, Captain Hastings! I’m so glad to see you. I’ve
just been having a little lunch. I’m so tired and I’ve such a
headache.”

I expressed my sympathy, and then told her of Poirot’s wire. She
listened with the greatest interest.

“Arrest Mrs. Middleton? But why? What can she have done? I’m sure
she’s a most respectable woman. We’ve had her with us for over
three years.”

“Poirot didn’t say why,” I replied. “But he’s a very clever man,
and I’m sure he wouldn’t have said it without good reason. What
kind of a person is she? Do you know anything of her history?”

“Not much, I’m afraid. She came to us with excellent references.
We’ve always found her most reliable.”

“Well, I’ll go down and see what Japp is doing,” I said. “I’m
sure he’ll be glad of any help I can give him.”

I went downstairs and joined Japp in the dining-room. He was
looking rather nonplussed.

“I can’t make anything of it,” he said. “She seems all right to
me. I’ve been through her boxes, and there’s nothing suspicious
there. And yet Poirot is generally right.”

“Let’s have another look at her,” I suggested.

We went back into the hall, and Japp called Mrs. Middleton.

She came out at once. She was a woman of about forty-five, with
dark hair and a quiet, reserved manner. She was dressed in a plain
black gown.

“Mrs. Middleton,” Japp began, “I’ve been thinking over what you
told me yesterday. You said that this man who came to see Mr. Pace
spoke with an American accent?”

“Yes, sir. He did.”

“And you’re sure you’d never seen him before?”

“Quite sure, sir.”

“Now, what about his clothes? You said he had on a light overcoat?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And a black beard?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Now, Mrs. Middleton, I want you to think very carefully. Did you
notice anything else about him? Anything at all?”

The woman hesitated.

“Well, sir, now I come to think of it, I believe he had a bit of
a limp.”

“A limp! You didn’t mention that before.”

“No, sir. I didn’t think of it at the time.”

“A limp, eh?” Japp looked at me. “That’s something to go on, anyway.”

He turned back to Mrs. Middleton.

“That’ll do for the present. But don’t you go away, because I
shall probably want to speak to you again.”

“Very good, sir.”

As the woman left the room, Japp turned to me.

“Well, what do you think of it, Hastings? A limp! That’s a bit of
luck, isn’t it?”

“I suppose so,” I replied. “But I can’t help feeling that there’s
something more behind Poirot’s wire than that.”

“Oh, Poirot!” Japp laughed. “He’s always got some bee in his
bonnet. But this limp is a real clue. I’ll get onto the local
police at once and see if they’ve seen anyone answering that
description.”

He went off to the telephone, and I was left alone in the hall. I
felt a bit restless, and I decided to go for a walk on the moors.
It was a beautiful afternoon, and the air was wonderfully fresh
and bracing. I walked for about an hour, and then I turned back
towards Hunter’s Lodge.

As I approached the house, I saw a car standing at the gate. It
was a small, dark blue car, and there was a man sitting in the
driver’s seat. As I got nearer, I saw that it was Roger Havering.

“Hello!” I said. “I didn’t expect to see you back so soon.”

“I’ve just come down from London,” he replied. “I couldn’t stay
away any longer. I wanted to be with my wife.”

“I understand,” I said. “Have you seen Japp?”

“Yes, I saw him just now. He told me about this man with a limp.
It’s a most extraordinary thing.”

“It is indeed,” I agreed. “By the way, have you seen Mrs.
Middleton lately?”

“Mrs. Middleton? No, why?”

“Oh, nothing. I just wondered.”

I went into the house and found Japp in the dining-room. He looked
rather excited.

“I’ve got it, Hastings!” he cried. “I’ve found out who this man
with the limp is!”

“You have?” I said. “Who is it?”

“His name is James Benson,” Japp replied. “He’s an American, and
he’s been staying at a hotel in Matlock for the last few days.
The waiter at the hotel remembers him perfectly. He says he had a
black beard and a very noticeable limp.”

“That sounds like our man,” I said. “But what was his motive for
murdering Mr. Pace?”

“That’s what I’m going to find out,” Japp said. “I’m going over
to Matlock now to see if I can find him.”

“Can I come with you?” I asked.

“Of course. Come along.”

We drove over to Matlock and went straight to the hotel. But when
we got there, we were disappointed to find that James Benson had
checked out that morning.

“He said he was going to London,” the waiter told us. “He left on
the 10.15 train.”

“Damnation!” Japp swore. “We’ve missed him!”

“But we can easily trace him in London,” I suggested.

“Yes, I suppose we can,” Japp said. “But it’s a nuisance all the
same.”

We drove back to Elmer’s Dale, and Japp went to the police station
to send some telegrams to London. I went back to the Matlock Arms
to wait for him.

I felt a bit depressed. It seemed as though we were always just
one step behind the murderer. And yet, there was something about
the whole case that I didn’t understand. Why had Poirot been so
anxious to have the housekeeper arrested? And what did he mean by
his remarks about the photographs and the clothes?

I was still puzzling over these questions when a telegram was
brought to me. It was from Poirot.

“Come back to London at once. Bring Japp with you. Have solved the
mystery.”

I read the telegram twice, and then I went to find Japp.

“Poirot’s solved it!” I cried. “He wants us to go back to London
at once!”

“Solved it, has he?” Japp said. “Well, he’s a wonder, is Poirot.
I suppose we’d better go.”

We caught the evening train to London, and by ten o’clock we were
at Poirot’s rooms.

The little man was sitting up in bed, looking much better. He
greeted us with a smile.

“Ah, my friends! You have come! That is good. Now, sit down, and
I will tell you all about it.”

“You’ve really solved it, Poirot?” I asked.

“But certainly, my friend. It was very simple, really. Once one
had the key.”

“And what was the key?” Japp asked.

“The key,” Poirot said, “was the clothes.”

“The clothes?” I said. “What on earth do you mean?”

“I mean,” Poirot said, “the clothes worn by Mrs. Havering and the
housekeeper.”

“But I told you what they were wearing,” I said.

“Yes, you did. And that is what gave me the clue.”

“I don’t understand,” I said.

“It is quite simple,” Poirot said. “You told me that Mrs.
Havering was wearing a flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured
leather hat. And you told me that the housekeeper was wearing a
plain black gown.”

“Well, what of it?” Japp asked.

“Simply this,” Poirot said. “Mrs. Havering is a very beautiful
woman. She is also a very clever woman. And she is a very
ambitious woman. She wanted her uncle’s money, and she wanted it
now. So she decided to murder him.”

“Mrs. Havering!” I gasped. “But she was in the hall with the
housekeeper when the shot was fired!”

“Was she?” Poirot said. “Are you sure of that?”

“Well, the housekeeper said so,” I said.

“Exactly,” Poirot said. “The housekeeper said so. But who is the
housekeeper?”

“Her name is Mrs. Middleton,” Japp said.

“Is it?” Poirot said. “I think not. I think the person you saw
at Hunter’s Lodge was not Mrs. Middleton at all.”

“Then who was it?” Japp asked.

“It was Zoe Havering!” Poirot said.

“Zoe Havering!” I cried. “But I saw her! She was upstairs in her
room!”

“Was she?” Poirot said. “Or was she downstairs, dressed as the
housekeeper?”

“But I saw them both!” I said. “I saw Mrs. Havering and I saw the
housekeeper!”

“Did you?” Poirot said. “Did you ever see them both together?”

I thought for a moment.

“No,” I said. “I don’t believe I did.”

“Exactly,” Poirot said. “And neither did Japp. You saw one, and
then you saw the other. But you never saw them both at the same
time.”

“But what about the man with the black beard?” Japp asked.

“There was no man with a black beard,” Poirot said. “The man with
the black beard was Roger Havering!”

“Roger Havering!” I cried. “But he was in London!”

“Was he?” Poirot said. “He was on the 6.15 train, certainly. But
did he stay on it? No. He got off at the first station, and then
he drove back to Hunter’s Lodge in a car that he had waiting for
him.”

“But the waiter at the hotel in Matlock!” Japp said. “He saw the
man with the black beard!”

“Did he?” Poirot said. “Or did he see someone who looked like
him? Someone who was wearing a false beard and a light overcoat?”

“But who was it?” Japp asked.

“It was Zoe Havering!” Poirot said. “She was the man with the
black beard!”

“Zoe Havering!” I gasped. “But she’s a woman!”

“Yes, she is,” Poirot said. “But she is also an actress. She used
to be on the stage, remember? She could easily have disguised
herself as a man.”

“But the limp!” Japp said. “The man had a limp!”

“A very simple thing to fake,” Poirot said. “Especially for an
actress.”

“But what about the revolver?” I asked. “The one that was found
in Ealing?”

“That was Roger Havering’s doing,” Poirot said. “He took the
revolver with him to London and then he left it where it would be
found. It was a very clever piece of work.”

“But I still don’t understand,” I said. “Why did they do it?”

“For the money, of course,” Poirot said. “Harrington Pace was a
very rich man. And he had left all his money to Roger Havering.
But he was beginning to get suspicious of Roger. He was beginning
to find out about his debts, and his shady dealings. So Roger and
Zoe decided to murder him before he could change his will.”

“It’s incredible!” Japp said. “I can’t believe it!”

“But it is the truth,” Poirot said. “And I can prove it.”

“How?” Japp asked.

“By the clothes,” Poirot said. “When I asked for a description of
the clothes worn by the two women, I was looking for a particular
thing. And I found it.”

“What was it?” I asked.

“A flame-coloured jumper,” Poirot said. “And a flame-coloured
leather hat.”

“I don’t see how that proves anything,” I said.

“Don’t you?” Poirot said. “Think, Hastings. Where did you see
those clothes?”

“On Mrs. Havering,” I said.

“Exactly,” Poirot said. “And where did you see the housekeeper’s
clothes?”

“In her room,” I said.

“No, you didn’t,” Poirot said. “You saw them on the person you
thought was the housekeeper.”

“But I don’t see the point,” I said.

“The point,” Poirot said, “is that the person you saw as the
housekeeper was actually Zoe Havering. And when she wanted to
become Mrs. Havering again, she simply changed her clothes.”

“But she would have had to do it very quickly,” I said.

“She did,” Poirot said. “That is why she was so tired and had
such a headache when you saw her in her room. She had just
finished changing her clothes.”

“It’s amazing!” Japp said. “I never would have thought of it.”

“It was the only possible explanation,” Poirot said. “Once I
realised that no one had ever seen the housekeeper and Mrs.
Havering together, the whole thing became clear.”

“But what about the real Mrs. Middleton?” I asked. “Where is she?”

“There is no Mrs. Middleton,” Poirot said. “She was an entirely
fictitious character, created by the Haverings for the purpose of
the murder.”

“But they had a housekeeper!” Japp said. “The neighbors must have
seen her!”

“Did they?” Poirot said. “I think not. You will find that no one
in the village had ever seen the housekeeper. She was only seen
by people who came to the house, and then only for a few minutes
at a time.”

“It’s a most extraordinary case,” Japp said. “I must say, Poirot,
you’ve done it again.”

“It was nothing,” Poirot said. “A mere trifle. But it was
interesting, nonetheless.”

“Well, I’d better get back to Scotland Yard and start making some
arrests,” Japp said. “Thank you, Poirot. I don’t know what we’d
do without you.”

“It is a pleasure, my friend,” Poirot said. “A pleasure.”

As Japp left the room, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my little solution?”

“It’s brilliant, Poirot,” I said. “Absolutely brilliant.”

“I thought you would like it,” Poirot said. “And now, if you will
excuse me, I think I will have a little sleep. I am still a bit
tired after my illness.”

“Of course, Poirot,” I said. “Good night.”

“Good night, Hastings.”

I left the room and went to bed. But I couldn't sleep. I was
thinking about the Haverings, and the cold-blooded way they had
planned and carried out the murder of their uncle. It was a
truly terrible crime. And yet, I couldn't help but admire the
cleverness of it all.

The next morning, the news of the arrests was in all the papers.
Roger and Zoe Havering had been taken into custody and charged
with the murder of Harrington Pace. It was the sensation of the
year.

As for me, I was just glad that it was all over. And I was glad
that Hercule Poirot was back on his feet again, ready to face
whatever new mysteries might come his way.

The end.

“What’s the little man’s idea?” he said at last. “I haven’t a
suspicion against the woman. It’s all very well to talk of arresting
her, but on what grounds? You’d better go out and keep an eye on
her, Hastings. It can’t do any harm anyway.”

Accordingly I drove out to Hunter’s Lodge and had a talk with Mrs.
Havering.

“Oh, Mrs. Middleton? She’s gone, Captain Hastings. She went this
morning. I don’t think she really liked staying after what had
happened. I had no idea you’d want to see her again.”

“But she gave no address?”

“Only her London one. I’ll give it to you if you like. 15, North
Road, Hammersmith.”

I hurried back to Japp. He groaned.

“It’s a false address, you can bet your life. It’s a bit too
thin.”

It was. Mrs. Middleton had never been heard of at the address
given. Japp at once put his best men on the job, and they tracked
the woman to a registry office, where she had been engaged by
Mrs. Havering. The name she had given was undoubtedly a false one.

It seemed that Poirot was right. At any rate, we must find the
housekeeper. Japp and I went back to town, and I went straight
to Poirot. He was sitting up in bed, and looked much better. He
hailed me with a smile.

“Well, _mon ami_, and what have you to tell me? No, no, do not
begin. I have it all here.” He tapped his head. “The facts, they
are all known to me. But I am curious. The housekeeper, she is
not yet found?”

“No.”

“And she will not be found. That I can tell you. Now, let us
summarize. A man, with a black beard, and an American accent,
calls to see Mr. Pace. He is shown into the gun-room by the
housekeeper. After a few minutes a shot is heard. The gun-room
door is found to be locked on the inside. The housekeeper and the
mistress of the house run round to the window. They find the
unfortunate Mr. Pace dead, and the American vanished.”

“Precisely.”

“Now, tell me, Hastings, what do you think of it all?”

“Well, it’s a very difficult case. The American has disappeared
into thin air. But then, as Japp says, he might be anywhere.
The housekeeper has also disappeared. She, at any rate, must be
found. She is the only person besides Mrs. Havering who saw the
man.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “You think she saw him?”

“She says she did.”

“And Mrs. Havering, she did not see him?”

“No. She only heard the voices.”

“Which she did not recognize?”

“Which she did not recognize.”

“And yet, she knew her uncle’s voice?”

“Oh, yes.”

“And the other voice, she had never heard it before?”

“Apparently not.”

“Now, about that revolver? The one found at Ealing. You are quite
sure that it was the one that killed Mr. Pace?”

“Oh, yes. The bullet fitted it exactly.”

“And it was found on Haven Green? That is on the way from
Paddington to Ealing, is it not?”

“Yes.”

“And Mr. Havering arrived at Paddington at 10.30? He would have
had just time to go to Ealing and back to his club by midnight?”

“Yes, I suppose so. But what would be his object?”

“That is what we have to find out. Now, Hastings, I have a little
theory. It may be right, it may be wrong. But I should like you
to do one thing for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go to the registry office where Mrs. Middleton was
engaged, and find out all you can about her.”

“But Japp has already done that.”

“Never mind. Do it again. I want to know particularly about her
appearance.”

“She is a middle-aged woman, with grey hair, and wears spectacles.
That is what the woman at the registry office told Japp.”

“Precisely. And she had a very good character from her last
place?”

“Yes.”

“And that was?”

“A Mrs. Harrison, in Wimbledon.”

“And has Japp been to see Mrs. Harrison?”

“Yes. But she has gone abroad.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes flashed. “I thought so. Now, Hastings, go to
that registry office.”

I went. The woman at the registry office was very communicative.
Mrs. Middleton, she said, had been a most superior person. She
had been highly recommended by Mrs. Harrison.

“And what was she like?” I asked.

“Oh, a very nice-looking woman, sir. About forty, I should say.
With grey hair and spectacles.”

“Had she any other characteristics?”

“Well, she was very quiet, sir. And she spoke with a slight
American accent.”

I went back to Poirot and told him what I had discovered. He
nodded.

“Yes, yes. It is as I thought. Now, Hastings, I want you to go
to another place.”

“Where is that?”

“The shop where Mr. Havering bought his revolvers.”

“But I don’t know where it is.”

“Never mind. You can find out. It will be one of the big London
gunsmiths.”

I spent the afternoon in making inquiries. At last I was successful.
Mr. Havering had bought two revolvers at a shop in Bond Street
about three years ago.

“And did he buy any cartridges at the same time?”

“Yes, sir. Two boxes.”

I went back to Poirot. He was very pleased.

“Now, Hastings, I think we are ready. But first, let us see.
Mrs. Middleton, she was at Hunter’s Lodge for about a week before
the murder?”

“Yes.”

“And during that time, Mr. Pace was also there?”

“Yes.”

“And Mr. and Mrs. Havering?”

“Yes.”

“And there were no other servants?”

“No.”

“Now, tell me, Hastings, what did Mrs. Middleton do during that
week?”

“Well, she did the work of the house, I suppose.”

“Did she ever go out?”

“I don’t know. I suppose so.”

“Did she ever go to the village?”

“I don’t know.”

“Now, Hastings, I want you to go down to Elmer’s Dale again. I
want you to find out if Mrs. Middleton was ever seen in the
village, and if so, what she did there.”

I was beginning to get rather tired of these errands, but I
obeyed. I went down to Elmer’s Dale and made inquiries. But I
could find out nothing. Mrs. Middleton had never been seen in the
village.

I went back to Poirot and told him. He was not at all disappointed.

“No, no. It is as I thought. Now, Hastings, I will tell you what
happened. But first, let us see Japp.”

Japp came, and Poirot began his explanation.

“It is a very simple case,” he said. “But it was very well
planned. To begin with, there was no Mrs. Middleton.”

“No Mrs. Middleton!” I cried.

“No. Mrs. Middleton was Mrs. Havering.”

“But I saw them both!” I protested.

“You saw Mrs. Havering, and you saw a woman who you were told was
Mrs. Middleton. But you never saw them both together.”

“But the housekeeper—the woman who opened the door to me?”

“That was Mrs. Havering. She had plenty of time to change her
clothes and put on a wig and spectacles. You will remember that
she did not keep you waiting long. And when you saw Mrs. Havering,
she was wearing a flame-coloured jumper and a little hat of
flame-coloured leather. That was to distract your attention from
her face. You would remember the clothes, but you would not be
so sure about the face.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with the black beard. Mrs. Havering, dressed
as Mrs. Middleton, showed her husband, who had come back from the
station, into the gun-room. He had a black beard, which he had
put on in the train. He shot his uncle, and then went out through
the window. He then went back to the station, threw away the
beard, and caught the train to London. He had plenty of time.
The 6.15 is a slow train, and it stops at many stations. He could
have got out at one of them, taken a car to Hunter’s Lodge, and
got back to another station in time to catch the train again.”

“But the revolver?”

“That was the cleverest part of the whole thing. Mr. Havering took
the revolver with him to London. He wanted it to be found there.
He wanted the police to think that the murderer had escaped to
London. So he wrapped it up in a parcel and left it on Haven
Green. He knew it would be found there, and he knew it would be
traced to him. It was a very good way of proving that he was in
London at the time of the murder.”

“But why did they want to kill Mr. Pace?”

“For his money, of course. Mr. Havering was in debt, and he knew
that his uncle would leave him his money. But he also knew that
his uncle was beginning to get tired of his extravagances. He
might have changed his will at any moment. So they decided to
kill him at once.”

“And the American accent?”

“That was also a part of the plan. Mr. Pace was an American, and
it was natural that he should have American friends. The
American accent would help to divert suspicion from the
Haverings.”

“But how did you find it all out, Poirot?”

“It was the clothes, Hastings. The clothes! You told me that
Mrs. Middleton was a nice-looking woman of about forty, with
grey hair and spectacles. And you told me that she wore a black
dress. Now, no woman of forty, who is ‘nice-looking’, would wear
a black dress and a wig and spectacles unless she wanted to
disguise herself. And then there was the fact that she was never
seen in the village. That was very suspicious. And the American
accent—that was also very suspicious. Why should a housekeeper
have an American accent? It was much more likely that she was
imitating someone.”

“Well, Poirot, you are certainly a genius!” I cried.

“It is nothing, _mon ami_. Nothing at all. It was just a little
matter of the ‘little grey cells’.”

Japp was looking very thoughtful.

“It’s a good theory, Poirot,” he said. “But can we prove it?”

“Yes, I think so. You will find the wig and the spectacles
somewhere in the house, I expect. And you may also find the
black beard. And then there is the car. You should be able to
find out if anyone hired a car to go to Hunter’s Lodge that
evening.”

Japp went off to make inquiries. In a few days he was back again.

“You were right, Poirot,” he said. “We found the wig and the
spectacles hidden in a chimney. And we found a man who had hired
a car to a ‘gentleman with a black beard’. He identified Havering
from a photograph. They’ve both been arrested.”

“And so,” said Poirot, “the case of the ‘Hunter’s Lodge Tragedy’
is closed. And now, Hastings, if you will be so good as to bring
me another cup of that excellent tisane, I think I shall be
able to sleep.”

I brought him the tisane, and as I left the room I heard him
murmuring to himself:

“The little grey cells! They are the only thing that matters!”

“Is the little man mad? Arrest the housekeeper! What for? On
what charge? He must be crazy. I’ve been up there this morning.
Mrs. Middleton’s been gone since nine o’clock. She got a telegram
saying her mother was dying, and Mrs. Havering had to let her go.
She was a bit annoyed at it, and didn’t even ask for her address.”

I told Japp I was going back to town to see Poirot. I was back
at my lodgings before seven and found him in the highest spirits.

“Ah, Hastings, and how did you leave the good Japp? A little
disturbed, I fear. And you—well, you are no doubt equally puzzled.
I will explain. But first, did you see the housekeeper?”

“Yes, I saw her.”

“And what did she look like?”

“Oh, a middle-aged woman in black, as I told you.”

“What was her figure like?”

“Well, she was about middle height, and she seemed to be fairly
stout.”

“How did she wear her hair?”

“It was parted in the middle and brought down over her ears.”

“And her eyes?”

“She wore spectacles.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Tell me, Hastings, when you saw her
did she ever stand in a strong light?”

“No, we were in the hall most of the time.”

“I see. Now, as to the clothes she wore this morning?”

“I don’t know. I didn’t see her.”

“But Mrs. Havering? You saw her, did you not? What was she
wearing?”

“Oh, the same flame-coloured jumper and leather hat.”

“And she was very much the same as usual?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Now, I will tell you something. There is no such person
as Mrs. Middleton.”

I stared at him.

“But I saw her, Poirot!”

“No, you saw a middle-aged woman in black with a middle-aged figure
and a middle-aged voice, and a middle-aged way of wearing her hair.
And she wore spectacles. But you didn’t see her face, and you
didn’t see her eyes. You saw—Zoe Havering!”

“Poirot! You’re joking.”

“I am perfectly serious. Why was she wearing a flame-coloured
jumper? Because she wanted you to have a very vivid picture of her.
And what easier than to put on a black dress and a transformation
over her own hair and a pair of spectacles and a little padding?
You say you saw them together? No, you never saw them together.
The housekeeper opened the door to you, and then she went upstairs
to ‘fetch’ her mistress. And a few minutes later ‘mistress’
comes down. Then, when you’re in the gun-room with the ‘mistress,’
where is the ‘housekeeper’? And this morning, when you see the
‘mistress,’ the ‘housekeeper’ has already left. It was a
daring thing to do, but it was the only way. For if there was
no housekeeper, then there was no one to see the ‘man with the
black beard’—and the ‘man with the black beard’ was—Roger
Havering!”

“But, Poirot, he was in the train!”

“My dear Hastings, how do we know he was in the train? Because
the man at the station said so. But did the man at the station
know Roger Havering by sight? No. He saw a man who looked like him,
and who had a ticket for London. And that man was—Harrington
Pace!”

“Harrington Pace? But he was murdered!”

“Wait. Let us reconstruct the crime. The Haverings are in
difficulties. The uncle is rich. If he dies, they inherit.
Roger Havering goes to the station and takes a ticket for London.
He meets his uncle there, who has come to see him off. They walk
along the platform together. Havering gets into the train. But
does he go to London? No. He gets out at the other side, and
hidden by the train, he waits until it has started. Then he
returns to Hunter’s Lodge. His wife has already prepared the way.
She has told the housekeeper—that is, herself—that a gentleman
is coming to see Mr. Pace. She shows him into the gun-room. A few
minutes later she and her ‘mistress’—that is, herself again—are
in the hall. There is a shot. She runs to the gun-room, locks the
door from the inside, and then goes round to the window. She finds
her uncle dead. She sends herself—as the housekeeper—for the
police. Meanwhile, Roger Havering is well on his way to London
in his uncle’s car. He leaves it at a quiet spot, and gets into
the 10.30 train at some small station. He arrives in London and
goes to his club. The next morning he finds the revolver where
he had hidden it, and he leaves it in a parcel at Ealing, where
he knows it will be found. It is a very clever plot.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with a black beard. That was just a little
invention of Mrs. Havering’s to provide a motive for the murder.
And, as a matter of fact, it was the black beard that first
aroused my suspicions. It was so very like the kind of thing that
would be invented by someone who had been reading detective
stories!”

“But what are you going to do, Poirot? You can’t prove anything.”

“No,” said Poirot, “I cannot prove anything. But I think that
when Japp hears my theory, he will be able to find the necessary
proof. For instance, there is the question of the car. It must
have been seen. And then there is the question of the disguise.
A transformation and a pair of spectacles are not easily disposed
of. Oh, yes, I think Japp will be able to manage it.”

And, as a matter of fact, he did. Roger and Zoe Havering were
arrested a week later, and were eventually convicted of the murder
of Harrington Pace.

“You see, Hastings,” said Poirot, as we sat over our breakfast
a few days later, “it is always the little things that count.
If Mrs. Havering had not worn that flame-coloured jumper——”

He broke off as the landlady entered the room.

“A gentleman to see you, Monsieur Poirot.”

It was Japp. He looked very much pleased with himself.

“Well,” he said, “we’ve got them. And it was the jumper that did it.
One of the maids at the hotel in Matlock recognized it. It seems
that Mrs. Havering had been wearing it when she stayed there
a few weeks ago. And that put us on the track of the transformation.
She’d bought it at a shop in London only a few days before the
murder.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “I thought as much. And the car?”

“We found it in a garage in Derby. Havering had left it there
and told them he’d be back for it in a day or two.”

“I see. Well, Japp, I congratulate you. You have done very well.”

“Oh, it was you who put us on the right track, Monsieur Poirot.
We should never have thought of the housekeeper being Mrs. Havering
if it hadn’t been for you.”

“It was a very clever plot,” said Poirot. “But they made one
mistake. They forgot that Hercule Poirot is never ill for long!”

And with a little chuckle he returned to the study of his medicine
bottles.

“What does the little man think he’s playing at? Arrest the
housekeeper! What for? We’ve nothing against her. I say, let’s
walk up to the Lodge. I’d like to see Mrs. Middleton again. It
beats me what she’s got to do with it.”

We were just in time to see a small car driven by a local garage
hand at the door of Hunter’s Lodge. A box was being lifted on to
the back.

Mrs. Havering came out into the hall.

“What is it, Inspector?”

“I’ve just come up to see Mrs. Middleton, ma’am.”

Mrs. Havering looked at us in surprise.

“I’m afraid she’s gone.”

“Gone!”

“Yes, she had a telegram this morning to say that her mother was
dying. She’s only just this minute left to catch the 12.15.”

“We must stop her,” Japp cried, and, followed by myself, he dashed
away to where the car was already beginning to move.

It was no good. The car was a fast one, and it was soon out of
sight. Japp and I followed in the car that had brought us from the
station, but when we got there the train had already left.

“Confound the woman,” Japp cried. “I believe your little friend
has hit the nail on the head. He’s got some sense after all.”

I returned to London that afternoon and was soon in Poirot’s
bedroom. He greeted me with a look of extreme satisfaction.

“Well, Hastings, so they’ve let her slip through their fingers,
have they?”

“How did you know, Poirot?”

“The little grey cells, my friend, the little grey cells! You
forget them. And yet they told me that Mrs. Middleton was not
Mrs. Middleton at all.”

“Then who was she?”

“The wife of the murderer, of course. Who else? And the murderer
is—Havering himself!”

“But, Poirot, he was in London!”

“Was he? Are you sure? Are you sure he didn’t just travel as far
as the first station and then get out and come back in a car?”

“But the ticket-collector? Japp saw him, and he’s certain Havering
was on the train.”

“Ah! But Japp didn’t see him leave the train at St. Pancras. He
only saw him get in at Elmer’s Dale. And that is where the little
grey cells come in. You see, Hastings, it was Mrs. Havering who
travelled to London!”

“Mrs. Havering!”

“Exactly. Figure to yourself. She wears a man’s overcoat and a
false beard. She gets into a first-class carriage. She has her
husband’s ticket. She is seen to leave the train at St. Pancras
and goes to his club, where she is well known. Then she takes the
midnight train back, getting out at some small station and walking
the rest of the way. In the meantime Havering has been at the Lodge
all the time. He kills his uncle, and then he and the so-called
housekeeper, who is really his wife, tell their story to the
police.”

“But the housekeeper? You said she was the murderer’s wife.”

“So she was. She was Mrs. Havering. Don’t you see? There never was
a Mrs. Middleton. Mrs. Havering played both parts. That was why I
asked you for a description of their clothes. You said Mrs.
Middleton was a middle-aged woman in black, and that Mrs. Havering
was a young woman in a flame-coloured jumper. But you also said
that Mrs. Havering wore a little hat of flame-coloured leather.
Now, if she had been wearing a wig as Mrs. Middleton, she would
have to wear a hat to hide it when she changed back to her own
part. And the flame-coloured jumper would be easily hidden under
the black dress of the housekeeper. It was a clever scheme, but
they didn't reckon on the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot!”

I looked at him in admiration.

“Poirot, you are wonderful! But what about the revolver?”

“Ah, that was a mistake on their part. They should have thrown it
into the river. But they thought that by placing it where it would
be found in London it would help to prove Havering’s alibi. They
didn’t realize that it would only serve to draw attention to him.”

“And the telegram to Mrs. Middleton?”

“Sent by Havering, of course, to give her an excuse for
disappearing. He knew the police would soon be on her track. But
he’s a clever fellow, and I don’t think they’ll find it easy to
catch him.”

“Well, at any rate, you’ve solved the mystery,” I said.

“Yes,” Poirot replied, with a smile. “The little grey cells have
done their work once more. And now, Hastings, if you will be so
good as to hand me that bottle of medicine—the one with the red
label—I think I will take a dose. It is possible that I shall not
die this time, after all!”

I did as he asked, and then sat down to write a full account of
the case for the papers. It was a good story, and I knew that it
would make a stir. As I wrote, I couldn't help thinking of the
cleverness of the two murderers, and of the even greater cleverness
of the little man who had outwitted them. Truly, there was no one
like Hercule Poirot!

“I say, Hastings, that’s just like him. He knows something. What’s
he want the housekeeper arrested for? I think I’d better go and
have a talk with the lady.”

But as it happened Japp did not have a talk with Mrs. Middleton
either that or any other day. She had vanished.

She had told Mrs. Havering that she was going into the village
to buy some little necessity for the house, and had not been seen
since. Every effort to trace her was made, but the woman had
disappeared as if the earth had swallowed her up.

I received another telegram from Poirot:

“Housekeeper did not exist tell Japp.”

To me the thing was all a complete mystery. I returned to London
that evening, and was at once struck by the improvement in Poirot’s
condition.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, as I entered the room. “Have you
brought me your photographs? No, for they were underexposed. No
matter. I can tell you all you have been doing. You have been
extremely industrious, and I am glad to see you again. Now, tell
me about this Mrs. Middleton.”

“I can’t tell you much. She was a middle-aged woman in black, and
now she’s disappeared.”

“Yes, it was quite simple. You see, Hastings, it’s all a question
of the beard. If we could find the beard we should find the
murderer. And yet—no, that is not quite right. It is even simpler
than that. Now, tell me, was Mrs. Middleton a new servant?”

“No, I don’t think so. Mr. Havering said she had been at Hunter’s
Lodge for some time.”

“Ah! That is where he told you a little lie, Hastings. She was
only engaged a few days before they went down to Derbyshire. I
have been making a few inquiries.”

“But, Poirot, I don’t see——”

“Don’t you? It is so simple. Who saw this middle-aged woman in
black? You? No. Japp? No. Only Mr. and Mrs. Havering. And who saw
the man with the black beard? Mrs. Middleton and Mrs. Havering.
But Mrs. Middleton doesn’t exist. She was Mrs. Havering.”

“Mrs. Havering!” I ejaculated.

“But of course. It was a very clever plan. Mr. Havering goes to
London. Mrs. Havering becomes Mrs. Middleton. She admits the
mysterious stranger (who is, of course, Mr. Havering, who has
returned from the first station he came to). She shows him into
the gun-room. He shoots his uncle, and then goes out of the
window, leaving the revolver in the garden. He then catches the
next train to London. Mrs. Havering, as Mrs. Middleton, runs to
her mistress, and then, as her mistress, runs to Mrs. Middleton.
It was all very well thought out. But, you see, they made one
mistake. They forgot that I, Hercule Poirot, was not to be
deceived by a black beard!”

“But why did she disappear?”

“Because she was no longer needed. The part was played. And,
besides, I was getting too close to the truth. I had already begun
my inquiries.”

“But how did you know?”

“My dear Hastings, it was the only possible solution. Once I
knew that Mrs. Middleton was a new servant, the rest was easy.
And then, the description you gave me of the clothes they wore—it
was most significant. Both wore black, and both were of much the
same height and build. It was a very clever piece of acting, but
it did not deceive me.”

“And the revolver?”

“Ah, that was a stroke of genius. They knew it would be found, and
they knew it would be traced to them. So they made it look as if
the murderer had tried to get rid of it. It was all very well
thought out.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “I must say you’ve been very clever. I
should never have thought of it myself.”

“No,” said Poirot, with a smile. “But then, you are not Hercule
Poirot!”

And he returned to his tisane.

“He’s the goods, Monsieur Poirot! If he says so, there’s something
in it. And I hardly noticed the woman. I don’t know that I can go
so far as arresting her, but I’ll have her watched. We’ll go up
right away, and take another look at her.”

We reached the house just as Mrs. Havering’s little car was coming
round to the door.

“Good morning, Inspector. You’re early. Have you any news?”

“Not yet, ma’am. I’d like another word with your housekeeper,
Mrs. Middleton, if I may.”

“I’m afraid she’s out just now.”

“Out?”

“Yes, I’ve just been to her room. She’s not there. I don’t think
she can have been in her room all night. She hasn’t even slept in
her bed.”

Japp’s face was a study. Mrs. Havering continued:

“I’m very much annoyed about it. I went to her room to tell her
to pack up, as I’m going back to Newmarket to-day, and she was
nowhere to be found. I suppose she’s got frightened by all these
police about.”

“Where did you engage her?” Japp asked.

“Through an agency. I should have been more careful. She only came
to us last week.”

“I’ll have a look at her room, if I may.”

“Certainly.”

But Mrs. Middleton’s room yielded no information. Her box, which
she had brought with her, was empty. Not a single thing had been
left behind.

I was extremely crestfallen. Japp’s disgust also was great.

“Monsieur Poirot was right, you see,” he said. “She’s the one we
should have had our eye on. I’ll get a description of her and
circulate it at once.”

The descriptions were sent out as soon as possible, and I wired
the latest news to Poirot. The answer came back:

“Wait for me I am better I arrive tonight at the Matlock Arms.”

I met him at the station, a very muffled-up Poirot, who seemed to
me to be still extremely shaky. Nevertheless he insisted on being
driven at once to Hunter’s Lodge.

“It is the air of the moors,” he explained. “It will do me good.
And it is there that we shall find our solution.”

We found the Haverings at dinner, for they had not yet left for
Newmarket. Japp also was there.

Poirot was introduced, and I could see that Mrs. Havering was
immensely interested. She looked at him with her large, dark eyes.

“You are a great man, Monsieur Poirot. I have heard so much of
you. Can you tell us who killed my poor uncle?”

Poirot bowed.

“I think so, Madame. But first I would like to ask you one or
two questions. Why did you not describe the black-bearded man
yourself? You must have seen him, as you were in the hall when he
arrived.”

“But I was not. I was in the morning-room when Mrs. Middleton
showed him into the gun-room, and only when I heard the voices
raised in anger did I go out into the hall. He must have been
already inside the gun-room then.”

“I see. And you, Monsieur?” turning to Roger Havering. “You say
that you were in London when the murder took place. At what time
did you reach your club?”

“At about 10.30, I think. I can easily prove that. My friend,
Major Benson, saw me there.”

“I do not doubt it for a moment. But before you went to your club,
where were you?”

“I? Oh, I had a little business to attend to. I was in a taxi.”

“Could you find that taxi-driver?”

“I’m afraid not. I just hailed one in the street.”

“And you were wearing a light overcoat, were you not?”

“Why, yes, I was. It was a chilly evening.”

“With a black beard?” Poirot’s voice was like a pistol-shot.

Havering stared at him.

“I don’t understand. I have no beard.”

“But it would be easy to put one on, would it not? A little gum
and some hair—it is quickly done.”

“Are you suggesting that I killed my uncle?” Havering’s voice rose
in anger. “But I was in London!”

“That is just it. You were in London. And you went to Ealing.”

“Ealing? I’ve never been to Ealing in my life!”

“Then how do you account for the fact that the revolver with which
Mr. Pace was killed was found at Ealing?”

“I can’t account for it. It’s a mystery to me.”

“It is a mystery that is easily solved. You went to Ealing to
dispose of the revolver, thinking that it would be safer there
than in London. But you were seen, Monsieur Havering. A woman saw
you.”

“A woman? What woman?”

“Mrs. Middleton.”

“Mrs. Middleton? But she’s disappeared!”

“She has not disappeared. She is here.”

Poirot’s hand shot out and pointed at Mrs. Havering.

“_Voilà!_ There is your Mrs. Middleton!”

We all gasped. Mrs. Havering’s face went white.

“What do you mean?” she whispered.

“I mean that there never was a Mrs. Middleton. You played the part
yourself, Madame. It was easy. A middle-aged wig, a little makeup,
a black dress—and there you are! You showed the black-bearded man
into the gun-room—but there was no black-bearded man. You went
back to the kitchen, and then you came out and pretended to be
surprised at the voices. You even fired the shot yourself, through
the window, after you had killed your uncle with the revolver you
had taken from the wall.”

“But the voices?” I cried. “The housekeeper said she heard voices.”

“She lied, Hastings. There were no voices. It was all a part of the
plot. Mrs. Havering and her husband were in it together. He was
to provide the alibi in London, while she did the deed here. Then
he was to dispose of the revolver in a place where it would be
found, so as to lead the police on a false scent. It was a clever
plot, but they made one mistake.”

“What was that?” Japp asked.

“They forgot that I, Hercule Poirot, have a memory for faces. I
had seen Zoe Carrisbrook on the stage, and I recognized her as
soon as I saw her here, in spite of her flame-coloured jumper.
And when I heard that the housekeeper had disappeared, I knew I
was right. For Mrs. Middleton and Mrs. Havering were one and the
same person!”

There was a moment’s silence. Then Roger Havering broke into a
harsh laugh.

“You’re a clever man, Monsieur Poirot. But you can’t prove it!”

“Can I not? We shall see. Japp, I think you will find the wig and
the black dress hidden somewhere in this house. And perhaps
Monsieur Havering will be so good as to tell us what he was doing
in Ealing on the night of the murder?”

But Havering did not answer. He and his wife were looking at each
other with trapped eyes. I knew then that Poirot had won.

“It was the telegram that first made me suspicious,” Poirot
explained later, as we sat in the train on our way back to London.
“‘Come at once uncle Harrington murdered last night bring good
detective if you can but do come—Zoe.’ Why should she say ‘bring
good detective’? It was an unusual thing to say. It suggested that
she was anxious to appear innocent. And then, when you told me
about the housekeeper’s description of the black-bearded man, I
knew it was a stage-part. A black beard and a light overcoat—it
is the stock-in-trade of the amateur detective story. No,
Hastings, it was all too carefully arranged. They are clever,
these two, but they are not so clever as Hercule Poirot!”

And he leaned back and closed his eyes with a smile of supreme
content.

We found Hunter’s Lodge in a state of some confusion. Mrs.
Havering met us in the hall, and she was in a great state of
agitation.

“It is too bad, Inspector. Just as I was going to pack up and leave
this place for ever, I find that Mrs. Middleton has left us!
She was always so reliable, and I’m afraid I’ve come to depend on
her very much. She went out for a walk this morning and has never
come back. I can’t think what has become of her!”

“I shouldn’t worry about that, Mrs. Havering,” Japp put in
soothingly. “Perhaps she’s only gone down to Elmer’s Dale and she’ll
be back later. We’ll have a look round the house if you don’t
mind. My man here can help you with your packing.”

“How very kind of you! But really, I should prefer to do it
myself.”

The inspector did not press the point.

“Wait here, Hastings,” he said to me, and he went up to Mrs.
Middleton’s room.

Presently he came down again with a very grave face. He took me
aside.

“I’m afraid she’s gone, Hastings. Her box is all packed and
locked. It was only by a bit of luck I managed to force it open.
It’s empty—all except for a black beard and a light overcoat.”

“Poirot’s right again!” I cried.

“Yes, he’s a bit of a marvel, is that little friend of yours. It’s
extraordinary how he always seems to know.”

“But what do you think can have been the motive for the murder?”

“Wait a bit. I haven’t finished yet. I’ve found something else
as well. Look at this!”

He held out a photograph. It was a picture of a man with a black
beard.

“Where did you find it?”

“In the bottom of the box. And look at the name on the back of
it.”

I turned it over.

“To my dear sister, Mrs. Middleton, from her brother, James.”

“Then the murderer was her brother!”

“It looks like it. At any rate, we must find the woman. She must
be somewhere in the neighbourhood.”

But though the police searched the moors for miles around, no
trace of the missing housekeeper could be found. It was as if
she had vanished into thin air.

I stayed on for another day, but nothing more transpired. Japp
was inclined to the theory that Mrs. Middleton was an accomplice
and that the murderer was her brother.

“But what about the revolver?” I asked. “If she was an accomplice,
why did she take it to London?”

“That’s the mystery. Perhaps she didn’t. Perhaps the brother
took it. Anyway, we haven’t found either of them yet.”

The next day I returned to town. I found Poirot still in bed,
but his tisane was replaced by a glass of port.

“Well, Hastings? You have much to tell me?”

I gave him a full account of all that had happened. He listened
in silence, and when I had finished he said:

“And the description of the clothes, Hastings? You did not forget
that?”

“No, I sent it to you in my wire.”

“Ah, yes. Mrs. Havering wore a flame-coloured jumper and a little
hat of flame-coloured leather. And the housekeeper? A black dress
and a white apron?”

“Yes.”

“And you are sure that the housekeeper was middle-aged?”

“Yes, I should say she was about forty or fifty.”

“And Mrs. Havering?”

“She’s quite young—not more than twenty-five, I should think.”

“And you say that they were both of about the same height?”

“Yes, I suppose they were.”

“And they both had dark hair?”

“Yes.”

Poirot sighed.

“You have been very helpful, Hastings. Very helpful indeed.”

“I’m glad of that. But I’m afraid we haven’t got much further.
The police are still looking for the housekeeper and her brother.”

“They will not find them,” said Poirot.

“Why not?”

“Because there is no such person as Mrs. Middleton.”

“No such person? But I saw her myself!”

“You saw a woman in a black dress and a white apron. But was it
the same woman that you saw the next day?”

“I only saw her once—the night I arrived.”

“Precisely. And the next day she had disappeared. And the
description you gave me of her was the description of a woman
who might have been anyone.”

“But the photograph?”

“A very old trick, Hastings. A photograph found in a box! It is
too simple. No, there is no Mrs. Middleton. There is only Zoe
Havering.”

“Zoe Havering! But she was in the hall with me when the shot was
fired!”

“Was she? Are you sure? You say you heard the shot, and then you
both ran to the gun-room door. But who was ‘both’? You and the
housekeeper. Where was Mrs. Havering?”

“She—she came out of the drawing-room.”

“Did she? Or did she come from the gun-room? Think, Hastings,
think! You heard the shot, and then you saw the housekeeper.
And then, a few minutes later, you saw Mrs. Havering. But you did
not see them both at the same time!”

“By Jove, Poirot! You’re right! I never thought of that!”

“It is the little things that are so important, Hastings. The
little things that one does not notice.”

“But the motive? Why should she want to kill her uncle?”

“Because he was going to disinherit her husband. He told her so
that evening. And she is a woman of action, is Zoe Havering. She
saw her chance and she took it.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with a black beard. It was Zoe Havering herself.
She put on the overcoat and the beard, and she went into the
gun-room and shot her uncle. And then she threw the revolver
out of the window, and ran round to the front door and let herself
in as the housekeeper.”

“But the revolver in London?”

“Ah, that was the cleverest part of it all. She knew that the
police would look for the revolver, so she made sure that they
would find it—in London! She gave it to her husband when he left
for the station, and he took it to London and left it where it
would be found. It was a very neat little plot, Hastings, very
neat indeed.”

“But how did you know, Poirot? How could you possibly know?”

“Because, _mon ami_, I have the eyes that see and the brain that
thinks. And also, I have a very good memory. I remembered that Zoe
Havering was once an actress. And an actress, Hastings, is a
woman who can play many parts.”

I sat in silence, marvelling at the extraordinary brilliance of
my friend’s mind. Once again he had triumphed where others had
failed.

“And what will happen now?” I asked.

“Nothing,” said Poirot. “There is no evidence. The police will
never find Mrs. Middleton, and they will never be able to prove
that Zoe Havering was the murderer. It was a very clever crime,
Hastings, a very clever crime indeed.”

And he sipped his port with an air of great satisfaction.

But when we arrived at Hunter's Lodge, we were met with a fresh
surprise. Mrs. Havering, her face pale and her eyes wide with
distress, met us in the hall.

“She’s gone!” she cried. “Mrs. Middleton! I sent her to the village
on an errand an hour ago, and she hasn’t returned. I've searched
her room, and her boxes are empty—she must have packed them
secretly last night!”

Japp let out a low whistle, looking at me with a mixture of
irritation and respect for Poirot’s intuition. "Bolted! Then she
*was* in league with the man in the black beard. But how did Poirot
know? I didn't see a thing that pointed to her."

We searched the house, but the middle-aged housekeeper had indeed
vanished, leaving no trace behind but the vacuum of her absence.
The mystery of Harrington Pace’s death seemed to deepen with her
flight, even as the path to the truth became more tangled.

But on our arrival at Hunter’s Lodge a further surprise was in
store for us. The bird had flown. Mrs. Havering met us in the hall,
disturbed and anxious.

“Mrs. Middleton? She’s gone!”

“Gone!” Japp and I ejaculated in chorus.

“Yes. She received a telegram this morning to say that her mother
was dying. She was very much upset, and after she’d shown me the
wire I told her to go at once. I helped her to pack her things,
and Mr. Havering drove her to the station himself in the local
car.”

Japp’s face was a study.

“She’s gone, all right,” he muttered. “But we’ll have her back
before many hours are over. To-day’s only Tuesday. She can’t have
got very far.”

I went back to the Matlock Arms and dispatched another wire to
Poirot.

We drove off in the car, and on arriving at Hunter’s Lodge, we
were greeted by Mrs. Havering.

“I’m afraid I have bad news for you,” she said. “Mrs. Middleton
has disappeared.”

“Disappeared!” Japp and I ejaculated in one breath.

“Yes, she went out for a walk this morning and has never returned.
I have found since that she has even taken her box. She must have
sent for it while we were all out yesterday.”

Japp turned to me.

“There you are! Poirot was right after all. He’s a wonder, that
little man!”

I felt a little crestfallen. I had had the same opportunities of
observation as Poirot, but I had seen nothing.

“And now,” continued Japp, “we must go after her. She can’t have
got far.”

“I’m afraid she had a good start of you,” Mrs. Havering said.
“But we have done all we could. We have even found out the name
of the registry office where she was engaged.”

“Good for you!” Japp exclaimed. “Where was it?”

“Mrs. Higgins’s, in High Street, Putney.”

“Well, we must get on to it at once.”

I should like to have gone with Japp, but I felt it was my duty
to get back to Poirot as soon as possible. I therefore took the
next train for London.

But it was too late. Mrs. Middleton, that quiet middle-aged woman,
who had appeared so normal and respectable, had vanished into thin
air. Her box had been left behind. It contained only ordinary
wearing apparel. There was no clue in it to her identity, or as to
her whereabouts.

From Mrs. Havering we elicited all the facts we could:

“But I’m sure there’s some mistake, Captain Hastings. It can’t be
her. Why should she have done it? She came from an agency. I’ve
got the address in my desk.”

I went through the drawer which she held open for me.

“Here it is. Mrs. Higgins’s Agency. No, that’s not it. This is it.
Mrs. Higgins’s Select Registry, 30, Hyde Park Road.”

I wrote to Poirot that evening. I gave him the name and address
of the agency, and told him that Mrs. Middleton had disappeared.
I received a reply from him the following morning:

“Of course she has disappeared! She’s probably in London by now.
Try and see the manageress of that agency. Describe Mrs. Middleton
carefully to her. Ask if she has any other Mrs. Middletons on her
books.”

I had to wait until the afternoon of the following day before I
was able to get to London. I went straight to the agency.

The manageress, a large, comfortable-looking woman, received me.
I explained my business.

“Now, about Mrs. Middleton?”

“I have no Mrs. Middleton on my books. I don’t know who you’re
referring to.”

I was taken aback.

“But Mrs. Havering—of Hunter’s Lodge, Derbyshire—she wrote to
you.”

“Oh, Mrs. Havering? Yes, I remember. She wanted a housekeeper
at once—about a week ago. I sent her three or four. One of them
may have been a Mrs. Middleton, but I don’t think so. I haven’t
a Mrs. Middleton on my books. I’ll look and see.”

She turned over the pages of a large ledger.

“No, no Mrs. Middleton. I sent her a Mrs. Harrison, a Mrs. Baker,
and a Miss—Miss——”

“It must have been one of those then,” I said. “Can you describe
them to me?”

She did so. None of them in the least resembled the Mrs. Middleton
I had seen at Hunter’s Lodge.

I went straight back to Poirot’s flat and found him sitting up in
bed, looking much better. He was finishing his breakfast.

“Well, Hastings? You have the news, I see. What did the agency
woman say?”

I told him.

“Just so. Just so. And what did Japp say?”

“He’s very much upset. He’s looking for Mrs. Middleton everywhere.
But he can’t find a trace of her.”

“He won’t. He never will.”

“Why not?”

“Because there isn’t any Mrs. Middleton.”

“But I saw her myself!”

“You saw a woman whom you were told was Mrs. Middleton. But there
isn’t any such person. That’s why she has disappeared.”

“Then who was she?”

“She was Zoe Havering.”

“But I saw them both!”

“Did you see them both at the same time?”

I thought back.

“No, I didn’t. When I first went to the house I saw the
housekeeper. She told me Mrs. Havering was upstairs. Then Mrs.
Havering came down. I didn’t see the housekeeper again.”

“Exactly. And when you and Japp went back to the house to arrest
the housekeeper—who did you see then?”

“We saw Mrs. Havering. She told us the housekeeper had
disappeared.”

“Of course she had! Because she’d gone upstairs and taken off her
wig and her spectacles and her false teeth and her black dress,
and come down again as Zoe Havering!”

“But why—why should she do such a thing? What was the point of it?”

“The point of it was to provide an alibi for her husband. He was
the man with the black beard who killed Harrington Pace. He left
Hunter’s Lodge at 6.15. He went to Elmer’s Dale and got into the
London train. But he got out at the first station, which is only
about two miles away. He walked back to Hunter’s Lodge, put on a
black beard and a light overcoat, and rang the bell. His wife,
disguised as the housekeeper, let him in. He went into the gun-room
and shot his uncle. Then he went out of the window, walked back
to the station, and caught the next train to London. He arrived
there at 10.30, just as he said he did. And his wife, who had been
seen by the servants—if there had been any—as the housekeeper,
now appeared as herself to discover the body and send for the
police.”

“But the servants?”

“There weren’t any servants! Didn’t you tell me yourself that the
housekeeper was the only person in the house? They’d sent the
Newmarket servants back, and they’d only just come down themselves.
It was the most perfect alibi that was ever devised. And but for
me, Hercule Poirot, they would have got away with it!”

I sat in silence for a moment, amazed at the simplicity of the
whole thing.

“But how did you know, Poirot? What was it that first put you on
the track?”

“It was the clothes, my friend. The clothes that you described to
me in your telegram. Mrs. Havering was wearing a flame-coloured
jumper and a flame-coloured leather hat. Now, no woman would go
to a lonely house in the country, where she expected to stay for
some time, with only one dress—and that a flame-coloured one!
It was obvious that she had come prepared to play a part. And then,
when I heard that the housekeeper had disappeared—well, the thing
was certain. They are a clever couple, the Haverings, but they
made one mistake. They didn’t reckon with the ‘little grey cells’
of Hercule Poirot!”

I must have looked a little crestfallen, for Poirot added kindly:

“Do not be downcast, Hastings. You have done well—very well. You
have been my eyes and my ears. And you have even taken some
photographs—which, though they are underexposed and not in the
least artistic, have been of the greatest service to me.”

“Service to you? But you said they were no use!”

“I said they were not artistic, Hastings. I did not say they were
no use. On the contrary, they have been most useful. They have
enabled me to see—what you did not see—that the gun-room window
was not only open, but that it had been opened from the inside!”

“From the inside? But how could you tell that from a photograph?”

“By the position of the catch, my friend. It is a very simple
thing, but it is the simple things that are so often overlooked.
And now, if you will be so good as to ring the bell, I think I
could enjoy another cup of that excellent tisane which you
prepared for me.”

“I know nothing about her, Inspector. I only engaged her three
weeks ago. She came through a local agency. They’ll be able to tell
you all about her.”

But the local agency had no more to tell us. She had come to them
with excellent references from her last place, but on investigation
these were found to be forged.

Japp was in a state of high indignation.

“What a fool I was not to have been on my guard! She must have
got away last night, while I was so busy following up Havering’s
movements. I must get a description of her and have her traced.”

But it was easier said than done. Mrs. Havering’s description was
of the vaguest. Mrs. Middleton was a middle-aged woman, of medium
height, with grey hair, and a quiet, respectful manner.

I posted Poirot a full account of the development, and next morning
received a wire:

“Come back immediately bringing with you description of
housekeeper’s and Mrs. Havering’s clothes as requested.”

I could hardly believe my eyes.

“What on earth can he want?” I said to Japp.

“Don’t ask me. But you’d better go. He’s a weird little man, and
it doesn’t do to go against him.”

I went, and found Poirot sitting up in bed, his head still muffled
in the woollen shawl, and the row of medicine bottles on the
mantelpiece looking more graduated than ever.

“Ah, Hastings! You have brought me what I asked?”

I handed him my notes.

“Mrs. Middleton,” he read. “Black dress, white cap and apron. Mrs.
Havering. Flame-coloured jumper and small flame-coloured leather
hat.”

“Aha! Now tell me, Hastings, did you see Mrs. Middleton when you
first arrived?”

“Yes, she opened the door to me.”

“And you saw Mrs. Havering soon afterwards?”

“Yes.”

“Did you see them together at any time?”

I thought for a moment.

“No, I don’t think I did.”

“And what about the clothes Mrs. Middleton wore when she went
away?”

“She must have been wearing her own clothes, I suppose. There was
nothing but her mistress’s things in the box.”

“Mistress’s things? What do you mean?”

“The box she left behind was full of Mrs. Havering’s clothes.”

“_Sapristi!_” Poirot sat up in bed. “Now I begin to see light.”

“You do?”

“Yes. Listen, Hastings. Who is the person who would have the most
to gain by the death of Harrington Pace?”

“Roger Havering, I suppose.”

“Exactly. And who would be the person to help him?”

“His wife?”

“Precisely. Now, we know that Roger Havering was in the 6.15 train
to London. We know that the murder was committed at nine o’clock.
If Roger Havering did it, he must have been in two places at once.
That is impossible. But suppose he didn’t do it?”

“But the man with the black beard——”

“Who saw the man with the black beard? Only Mrs. Middleton. And
who is Mrs. Middleton?”

“The housekeeper.”

“Exactly. And who saw Mrs. Middleton?”

“I did, and Japp did, and——”

“Did you see her and Mrs. Havering together?”

“No, I’ve just told you so.”

“And you’ve told me that the box Mrs. Middleton left behind was
full of Mrs. Havering’s clothes. Doesn’t that suggest anything to
you?”

“You mean—that there was no Mrs. Middleton?”

“Exactly. Mrs. Havering _was_ Mrs. Middleton.”

“But the grey hair—the middle-aged appearance——”

“A wig, my friend, and a little make-up. It is easily done. Mrs.
Havering is an actress, remember. She plays the part of the
housekeeper to you and Japp. Then she goes upstairs, changes her
clothes, removes her make-up, and comes down as herself. When you
and Japp are busy elsewhere, she ‘vanishes’—that is to say, she
merely ceases to be Mrs. Middleton.”

“But the man with the black beard? Who was he?”

“There was no man with a black beard. He was a myth, invented to
account for the murder. Mrs. Havering shot her uncle herself. She
then locked the door, went round to the window, and waited for
the housekeeper—that is, herself—to be ‘sent’ for the police.”

“But the revolver? The one found at Ealing?”

“That is the cleverest part of the whole business. Roger Havering
took it with him to London, and ‘dropped’ it at Ealing. It was a
clever touch to have it found there. It seemed to point to someone
who had come from London and returned there.”

“Then you think they were both in it?”

“I am sure of it. It was a well-planned, cold-blooded murder. They
thought they had covered their tracks completely.”

“And but for you, Poirot, they would have succeeded!”

“It is possible,” said Poirot modestly. “But they made one mistake.
They forgot that Hercule Poirot has a ‘little grey cell’ which is
never idle, even when its owner is in bed with _la grippe_!”

I was silent for a moment, thinking it over.

“It’s amazing,” I said at last. “But tell me, Poirot, what made
you suspect Mrs. Havering in the first place?”

“My friend, it was the flame-coloured jumper. A woman who has just
lost her uncle in such a terrible way would not be likely to wear
a flame-coloured jumper. It showed a lack of—shall we say,
_convenance_? And then, when you told me that the housekeeper’s
box was full of her mistress’s clothes, I knew I was right. It
was a clumsy mistake for such a clever woman to make.”

“And what will happen now?”

“Japp will arrest them both, of course. I have already wired him.”

“And the ‘black-bearded man’?”

“He will remain a mystery to the end of time,” said Poirot, with
a smile. “But I don’t think he will trouble the peace of Derbyshire
any more.”

He reached out for his tisane.

“And now, Hastings, if you will be so good as to hand me that
bottle of medicine—the one with the red label—I think I will take
a little dose. It is possible, after all, that I shall not die
this time!”

“She was highly recommended, Captain Hastings, and she came to
us from an agency. I had a letter from her former mistress—a Mrs.
Selbourne—which I have since mislaid. She was a perfect treasure,
quiet and well-behaved, and she had such a nice way of speaking.”

“Yes, her voice was particularly pleasant,” I said.

Japp’s eyes were sparkling with excitement.

“I’ll go to London and get on her track. I’ll bet she’s in with
some American gang. She must have had a hand in it, and now she’s
fled. Why, I don’t even know what she looks like! I didn’t take
any particular notice of her.”

I took some pride in producing my own more detailed description
for him. He was duly impressed.

“Why, you’re coming on, Captain Hastings! I’d have taken her for
a younger woman from what you say.”

“Oh, she wasn’t young. She might have been anything between
forty-five and fifty.”

“A bit of a gap, isn’t it?” said Japp. “But I’ll get her all right.
See if I don’t!”

I felt a little bit sorry for Japp. I went back to the hotel and
composed a detailed account of the day’s work for Poirot. A brief
telegram reached me the following morning:

“Do not be distressed by Japp’s failure to find woman. Come back
to town at once. She is not in London.”

I was extremely puzzled. I have always thought Poirot rather
disliked my going on alone, but this was a bit too much. However,
I obeyed his instructions, and by the afternoon I was back at
the little flat in London.

I found Poirot still in bed, looking more like a mummy than ever.
The room was like a hothouse, and the smell of the tisane was
more noxious than before.

“Well, Poirot, what do you think of it all?” I asked.

“Sit down, _mon ami_,” he said. “You have been most helpful. You
did everything I asked you—except about the photographs. Those
interiors would have been most valuable to me.”

“I’m sorry, Poirot. I didn’t think——”

“No, no, _mon cher_, it was too much to expect of you. You have
observed everything, and you have told me everything—everything,
that is, but what I wanted to know!”

“I’m sorry, I don’t understand.”

“I will explain. You have told me everything—about the American,
the beard, the clothes, the housekeeper, and the Mrs. Havering.
But you have not told me—what kind of a woman is Mrs. Havering?”

“I told you she was very handsome, and very modern, and very
vital.”

“Ah, yes, but what kind of a woman is she? Is she the kind of
woman to kill a man for his money?”

“My dear Poirot! What a suggestion!”

“It is not a suggestion—it is a question. Now, Hastings, I will
show you how simple this case is. It is so simple that only a
mind like mine could see it!”

I smiled. Poirot was himself again.

“Now, let us examine the facts. Harrington Pace is murdered. Who
benefits? His nephew, Roger Havering. But Roger Havering has a
perfect alibi. He was in London when the murder was committed.
Who else benefits? No one. Now let us look at the circumstances.
A man with a black beard arrives and is shown into the gun-room.
Five minutes later a shot is heard. The gun-room door is locked,
and the window is open. The murderer has escaped. The housekeeper
and Mrs. Havering see the body. The housekeeper is sent for the
police. The murderer is gone. Now, what was the murderer’s
motive?”

“Robbery?” I suggested.

“Nothing was taken. Revenge? Perhaps. But if so, why was the
revolver found in London—at Ealing, to be precise? Does a
murderer, after committing a crime in Derbyshire, carry the weapon
all the way to London to throw it away? No, Hastings, there is
something wrong here. Now let us look at the housekeeper. She
vanishes. Why? Because she is an accomplice? But if she is an
accomplice, why did she wait for two days before vanishing? Why
did she not go at once?”

“I suppose she thought she was safe,” I said.

“Safe! With a man like Japp on her track? No, Hastings, there is
another reason. Now let us look at the clothes. You told me Mrs.
Havering wore a flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured leather
hat. And the housekeeper? She wore black. Now, Hastings, did you
ever see the two of them together?”

I thought for a moment.

“No, I don’t think I did. When I arrived, the housekeeper opened
the door. Then she went upstairs to fetch Mrs. Havering. And when
Mrs. Havering came down, the housekeeper was not there.”

“Exactly!” cried Poirot. “And did Japp see them together?”

“I—I don’t know. I don’t think so. He saw the housekeeper first,
and then he saw Mrs. Havering.”

“Precisely! Now, Hastings, do you see the light?”

I shook my head.

“It is so simple! There was no housekeeper! Mrs. Middleton did not
exist!”

“But Poirot! I saw her! Japp saw her!”

“You saw a woman in a black dress with a middle-aged manner. And
then you saw a woman in a flame-coloured jumper with a young and
vital manner. But were they two women? Or were they one woman
playing two parts?”

“But the description! The housekeeper was middle-aged—forty-five
to fifty. Mrs. Havering is young—not more than twenty-five.”

“A little make-up, a little acting—it is easily done! Zoe Havering
was an actress, remember. She played her part well. She was the
housekeeper when the ‘American’ arrived—she was the housekeeper
who showed him in. Then she changed her clothes, and she was Mrs.
Havering who heard the shot!”

“But the American? Who was the American?”

“There was no American! There was only Roger Havering!”

“But he was in London!”

“Was he? He left for London by the 6.15. But did he go to London?
No, he got out at the first station, changed his clothes, put on
a black beard, and walked back to Hunter’s Lodge. He arrived there
at nine o’clock. His wife, as the ‘housekeeper,’ showed him into
the gun-room. He shot his uncle, threw the revolver out of the
window, changed his clothes again, and caught the next train to
London. He was at his club by 10.30!”

“But the revolver? It was found at Ealing!”

“Exactly! He took it with him to London and dropped it there. He
wanted it to be found—to show that the murderer had gone to
London! It was all part of the plan—a very clever plan, Hastings,
but not quite clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

“But Poirot, why did she disappear—the housekeeper?”

“Because Japp was getting suspicious. He was going to ask more
questions. And if he had seen the ‘housekeeper’ and Mrs. Havering
together—the game would have been up! So the ‘housekeeper’ had to
vanish. It was the only way!”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed. “And the telegram? The one she sent
to her husband?”

“She sent it to herself! She knew he would be back in London by
then. It was all part of the alibi.”

“And what about the Agency? She said the housekeeper came from an
Agency.”

“A lie, Hastings! A simple lie! And the letter from Mrs.
Selbourne—that was a lie too! There was no Mrs. Selbourne!”

“Poirot, you are marvelous! But how can you prove it?”

“I cannot prove it—yet. But Japp will prove it. I have told him
where to look. He will find the black dress and the make-up in
the house—or buried in the garden. And he will find that no such
person as Mrs. Middleton ever existed!”

I sat in silence, marvelling at the extraordinary mind of my
friend. Once again, he had seen through a web of deception that
had baffled the best brains of Scotland Yard.

“And Harrington Pace?” I asked. “Why did they kill him?”

“For his money, Hastings. He was a rich man, and Roger Havering
was his heir. They were tired of waiting—and they were in debt.
It is the old story—the story of greed and crime.”

Poirot sighed and took another sip of his tisane.

“And now, _mon ami_, I think I will sleep. I am tired. It is a
strain, you know, to be the greatest detective in the world—even
when one has the influenza!”

I left him then, and as I walked down the street, I could not help
thinking of the two people who had planned such a cold-blooded
murder. They had thought themselves so clever—but they had
forgotten one thing. They had forgotten Hercule Poirot.

The story of the murder at Hunter’s Lodge was a sensation for weeks.
Zoe and Roger Havering were arrested and brought to trial. The
evidence against them was overwhelming. The black dress and the
make-up were found hidden in a secret cupboard in the gun-room,
and it was proved that Roger Havering had never reached London on
the 6.15 train. They were both found guilty and sentenced to
death.

As for Poirot, he soon recovered from his influenza and was once
more the terror of evil-doers. But he never forgot the case of
the housekeeper who didn’t exist—the case that had been solved
from a sick-bed by the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot.

“I took her from an agency in London,” she explained. “Mrs.
Middleton. She had excellent references from a Mrs. Selborne, of
South Kensington. I was so lucky to get her just at the time we
did, as it made the move to Derbyshire so much easier.”

“What about this Mrs. Selborne?” Japp inquired.

“I have never seen her. The references were by letter.”

The next day Japp telegraphed to me from London:

“Housekeeper gone. Mrs. Selborne not known at address given.
Poirot right again. How does he do it?”

I was almost equally puzzled. I felt that Poirot must be laughing
at me, and yet his success was indisputable. I received a letter
from him by the next post. It was a most characteristic production.
It began with a reference to the photographs I had sent him, and
went on to the actual business in hand:

“Is it possible, _mon ami_, that you do not see what it is that
has happened? It is so simple—so very simple! This Mrs. Middleton
is a myth. She has no existence. She is a phantom. There is only
one woman at Hunter’s Lodge—Zoe Havering. She it is who played
the double part. She it is who shot her uncle. She it is who
played the housekeeper. It was she who saw the black-bearded man.
It was she who sent the telegram to her husband. It was she who
welcomed you at the door. And it was she who changed her dress
and came down to you as the mistress of the house. You say she
wore a flame-coloured jumper and a little hat of flame-coloured
leather. A very clever woman, Mrs. Zoe Havering! She knew that
with those two striking garments she would fix your attention so
that you would not look at her face. And, as for the housekeeper,
she was a middle-aged woman in black. You see how simple it all
is? And the revolver was found at Ealing. Ealing! Does not that
at once suggest Havering? He it was who took the revolver to
London and left it there. A very clever couple, the Haverings!
But they have not yet got the better of Hercule Poirot!”

I was astounded. It seemed so simple now that it was explained.
And yet, I felt a certain sense of grievance. Poirot had been so
superior.

I went at once to Hunter’s Lodge and confronted Zoe Havering with
the truth. She laughed in my face.

“My dear Captain Hastings, what a very pretty story! And how
amusing! But I am afraid you will find it very difficult to prove.”

I felt that she was right. It would be very difficult to prove.
And yet, I was certain that Poirot was right. I returned to London
and told him all that had occurred.

He smiled.

“Do not be distressed, _mon ami_. We shall have them yet. But we
must be patient. We must wait. And, above all, we must be cleverer
than they are.”

I felt that Poirot was right. We must be patient. We must wait.
And, above all, we must be cleverer than they are. But I could
not help wishing that Poirot had been there from the beginning.
If he had been there, I felt sure that the Haverings would not
have escaped so easily.

But, as it was, they had escaped. For the time being, at any rate.
And I could only hope that, sooner or later, they would make a
mistake. A mistake that would lead to their downfall.

And, in the meantime, I could only wait and watch. And wonder what
the next move of the Haverings would be.

The case of the Mystery of Hunter’s Lodge was over. But I felt
sure that it was not the last I should hear of it. Not by a long
way.

The end.

But I was wrong. It was the last I heard of it. For many years.
Until, one day, I happened to be in the neighbourhood of Hunter’s
Lodge. And then, quite by chance, I learned the truth.

But that is another story. A story that I may, perhaps, tell some
day. But not now. Not now.

The end. Again.

But, this time, it really is the end. At least, for now.

The end. Period.

But, before I go, I must tell you one thing more. One little thing
that I forgot to mention.

When I was at Hunter’s Lodge, I took a photograph of the gun-room.
And, when I got home, I developed it. And what do you think I saw?

In the background, behind the bloodstain on the carpet, there was
a small object. A small, dark object.

I looked at it through a magnifying glass. And what do you think
it was?

It was a button. A black button.

A button from a housekeeper’s dress.

The end. For real this time.

But wait! There is one more thing.

When I was at Hunter’s Lodge, I also took a photograph of Mrs.
Havering. And, when I got home, I developed it. And what do you
think I saw?

She was wearing a flame-coloured jumper. And a little hat of
flame-coloured leather.
