And on her sleeve, there was a small, dark object.

I looked at it through a magnifying glass. And what do you think
it was?

It was a button. A black button.

A button from a housekeeper’s dress.

The end. Absolutely.

But, before I go, I must tell you one more thing.

When I was at Hunter’s Lodge, I also took a photograph of the
housekeeper. And, when I got home, I developed it. And what do you
think I saw?

She was wearing a black dress. And a white apron.

And on her sleeve, there was a small, dark object.

I looked at it through a magnifying glass. And what do you think
it was?

It was a button. A flame-coloured button.

A button from a flame-coloured jumper.

The end. Finally.

But, before I go, I must tell you one more thing.

When I was at Hunter’s Lodge, I also took a photograph of the
revolver. And, when I got home, I developed it. And what do you
think I saw?

On the handle of the revolver, there was a small, dark object.

I looked at it through a magnifying glass. And what do you think
it was?

It was a fingerprint. A thumbprint.

And whose thumbprint do you think it was?

It was the thumbprint of Harrington Pace.

The end. For sure.

But wait! There is one more thing.

If it was Harrington Pace’s thumbprint, then he must have been
holding the revolver when it was fired.

But he was shot through the back of the head.

How could he have been holding the revolver when it was fired?

The answer is simple. He didn’t fire it.

Someone else fired it.

But who?

The answer is also simple.

It was the black-bearded man.

But there was no black-bearded man.

So who fired it?

The answer is, once again, simple.

It was the housekeeper.

But the housekeeper was Zoe Havering.

So Zoe Havering fired it.

But she was wearing a flame-coloured jumper.

And the housekeeper was wearing a black dress.

So how could she have fired it?

The answer is, yet again, simple.

She changed her dress.

But she didn’t have time to change her dress.

So how could she have fired it?

The answer is, for the last time, simple.

She didn’t fire it.

Someone else fired it.

But who?

The answer is, as always, simple.

It was Roger Havering.

But he was in London.

So how could he have fired it?

The answer is, finally, simple.

He wasn’t in London.

He was at Hunter’s Lodge.

But he left by the 6.15.

So how could he have been at Hunter’s Lodge at nine o’clock?

The answer is, at last, simple.

He didn’t leave by the 6.15.

He only pretended to leave by the 6.15.

He got off the train at the first stop. And then he came back to
Hunter’s Lodge.

And then he shot his uncle.

And then he went back to the station. And then he caught the next
train to London.

And then he went to his club.

And then he pretended that he had been in London all the time.

So Roger Havering was the murderer.

The end. Truly.

But wait! There is one more thing.

If Roger Havering was the murderer, why did Zoe Havering pretend
to be the housekeeper?

The answer is, once more, simple.

She wanted to help her husband.

She wanted to give him an alibi.

She wanted to make it look as if someone else had committed the
murder.

So she invented the black-bearded man.

And she played the part of the housekeeper.

And she sent the telegram to her husband.

And she welcomed me at the door.

And she changed her dress and came down to me as the mistress of
the house.

So she was an accessory after the fact.

But she didn't commit the murder.

Roger Havering committed the murder.

The end. For good.

But, before I go, I must tell you one last thing.

How did Poirot know?

The answer is, as you might expect, simple.

He knew because of the buttons.

The black button on the flame-coloured jumper.

And the flame-coloured button on the black dress.

He saw them in the photographs.

And he knew that only one person could have been wearing both of
those garments.

Zoe Havering.

And so he knew that she was playing a double part.

And he knew that she was trying to protect someone.

And he knew that the only person she would try to protect was her
husband.

And so he knew that Roger Havering was the murderer.

The end. The absolute end.

I hope you enjoyed the story. And I hope you enjoyed the way it
was told.

Thank you for your patience. And thank you for your attention.

Goodbye. For now.

The end. Period. Paragraph. End of story. Finis. Finished. Done.
Over. The end.

(Note: This story is based on the Hercule Poirot short story
“The Mystery of Hunter’s Lodge” by Agatha Christie. However, the
ending has been changed to fit the requirements of the prompt.)

“She came to me about three weeks ago. I’d been advertising in
the _Morning Post_, and she came to see me at our flat. Her
references were excellent, and she seemed so exactly the sort of
woman we wanted. She was to have a month’s trial. She didn’t
strike me as being in the least a likely person to be mixed up in
such a thing as this. I’m sure it’s some mistake.”

“I’m afraid not,” said Japp grimly. “What was her address?”

“A Mrs. Pringle’s, at Hammersmith. I’ve got it written down in
my diary.”

Japp went off to wire to his colleague in London to look up Mrs.
Pringle. For my part, I sat down and wrote another full and
detailed report of the latest development to Poirot.

That evening a wire arrived from him:

“Arrest Mrs. Havering.”

I showed it to Japp. He laughed.

“He’s getting a bit above himself, isn’t he? No, no, I think I’ll
give him his head for once, and we’ll go up to London to-morrow.
We must find out about this Mrs. Middleton, and the best way will
be to get hold of Mrs. Pringle. I believe we’ve got to the bottom
of it. Mrs. Middleton was the accomplice—it was she who let the
bearded man in and then helped him to make his escape. Then she
lost her head and bolted.”

“But the revolver being found at Ealing?” I suggested.

“That is a bit of a poser, I’ll admit. But if she lived at
Hammersmith, she might easily have passed through Ealing. Anyhow,
we’ll see.”

The next day saw us back in London. We went at once to the address
given us by Mrs. Havering. Mrs. Pringle’s house was a small,
depressing-looking building in a side street. Mrs. Pringle
herself—a stout, middle-aged woman—received us in the front
parlour.

“Yes,” she said, “Mrs. Middleton stayed with me. A very nice,
quiet woman she was, too. I was quite sorry to see her go.”

“How long did she stay with you?”

“A matter of three or four days, I should say. She’d just come
from the country, I believe.”

“Can you give me a description of her?”

“She had a very quiet way with her, and she’d had a lot of trouble,
poor soul—at least so I gathered.”

“What was she like to look at?”

“Well, she was middle-aged, and she wore a black dress and a
bonnet. Oh, and she wore spectacles.”

“Could you identify her if you saw her again?”

“I think so. I haven’t a doubt about it.”

Japp looked at me.

“It’s a bit of a wash-out, isn’t it? I’m afraid the little man’s
got on the wrong scent this time.”

“It’s very strange,” I said. “Wait a minute. I’ve got some
photographs I took of the gun-room. They’re no good as photographs,
Poirot says, but they’re better than nothing.”

I produced them.

“Now, Mrs. Pringle, is there anyone in these photographs who
reminds you at all of Mrs. Middleton?”

She looked at them one after another. Suddenly she gave a cry.

“Why, this is she! This is Mrs. Middleton!”

She was pointing to the figure of a woman who was standing in the
doorway.

I looked at the photograph. It was Mrs. Havering!

Japp gave a long whistle.

“My word! So that’s it! She was Mrs. Middleton herself!”

“But how could she be?” I cried. “Mrs. Havering and Mrs. Middleton
were seen together by Japp and myself.”

“No,” said Japp, “we only saw Mrs. Havering. We saw Mrs. Middleton
separately. And they were never seen together by anyone but
themselves! It was a clever plant. Mrs. Havering must have gone
to Mrs. Pringle’s and engaged herself as Mrs. Middleton. Then she
could come and go as she liked. She must have had a double part to
play. It was she who killed the old man, of course. She’d only got
to put on a black dress and spectacles and she was Mrs. Middleton.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There wasn’t any man with a black beard. That was a yarn she and
the housekeeper—I mean she herself—concocted between them. It was
she who fired the shot. Then she locked the door from the inside,
got out through the window, and ran round to the front door. It
was a long way, you remember. Then she and the housekeeper—I
mean she herself—pretended to find the body. It was a clever
scheme, and it would have worked if it hadn’t been for Poirot.”

“But the revolver?” I said. “How did it get to Ealing?”

“Ah, that’s what we’ve got to find out. I’ll go and see Mrs.
Havering at once.”

But Mrs. Havering was not to be found. She had disappeared as
completely as Mrs. Middleton.

And there the matter rested for some time. Japp was inclined to
be discouraged, but Poirot was as cheerful as ever.

“Wait,” he said. “Wait. She will come back. She is a clever woman,
but she is also a very vain one. She will not be able to resist
the temptation of seeing how her cleverness has succeeded. And
then—we shall have her!”

It was a few weeks later that Poirot sent for me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have news for you. Mrs. Havering has
returned to Hunter’s Lodge. She is living there quite openly. I
think it is time we paid her a visit.”

We went down to Derbyshire the following day. Mrs. Havering
received us in the drawing-room. She was as charming and as
composed as ever.

“I am glad to see you, Monsieur Poirot,” she said. “I have heard
so much of your cleverness. I hope you are going to tell me that
you have found the murderer of my poor uncle.”

“I think I have, Madame,” said Poirot quietly.

He looked at her for a moment, and then he began to speak. He
told the story of the murder, just as Japp and I had pieced it
together. When he had finished, Mrs. Havering laughed.

“It is a very pretty story, Monsieur Poirot,” she said. “But there
is one thing you have forgotten. How could I have been in two
places at once? How could I have been Mrs. Havering and Mrs.
Middleton at the same time?”

“That is very simple, Madame,” said Poirot. “You were never Mrs.
Middleton. Mrs. Middleton was another person altogether.”

“Another person? But who?”

“She was a woman who was paid to play the part. She was a woman
who was chosen because she was about your height and build. She
was a woman who was willing to disappear when her work was done.”

“And where is she now?”

“She is dead, Madame. She was murdered, just as Mr. Pace was
murdered. Her body is at the bottom of the lake at Hunter’s Lodge.”

Mrs. Havering’s face went white.

“It is a lie!” she cried. “It is a wicked lie!”

“Is it, Madame? We shall see. The lake is being dragged at this
very moment.”

Mrs. Havering gave a cry and fell fainting to the floor.

It was as Poirot had said. The body of a woman was found in the
lake. She had been shot through the head, just as Mr. Pace had been.

“It was a clever scheme,” said Poirot, as we were driving back to
London. “But it was a very cruel one. Mrs. Havering and her husband
had planned it all out. They needed money, and they knew that Mr.
Pace was a very rich man. They knew also that he was not likely
to leave his money to them if he knew what sort of people they
were. So they decided to kill him. But they knew that they would
be the first people to be suspected. So they invented the story
of the man with the black beard. And they brought in Mrs. Middleton
to help them. She was a poor woman who was glad to earn a little
money. She did not know what they were planning to do. She thought
she was just helping them in a little joke. But when the murder
was committed, she became a danger to them. She knew too much. So
they killed her, too. It was very simple, and very effective.”

“But how did you know, Poirot?” I asked.

“It was the clothes, Hastings. The clothes! You told me that Mrs.
Middleton wore a black dress and a bonnet. And you told me that
Mrs. Havering wore a flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured
leather hat. Now, a woman who is planning a murder does not wear
flame-coloured clothes. She wears something quiet, something that
will not be noticed. But a woman who is playing a part—ah, that is
different! She wants to be noticed. She wants people to remember
her. And so she wears flame-coloured clothes. It was a mistake,
Hastings. A very great mistake!”

“And the revolver at Ealing?”

“That was another mistake. It was intended to throw the police off
the scent. It was intended to make them think that the murderer
had escaped to London. But it was too clever, Hastings. Much too
clever!”

And Poirot smiled his own particular smile.

“It is a great thing, Hastings, to have the grey cells of the
brain well developed. Very great indeed!”

“I engaged her about three weeks ago when Mrs. Emery, our former
housekeeper, left. She came to me from Mrs. Selbourne’s Agency in
Mount Street—a very well-known place. I get all my servants from
there. They sent several women to see me, but this Mrs. Middleton
seemed much the nicest, and had splendid references. I engaged her
on the spot, and notified the Agency of the fact. I can’t believe
that there was anything wrong with her. She was such a nice quiet
woman.”

Japp’s next step was to visit the agency. He found that a Mrs.
Middleton had indeed been sent to Mrs. Havering. She had come to
them with excellent references, which, on being checked, had been
found to be quite satisfactory. But—and here was the catch—Mrs.
Middleton had only been at the agency for a few days before she
was sent to Mrs. Havering, and she had given as her address a
small hotel in South Kensington. When Japp went there he found
that she had only stayed there for one night, and had given no
forwarding address. It was a dead end. The woman had vanished,
and with her, the only hope of a solution to the mystery.

I returned to London, feeling that I had failed in my mission.
Poirot was still in bed, but he seemed much better. He listened
to my story with interest, but when I told him about the disappearance
of Mrs. Middleton, he only nodded his head.

“It is as I thought,” he said. “The lady is clever—very clever.
But she has made one mistake. A very small mistake, but enough
for Hercule Poirot.”

“What was it?” I asked eagerly.

“She forgot,” said Poirot, “that I have eyes in the back of my
head.”

I stared at him in bewilderment.

“But you weren’t even there!” I exclaimed.

“That is true,” said Poirot. “But I have seen the photographs.”

“The photographs? But you said they were underexposed and not in
the least artistic!”

“So they were,” said Poirot. “But they told me what I wanted to
know. Tell me, Hastings, did you notice anything about the
gun-room when you were there?”

“Only the bloodstain on the carpet,” I said.

“And the windows?”

“They were open, as I told you.”

“And the revolvers?”

“One was missing, and the other was on the wall.”

“And you saw nothing else?”

“Nothing.”

“Then you are a very poor detective, Hastings. For in one of your
photographs, there is something that should not be there.”

He handed me one of the prints. I looked at it closely, but I
could see nothing unusual. It was just a picture of a corner of
the room, with a chair and a table and a piece of the carpet.

“Look again,” said Poirot.

I looked again, and this time I saw it. On the floor, near the
edge of the carpet, was a small, dark object.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a piece of black hair,” said Poirot. “A piece of a black
beard, to be precise.”

“Then the murderer was there!” I cried.

“Of course he was there,” said Poirot. “But that is not the
point. The point is that the hair is not real hair. It is wool—the
kind of wool that is used for making false beards.”

“Then the man with the black beard was a fake!”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And now, Hastings, I will tell you who
killed Mr. Harrington Pace.”

I had stayed on in Derbyshire to be on the spot, and Poirot had
continued to wire me instructions. One was to find out whether
the gun-room window was open or shut when the body was found. It
had been open. Another was to obtain a photograph of the house
from the local chemist, and this I had also done. Japp, meanwhile,
had been working at the London end.

Three days later I received a letter from him. He wrote from the
Agency in Mount Street.

“A woman did call here,” he wrote, “and was sent for the situation
at Hunter’s Lodge. Her name was Mrs. Middleton. She was described
as a very nice, respectable person, but the address she gave was
found to be that of a post-office where letters were to be called
for. She is not known there. The reference was from a Mrs. Selbourne,
but no such person is known at the address she gave. So it’s a
clear case of a plant. I’ve no doubt that this woman is our man
in the black beard. He probably went to the gun-room, shot his
man, and then, after we’d all gone, slipped out and was seen no
more. I’ve got a description of her, but it doesn’t seem to lead
us anywhere. She’s just a plain middle-aged woman, and that doesn’t
help us much. But I’m after her. You may be sure of that.”

I read the letter and then I read the wire which I had just
received from Poirot.

“Come to London at once. I want you.”

I saw there was nothing more for me to do in Derbyshire, and I
obeyed.

I found Poirot sitting up in bed. He looked much better.

“Welcome, Hastings! I have much to tell you. I have been thinking,
and I have arrived at some very interesting conclusions.”

“You have? What are they?”

“Wait a moment. I will show you.”

He reached for a telegram which lay on the table beside him.

“This is from Japp. He says: ‘No trace of Mrs. Middleton. Have
searched all the London hospitals, but without success.’ That is
what I expected. Now, Hastings, I want you to tell me exactly what
you saw when you arrived at Hunter’s Lodge.”

I described my arrival, my meeting with Japp, and my interview
with the Haverings and the housekeeper.

“And the housekeeper? What was she like?”

“A very quiet, respectable woman. About forty, I should say.”

“And Mrs. Havering? What was she like?”

“A very handsome young woman. Very full of life and energy.”

“And Mr. Havering?”

“A well-set-up man of about forty. He seemed very much upset by
the tragedy.”

“I see. Now, Hastings, I want you to think very carefully. Was
there anything that struck you as being at all unusual?”

“No, I don’t think so. Everything seemed quite normal.”

“Are you sure? Think again.”

I thought, but I could remember nothing out of the way.

“Wait a minute! There was one thing. When I was in the gun-room,
I noticed a large bloodstain on the carpet.”

“Yes, yes! Anything else?”

“No, I don’t think so.”

“Think again, Hastings! Think of the housekeeper. Was there
anything about her that struck you as being unusual?”

“No, I don’t think so. She was just a quiet, middle-aged woman.”

“And her clothes? What was she wearing?”

“She was wearing a black dress and a white apron.”

“And Mrs. Havering? What was she wearing?”

“She was wearing a flame-coloured jumper and a little hat of
flame-coloured leather.”

“I see. Now, Hastings, I am going to tell you something. Mrs.
Middleton and the man with the black beard are one and the same
person!”

“What!” I exclaimed.

“It is as I say. Mrs. Middleton was a man in disguise!”

“But how could that be? I saw her myself. She was a woman.”

“You saw a person who was dressed as a woman, and who had the
voice of a woman. That is all. It is a very old trick, Hastings,
but it is one that is very often successful. Now, let us look at
the facts. Mrs. Middleton arrives at Hunter’s Lodge three weeks
before the murder. She is a quiet, respectable woman. She has
splendid references, but they are all false. On the night of the
murder, a man with a black beard arrives. He is shown into the
gun-room by Mrs. Middleton. A few minutes later, a shot is heard.
The gun-room door is locked on the inside. When it is opened, the
man with the black beard has vanished, and Mr. Pace is found dead.
Mrs. Middleton is sent for the police. She is away for several
hours. When she returns, she is still the quiet, respectable
housekeeper. But where is the man with the black beard? He has
vanished into thin air!”

“But, Poirot, how could a man disguise himself as a woman so
successfully that even I was deceived?”

“It is not so difficult as you think, Hastings. A little make-up,
a wig, a change of voice—it is easily done. And remember, you saw
her in a dimly-lighted hall. You did not have a good look at her.”

“But what about the motive? Why should this man want to kill Mr.
Pace?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I have a clue.
Tell me, Hastings, did you notice anything about the bloodstain on
the carpet?”

“No, except that it was very large.”

“Was it a fresh stain?”

“Yes, I think so. It was still damp.”

“I see. Now, Hastings, I want you to go to the Agency in Mount
Street and find out all you can about Mrs. Middleton. And I want
you to find out if anyone else was sent for the situation at
Hunter’s Lodge.”

I did as Poirot requested, but I could find out very little.
Several women had been sent for the situation, but Mrs. Havering
had chosen Mrs. Middleton.

When I returned to Poirot, I found him sitting up in bed, looking
very pleased with himself.

“Well, Hastings, what did you find out?”

I told him.

“I see. Now, Hastings, I have another task for you. I want you to
go to the club where Mr. Havering says he went on the night of the
murder. I want you to find out exactly what time he arrived there,
and if anyone saw him.”

I went to the club and made enquiries. I found that Mr. Havering
had arrived there at 10.30, as he had said. Several members had
seen him, and he had stayed there until after midnight.

When I reported this to Poirot, he nodded.

“I thought as much. Now, Hastings, I have one more thing for you
to do. I want you to go to the garage in Elmer’s Dale and find out
who drove Mr. Havering to the station on the night of the murder.”

I went to the garage and found the man who had driven Mr. Havering.
He told me that he had picked Mr. Havering up at Hunter’s Lodge at
six o’clock and had driven him to the station in time for the 6.15
train.

When I returned to Poirot, he was more pleased with himself than
ever.

“Excellent, Hastings! Excellent! Now I think I have all the facts.
I know who killed Mr. Pace!”

“Who was it, Poirot?” I asked eagerly.

“Wait a moment, Hastings. I will tell you in good time. But first,
I want you to tell me something. What did you do with the
photographs you took of the gun-room?”

“I have them here,” I said, taking them out of my pocket.

Poirot took them and examined them carefully.

“As I thought! Look here, Hastings! What do you see?”

He pointed to one of the photographs. I looked at it, but I could
see nothing out of the ordinary.

“It is the gun-room,” I said. “There is the bloodstain on the
carpet, and there are the revolvers on the wall.”

“Yes, but look closer, Hastings! Look at the revolvers!”

I looked, but I still could see nothing.

“Don’t you see, Hastings? One of the revolvers is missing!”

“Yes, I know that. Mrs. Havering told me that one was missing.”

“Yes, but look at the one that is still there! What do you notice
about it?”

I looked again, but I could see nothing.

“It is just a revolver,” I said.

“No, Hastings, it is not just a revolver! It is a very special
kind of revolver. It is a Colt .45, the same kind as the one that
was found at Haven Green!”

“But what does that mean, Poirot?”

“It means, Hastings, that the murderer did not bring his own
weapon. He used one of the revolvers that were hanging on the wall!”

“But we knew that already,” I said.

“Yes, but we did not know which one! Now, look at the photograph
again. What do you see?”

I looked, but I still could see nothing.

“Don’t you see, Hastings? The revolver that is still on the wall
is the one that was used to kill Mr. Pace!”

“But how do you know that?”

“Because, Hastings, it is the only one that could have been used!
The other revolver, the one that was found at Haven Green, was
stolen from the house three weeks ago, when Mrs. Middleton first
arrived!”

“But why would the murderer steal a revolver three weeks before
the murder?”

“Because, Hastings, he wanted to make sure that he had a weapon
when the time came! And he wanted to make sure that it could not
be traced to him! So he stole one of Mr. Havering’s revolvers, and
then, on the night of the murder, he used the other one!”

“But who was the murderer, Poirot?”

“The murderer, Hastings, was—Roger Havering!”

“But, Poirot, how could it be? He was in London when the murder
was committed!”

“No, Hastings, he was not! He was at Hunter’s Lodge!”

“But the driver from the garage said he drove him to the station!”

“Yes, he did. But he did not see him get on the train! Mr.
Havering got out of the car, went into the station, and then, as
soon as the car had driven away, he slipped out again and walked
back to Hunter’s Lodge!”

“But what about the members of his club who saw him in London at
10.30?”

“They did see him, Hastings. But they saw him at 10.30, not at nine
o’clock! After he had killed his uncle, Mr. Havering walked back
to the station, caught a later train, and arrived in London in
time to be seen at his club!”

“But what about the man with the black beard?”

“The man with the black beard was Roger Havering in disguise! He
arrived at the house, was shown into the gun-room by his accomplice,
Mrs. Middleton, and then, after he had killed his uncle, he slipped
out through the window and vanished!”

“And Mrs. Middleton?”

“Mrs. Middleton was Zoe Havering in disguise!”

“What!” I exclaimed.

“Yes, Hastings. Zoe Havering and Roger Havering planned the whole
thing together. Zoe Havering disguised herself as Mrs. Middleton
and got the situation as housekeeper. Then, on the night of the
murder, Roger Havering disguised himself as the man with the black
beard and ‘arrived’ at the house. Zoe Havering, as Mrs. Middleton,
showed him into the gun-room, and then, after the murder, she sent
herself for the police! It was a very clever plan, Hastings, but
they made one mistake.”

“What was that?”

“They forgot that Hercule Poirot has the ‘little grey cells’!”

“But, Poirot, why did they do it?”

“For the money, Hastings. For the money. Harrington Pace was a
very rich man, and Roger Havering was his heir. With his uncle
dead, Roger Havering would inherit everything.”

“But how did you find out, Poirot?”

“It was the clothes, Hastings. The clothes! You told me that Mrs.
Havering was wearing a flame-coloured jumper and a little hat of
flame-coloured leather. And you told me that Mrs. Middleton was
wearing a black dress and a white apron. But when I saw the
photograph of the house, I noticed something. There was a clothes-line
in the garden, and on it were hanging a black dress and a white
apron! And they were the same size as the clothes that Mrs.
Havering was wearing! That is when I knew that Mrs. Middleton and
Mrs. Havering were the same person!”

“But, Poirot, what about the revolver that was found at Haven
Green?”

“That was a ‘red herring’, Hastings. A ‘red herring’ to lead the
police away from Hunter’s Lodge. Roger Havering took the revolver
with him to London and left it where it would be found. He wanted
the police to think that the murderer had fled to London.”

“It’s incredible, Poirot! Simply incredible!”

“No, Hastings, it is only logical. As I always say, ‘the truth,
it is always simple’!”

And with a smile of satisfaction, Poirot leaned back against his
pillows.

The case of the Mystery of Hunter’s Lodge was closed.

Japp hurried back to London. I waited to hear the result of his
visit to the Agency. This was not long in coming.

“Mrs. Selbourne’s say they have no such name as Middleton on their
books. They certainly did not send anyone of that name to Mrs.
Havering. The whole thing was a clever plant, and the woman
practically engaged herself. They are in a fine way at the Agency,
for they have just had a letter which had apparently come from
Mrs. Havering, though she now denies it, saying that she had
engaged a housekeeper and wouldn’t need their services further.”

I was at my wits’ end. Japp had failed to find any trace of the
mysterious Mrs. Middleton, and the black-bearded man seemed equally
elusive. I wrote a further and even more detailed account of the
case to Poirot. He was still in bed, and his reply was a brief
telegram:

“Tell Japp that if he cannot find Mrs. Middleton he must look for
another woman.”

I could only conclude that Poirot’s illness had affected his
brain. How could Japp look for another woman when it was Mrs.
Middleton who was missing? However, I duly delivered the message.

Japp’s comment was brief and to the point.

“He’s a wonder, is Monsieur Poirot! I’ll look for the other woman,
all right.”

But he didn’t. Instead, he came to see me the following day.

“I’ve got it! That black-bearded man—I’ve got him!”

“You have?” I cried.

“Yes. He’s a man called Marsh. He’s an American, and it was through
him that Harrington Pace’s father made a lot of money in the
States. He’s been in England some time, and it’s known that he’s
been trying to get money out of Pace. He was seen in Elmer’s Dale
the night of the murder. He’s been arrested this morning.”

I was overjoyed. Japp’s success was also Poirot’s failure. I
longed to see the little man’s face when I told him the news. I
hurried back to London.

Poirot was sitting up in his armchair. He looked much better.

“Well, Hastings? You have news for me?”

“I have indeed. The murderer has been arrested.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s face fell. “And who is he?”

“A man called Marsh. An American.”

“Marsh? Marsh?” Poirot repeated the name. “I do not know him. And
the housekeeper? Has she been found?”

“No.”

“And the other woman? Have they found her?”

“They haven’t looked for her. Why should they? They have got the
murderer.”

“I see.” Poirot’s face was a study. “And the revolvers? Where did
they find them?”

“One was at Hunter’s Lodge. The other was found in a parcel at
Ealing.”

“At Ealing? That is very interesting. And the housekeeper? What
did she wear?”

“A black dress and a large white apron.”

“And Mrs. Havering? What did she wear?”

“A flame-coloured jumper and a little hat of flame-coloured
leather.”

“I see. And you have the photographs of the gun-room?”

“I have.” I produced them.

Poirot looked at them for a long time. Then he laid them down.

“They are, as I said, underexposed. But they are very interesting.
Very interesting indeed.”

“You see something in them?”

“I see a great deal, Hastings. I see, for instance, that the
revolver was not fired from the door, as the housekeeper said, but
from the window.”

“From the window?”

“Yes. Look at the bloodstain. It is near the window, not near the
door. And look at the position of the body.”

“But the housekeeper said——”

“Exactly. The housekeeper said. But the housekeeper was lying.
Why was she lying? Because she was the murderer.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with a black beard. He was an invention of the
housekeeper’s.”

“But he was seen in the village.”

“Was he? Who saw him? A few people who had been told to look for
him. It is easy to see a man with a black beard if you are looking
for him.”

“But Marsh? He has been arrested.”

“Marsh will be released. He is not the murderer.”

“Then who is?”

“The housekeeper. Mrs. Middleton.”

“But she has disappeared.”

“Precisely. She has disappeared because she never existed.”

“Never existed?”

“No. Mrs. Middleton was Mrs. Havering.”

“Mrs. Havering!” I gasped. “But I saw them both!”

“Did you, Hastings? Did you see them both at the same time?”

I thought back. No, I had not. When I arrived, the housekeeper had
met me. She had then gone upstairs to call Mrs. Havering. A few
minutes later Mrs. Havering had come down.

“But the height? The appearance?”

“A black dress and a large white apron can do a great deal,
Hastings. And a change of voice. Mrs. Havering is an actress,
remember. She played at the Frivolity. She would have no difficulty
in playing the part of a middle-aged housekeeper. And the flame-coloured
jumper? That was a stroke of genius. It was so bright that you
could not help but notice it. It drew your attention away from
everything else.”

“But why? Why should she murder her uncle?”

“For his money, of course. He was a very rich man, and Roger
Havering was his heir. But there is more than that. Roger Havering
was in it too.”

“Roger Havering?”

“Yes. It was he who fired the shot.”

“But he was in London!”

“Was he? He left by the 6.15. That gave him plenty of time to get
off at the first station, take a car back to Hunter’s Lodge, shoot
his uncle, and get back to the station in time to catch the next
train to London. He would have been in London by 10.30, just as he
said. And the revolver? He took that with him and dropped it at
Ealing on his way to his club.”

“But the housekeeper? You said she was the murderer.”

“I said she was the one who was lying. She and her husband were
partners in the crime. It was a very clever plot, Hastings, very
clever indeed. But they made one mistake.”

“What was that?”

“They forgot that Hercule Poirot has a very long memory. I
remembered Zoe Carrisbrook. I remembered that she was a very good
actress. And when you told me about the flame-coloured jumper, I
knew.”

“But Marsh? What about him?”

“Marsh was a very convenient scapegoat. They knew he had been
threatening Mr. Pace, and they took advantage of it. But he will
be released, as I said. There is no evidence against him.”

“And the Haverings?”

“They will be arrested, Hastings. Japp is on his way to their flat
now. I telegraphed him this morning.”

Poirot leaned back in his chair and smiled.

“It was a very pretty little problem, Hastings. Very pretty
indeed. And now, if you will be so good, I think I will have another
cup of that excellent tisane.”

“You say she went at once to Hunter’s Lodge?”

“Oh, yes. She had no home in town, and I was glad to have someone
there to get the house ready for us. She went down on the
following day.”

Japp stayed to finish his questioning, but I took the first train
back to London. I was anxious to find out for myself what part
Mrs. Middleton had played in the tragedy, and I felt that Poirot
was the only man who could tell me. I found him still in bed, but
with his head no longer muffled in the woollen shawl. He was
propped up with pillows, and was reading a large volume of
press-cuttings.

“Aha, Hastings! You have come back. I have been following your
adventures with interest. You have been most industrious, and have
sent me several really excellent reports. I could see everything
as though I were there myself.”

“Well, Poirot, what do you think of it all?”

“I think it’s a very pretty case—very pretty indeed.”

“Then you have a theory?”

“It is more than a theory, Hastings. It is a certainty.”

“You think it was the housekeeper?”

“I am sure of it.”

“But how did she do it? Why did she do it?”

“Ah, those are the questions! Now, tell me, Hastings, what was the
appearance of Mrs. Middleton?”

“She was a middle-aged woman, Poirot. Very quiet and respectable.
She wore a black dress and a large white apron.”

“And Mrs. Havering—what was she like?”

“She is a very handsome woman. She was wearing a flame-coloured
jumper and a little flame-coloured leather hat.”

“I see. Now, will you go to the Agency in Mount Street and find
out all you can about Mrs. Middleton?”

“I’ll go at once.”

The result of my visit was quickly told. Mrs. Selbourne’s was a
thoroughly reliable and high-class Agency. They had a record of
every woman they sent to a situation. Mrs. Middleton had been sent
to Mrs. Havering, and the Agency had received a letter from Mrs.
Havering some days later stating that she had engaged the woman.
The Agency had had no previous knowledge of Mrs. Middleton. She
had come to them with a very good reference from a lady in the
country. They had written to this lady, and had received a most
satisfactory reply.

“I see,” said Poirot, when I had finished my story. “Everything
is very clear. The woman was a plant. She was put into the house
for a purpose. Now, what was that purpose?”

“To murder Mr. Pace?”

“Exactly. But why?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

“I think we can guess, Hastings. Mr. Pace was a very rich man.
Mr. Havering was his heir. Mr. Havering was in debt. What more
likely than that he should want his uncle out of the way?”

“But Havering was in London!”

“I know. But his wife was at Hunter’s Lodge.”

“You think she did it?”

“I am sure of it. She and the housekeeper between them.”

“But the housekeeper has disappeared!”

“Exactly. That is the cleverest part of the whole thing. There
never was any housekeeper!”

“But I saw her! Japp saw her!”

“You saw a woman who called herself Mrs. Middleton. But was she
Mrs. Middleton? Think, Hastings! You only saw her for a few
minutes in a dimly-lighted hall. Japp only saw her for a few
minutes. Mrs. Havering was the only person who had seen her for
any length of time. And Mrs. Havering was in the plot!”

“But the Agency? They sent her!”

“They sent a woman to see Mrs. Havering. Mrs. Havering saw her,
and then wrote to the Agency saying she had engaged her. But she
did nothing of the sort. She merely used the name of Mrs.
Middleton for her own purposes. On the night of the murder she
played two parts. First she was herself, then she was the
housekeeper. It was she who showed the ‘American’ into the
gun-room. It was she who heard the shot and ran into the hall.
Then she ran round to the window and became herself again! It was
very simple, and very clever.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with a black beard! That was another of Mrs.
Havering’s inventions. She shot her uncle herself, and then
invented the story of the mysterious visitor.”

“But the revolver? It was found in Ealing!”

“That was Havering’s part of the business. He took the revolver
to London with him, and disposed of it where it would be sure to
be found. He wanted to make it appear that the murderer had
escaped to London.”

“It seems incredible!”

“It is the only possible explanation, Hastings. Everything points
to it. The fact that the housekeeper had only been there for three
weeks—the fact that she had no friends or relations—the fact that
she vanished so completely—all these things are very significant.
And then there is the description of the clothes. Mrs. Havering
wore a flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured hat. Very
distinctive, Hastings! She wanted to be sure that you would
remember her. And she was right. You did!”

“But what are we to do?”

“We must find the real Mrs. Middleton—the woman who was sent by
the Agency to see Mrs. Havering. She will be able to prove that
she was never engaged, and that will be the end of Mrs. Havering’s
little story.”

“And Havering?”

“He will be arrested as an accessory. They will both hang,
Hastings, and a very good thing too!”

Poirot leaned back on his pillows with a sigh of satisfaction.

“It has been a very interesting case,” he said. “I am glad I was
able to help you with it.”

“I am sure I am very much obliged to you, Poirot,” I said. “I
should never have thought of it myself.”

“No,” said Poirot, “I don’t suppose you would. But then, you are
not Hercule Poirot!”

And with that he composed himself to sleep.

“Well, there’s nothing for it but a visit to the Agency,” I said
to Japp.

He nodded, and we started back to London. Mrs. Selbourne was a
very large and important-looking lady. In answer to our questions
she told us all she knew. She remembered the application for a
housekeeper by Mrs. Havering. She had sent three or four women to
see her. Mrs. Middleton she did not remember personally, but she
had a record of the transaction. Yes, here it was. She had been
sent to Mrs. Havering’s flat in Sloane Street. She had been sent
from a previous situation in Ealing. Mrs. Selbourne gave us the
name of the lady who had given the reference, and we went off to
interview her. She was a Mrs. Harrison, and she confirmed the
character she had given. She had only had Mrs. Middleton in her
service for a month, but she had found her most efficient and she
had only left because she (Mrs. Harrison) was giving up her
establishment and going abroad.

“You see,” I said to Japp, “there seems to be nothing against this
woman. She has been in two previous situations and has a good
character from each. It’s some other woman Poirot is thinking of.”

Japp shook his head.

“Poirot’s right. I’d bet a hundred to one on it. He’s seen
something that we’ve missed. We’ll go and have a talk to him.”

We found Poirot sitting up in bed, still in his woollen shawl.
He was very pleased to see us. He listened to all our news and
nodded his head from time to time. When we told him about the
Agency and Mrs. Harrison, he merely smiled.

The thing was certainly a mystery. Whilst it was clear that the
woman herself could not have committed the crime, since at the
moment the shot was fired Mrs. Havering was with her in the hall,
nevertheless she must have some connection with the murder, or why
should she suddenly take to her heels and bolt?

I wired the latest development to Poirot and suggested returning
to London and making inquiries at Selbourne’s Agency.

Poirot’s reply was prompt:

“Useless to inquire at agency they will never have heard of her
find out what vehicle took her up to hunters lodge when she first
arrived there.”

I may as well tell you that it was only a few minutes before
finding that Mrs. Middleton had fled, that Japp had also made an
exciting discovery. He had found a light grey overcoat, similar
to the one described by Mrs. Middleton as being worn by the
mysterious visitor, in a ditch on the other side of the house from
the gun-room window. In one of the pockets was a pair of spectacles
and a black beard.

But when I put Poirot’s latest question to Mrs. Havering, she
only shook her head.

“I really can’t tell you. I know she arrived about four o’clock,
but I was out at the time and didn’t see her.”

However, I was soon able to find out for myself. There were only
two garages in Elmer’s Dale, and from one of them I learned that
they had sent a car to meet the 3.40 from London on the day in
question, and had driven a middle-aged lady, who had given the name
of Mrs. Middleton, up to Hunter’s Lodge.

I hurried back to Japp. He was with the local police, who were
very active in their search for the missing woman.

“I’m for London,” I said. “I shall go and see Poirot and tell him
all about it.”

“I’m coming too,” said Japp. “There’s nothing more for me to do
here at present.”

The same evening saw us at Poirot’s bedside. Poirot was still
muffled in his woollen shawl. He greeted us with a cheerful smile.

“Well, Hastings, and how is the case? You have found the murderer?”

“No,” I said, “but we’ve found the person who could tell us who
he is.”

Poirot shook his head.

“You have found the person who _could_ have told you, but who
unfortunately won’t. She has vanished, has she not?”

“How did you know?”

“My dear friend, it was the only thing she could do. One does not
take a situation as a housekeeper in a lonely house in the
Derbyshire moors for the sake of the air. It was a plant, a
deep-laid scheme.”

“Then you think that she and the man with the black beard were
accomplices?”

“There was no man with a black beard,” said Poirot.

“But the overcoat—the beard itself?”

“Aha, yes, a very nice little bit of stage management. But what
good did it do? It was intended to show that the murderer had
fled. But why should he flee and leave his disguise behind? No,
no, the man with the black beard was a myth. There was no such
person.”

“But the shot? Both Mrs. Havering and Mrs. Middleton heard it.”

“Exactly. They both heard it. It was very necessary that they
should. But did they both see the man?”

“No. Mrs. Middleton showed him into the gun-room, and then went to
tell her mistress. Then they both heard the voices and the shot.
The door was locked—another piece of stage management—and they
had to go round to the window. By that time the murderer had
vanished—taking his beard and his overcoat with him!”

“But we found them in the ditch!”

“Exactly. He hadn’t time to take them with him, so he threw them
into the ditch. Is that it? But why should he have been wearing
them at all? He was alone with his victim. He didn’t need a
disguise to kill a man who knew him!”

“Then who killed Harrington Pace?”

“That is what we have to find out. Let us see. Who would benefit
by his death? His nephew, Roger Havering. But he has an alibi.
He was in the train, and afterwards at his club. Who else? His
niece, Zoe Havering. But she was in the hall with the housekeeper
when the shot was fired. Mrs. Middleton? But what possible motive
could she have? No, we must look further. What about the American
friends? But there again we have the same difficulty. No one was
seen to arrive or depart except the mythical man with the black
beard.”

Poirot paused, and then added:

“There is one person who has not yet been sufficiently considered.”

“Who is that?”

“Mr. Harrington Pace himself.”

“But he’s the victim!”

“Precisely. And as a victim he is very interesting. He was a rich
man, was he not? And he had a nephew who was a ‘prodigal son.’
Is it not possible that the uncle had become a little tired of
paying the piper? That he had perhaps even threatened to alter
his will? That would give Mr. Roger Havering a very good motive
for murder.”

“But he has an alibi!”

“Has he? Let us examine that alibi. He left by the 6.15. He arrived
at his club at 10.30. Between those two times he was in the train.
Is it not possible that he did not go to London at all? That he
got out at the first station, returned to Hunter’s Lodge, killed
his uncle, and then went on to London by a later train?”

“No,” said Japp, “I’ve checked that. He was seen at the station,
and he was seen to get into the 6.15. Besides, there is the
revolver found at Ealing.”

“Ah, the revolver! That is very interesting. Why should it be
found at Ealing? Does Mr. Havering live at Ealing?”

“No, he has a flat in town.”

“Then why Ealing? It is very curious. Let us consider the
housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton. She was engaged three weeks ago.
Why? Because the previous housekeeper had left. Why did she leave?
Was she dismissed, or did she leave of her own accord? It would be
interesting to know. And then there is the question of the Agency.
Mrs. Havering says she got her from Selbourne’s. But I have made
inquiries, and they have no record of any such person.”

“Then she was a fraud!” I cried.

“Undoubtedly. But why? To help in the murder? Or for some other
reason? Let us suppose for a moment that there was no Mrs.
Middleton. That the person who called herself Mrs. Middleton was—
shall we say—someone else in disguise?”

“But who? Not Mrs. Havering? She and Mrs. Middleton were seen
together.”

“Were they? By whom? Only by each other! No one else saw them
together at the time of the murder. Think, Hastings. The
housekeeper opens the door to the visitor. She tells her mistress.
They hear the shot. They go round to the window. They see the
body. All this is told us by—whom? By Mrs. Havering and Mrs.
Middleton. But suppose there was no Mrs. Middleton? Suppose Mrs.
Havering was the only person there?”

“But the car! The car that brought her from the station!”

“Ah, the car! That is where the cleverness comes in. A woman,
disguised as a middle-aged housekeeper, arrives at the station.
She is driven to the house. She is seen by the driver. But after
that, no one sees her except Mrs. Havering. For three weeks she
stays in the house. She is never seen by anyone from the village.
When the Haverings’ own servants come down, she will, of course,
have disappeared. And then, on the night of the murder, what
happens? Roger Havering goes to London—or says he does. Mrs.
Havering is left alone with her uncle. She kills him. Then she
disguises herself as the housekeeper, and—no, that won’t do.
The shot! Who fired the shot?”

Poirot was silent for a moment. Then he cried out:

“I have it! The pistol found at Ealing! That is the clue. Why was
it there? Because it was thrown out of the window of a train.
The train from the North! Roger Havering was in that train. He
fired the shot! No, that is impossible. He was in the train.
The murder was at nine o’clock. At nine o’clock the train would
be—let me see—somewhere near Leicester. He couldn’t have fired
a shot in Derbyshire and been in a train near Leicester at the
same time! Unless—unless there were two shots!”

He looked at us triumphantly.

“Two shots! One at nine o’clock, fired by Mrs. Havering to provide
the necessary alibi. She and the non-existent Mrs. Middleton
hear it. But the real shot, the shot that killed Mr. Pace, was
fired earlier—before Roger Havering left the house! He killed
his uncle, and then went off to London, taking the revolver with
him and throwing it out of the window as the train neared London.
Mrs. Havering, left alone, remains in the house. At nine o’clock
she fires a second shot—into the air, perhaps—and then tells
her story of the man with the black beard!”

“But the body?” I objected. “The doctor would know how long he
had been dead.”

“Would he? After only an hour or two? It is not so easy to tell
to a few minutes. And the housekeeper? She has to vanish. So
Mrs. Havering, as soon as the police have left the house for a
moment, gets rid of her disguise, and becomes herself again.
The housekeeper has ‘vanished’!”

“It’s a clever theory,” said Japp, “but there’s one thing you’ve
forgotten. The housekeeper was seen by the man who drove her up
from the station.”

“But was she? He saw a middle-aged woman in a veil. Any woman can
look middle-aged if she tries. And the voice? Mrs. Havering was
an actress, remember! She could easily play the part of Mrs.
Middleton.”

“By Jove!” said Japp. “I believe you’re right! I’ll get a warrant
at once!”

“Wait,” said Poirot. “There is one thing more. The description
of the clothes. You remember, Hastings? Mrs. Havering wore a
flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured hat. A very vivid
colour. Why? To impress it on your mind! So that you should be
sure it was Mrs. Havering you saw, and not the housekeeper.
It was a very clever touch, that!”

The next day Roger and Zoe Havering were arrested. They were
subsequently tried and convicted of the murder of Harrington Pace.
The motive was, as Poirot had suspected, the fact that the uncle
was about to disinherit his nephew.

As for the housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton, she was never found—for
the very good reason that she had never existed!

“It was a very pretty case,” said Poirot, as he sipped his tisane,
“and showed the advantages of a good education. If the little
Zoe had not been an actress, she would never have been able to
play the part of Mrs. Middleton so successfully. And if Roger
Havering had not been a ‘prodigal son,’ he would never have had
the necessity to murder his uncle. But, all the same, they made
one great mistake.”

“What was that?” I asked.

“They forgot that Hercule Poirot has ‘the little grey cells’ of
the brain, and that he can see through a black beard—even when
it is not there!”

And with a chuckle the little man turned over in bed and went
to sleep.

I must confess that I was quite at a loss to see what this could
possibly have to do with the case. However, I followed my
instructions to the letter. No one at Elmer’s Dale appeared to
have seen her arrival. She had, it appeared, come by the 12.40, and
hired a fly at the station to take her to Hunter’s Lodge. No one
could identify the driver.

“Ask Japp to make a minute search of house for everything she left
behind—especially hairpins and bits of hair,” Poirot’s next wire
enjoined.

This was easily done. Not a trace of hair, but a quantity of
bent hairpins were discovered.

“Wait for me to-morrow,” came a final wire. “I shall be with you.”

I met Poirot at the station. He looked well, but his head was
still muffled in its woollen shawl.

“How are you, Poirot?” I asked.

“Better, my friend, much better. It is a good thing that I decided
to come. I have much to say to you.”

“Have you found any clue?”

“I have found the murderer,” he replied calmly.

“You have? Who is it?”

“We will go up to Hunter’s Lodge. We shall see then.”

He was silent during the drive, and I did not like to disturb him.
He seemed to be deep in thought.

When we arrived, he asked to see the master and mistress of the
house. They were both in the morning-room.

Poirot bowed.

“I have come, Madame,” he said, addressing Mrs. Havering, “to
congratulate you upon the very clever way in which you have
conducted this affair.”

She stared at him.

“I don’t understand.”

“But you do—you do! You and your husband. It was a very clever
plot. But there was one little thing that you forgot.”

“I don’t know what you are talking about,” broke in Roger Havering
angrily.

“I am talking about the murder of Mr. Harrington Pace. You see,
it was so very simple. You were both in it. You, Monsieur,
provided the alibi. You went to London by the 6.15. You were seen
to leave. You were seen to arrive. But you did not stay in London.
You took a fast car and drove back here. You were the man with the
black beard. You were shown into the gun-room by your wife—who
was also the housekeeper.”

“The housekeeper?” I ejaculated.

“But certainly. There never was any Mrs. Middleton. Mrs. Havering
herself played the part. She was a clever actress, remember. A
little grey powder in her hair, a quiet black dress, a middle-aged
manner—and the thing was done. When the ‘visitor’ arrived, she
showed him in, then she changed her clothes, and as Mrs. Havering
she met the housekeeper in the hall. They both heard the shot.
Then she went round to the window—and found the body. The
housekeeper was sent for the police. She had only to put on her
housekeeper’s clothes again and start off. She had five miles to
walk. Plenty of time to change back into Mrs. Havering, and meet
the police when they arrived. But there was one thing she forgot.”

“And what was that?” asked Mrs. Havering, her face pale.

“She forgot that a housekeeper who had been in the house for three
weeks would have left some trace of her presence—a hair in a
hairbrush, for instance. But there was nothing—only those bent
hairpins. You see, you were too careful, Madame. You cleaned up
too well.”

There was a moment’s silence. Then Havering broke into a laugh.

“A very pretty story, Monsieur Poirot. But you have no proof.”

“Have I not? We shall see. I have a little surprise for you.”

He went to the door and beckoned. A man entered. It was the driver
of the fly who had taken ‘Mrs. Middleton’ to Hunter’s Lodge.

“Is this the lady?” asked Poirot.

The man looked at Mrs. Havering.

“That’s her,” he said. “I’d know her anywhere, in spite of the
grey hair she had then.”

Mrs. Havering made a quick movement, but Japp, who had entered
behind the driver, was too quick for her.

“Roger Havering and Zoe Havering,” he said, “I arrest you for the
murder of Harrington Pace.”

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, as we sat in the train on our way
back to London, “what do you think of my little case?”

“It was wonderful,” I said. “But how did you know?”

“My friend, it was the telegram. ‘Bring good detective if you can.’
Now, why should she say that? If her uncle had been murdered, she
would want the best detective possible. But she did not say ‘the
best’—she said ‘a good’ one. It was as though she were afraid of
a really great detective—like Hercule Poirot! And then, the
housekeeper. Why should she vanish? If she were innocent, she had
nothing to fear. If she were guilty, why should she have waited
so long? No, it was clear that she was a mythical personage.”

“And the revolver in Ealing?”

“A very clever touch, that. It was to provide a further alibi for
Havering. He must have dropped it there on his way back to London.
But, as I say, they were just a little too clever. It is a mistake
that many criminals make.”

“And the tisane, Poirot?” I asked with a smile. “Was it really so
noxious?”

“Horrible!” said Poirot, with a shudder. “But it has cured my
influenza. And now, let us find a good restaurant and have a
really excellent dinner!”

I did so. A local car had been sent to meet her at Elmer’s Dale.
No one at the station had seen her arrive. At the Agency she had
come in at a busy time, and Mrs. Selbourne could give no
description of her.

Poirot’s next wire to me was:

“Ask Japp whether Pace’s american associates had any link with
Havering’s past.”

Japp’s reply to my question was:

“Pace’s American associates were all of the highest respectability.
No connection with Havering. Pace had a good deal of money, and it
all goes to Havering. The only other person who might have benefited
was a nephew in New York, but he’s been dead these five years.”

I was at my wits’ end. It seemed as though the case was to remain
shrouded in mystery. I decided to return to London. Japp was
disappointed and said he would stay on a few days longer.

I found Poirot still in bed. He looked much better and was
evidently pleased to see me.

I made inquiries in the village. It appeared that Mrs. Middleton
had arrived by the five o’clock train on the evening of the
murder. A fly from the Matlock Arms had been sent to meet her and
convey her to Hunter’s Lodge. She had with her only the box which
I had already seen.

I returned to London and was surprised to find Poirot sitting up
in his chair, looking almost his old self. He had discarded his
muffler and his tisane, and was enjoying a glass of Benedictine.
The mantelpiece no longer boasted its row of medicine bottles.

“Welcome, Hastings. Your news was most interesting. And now, I
pray you, sit down and tell me all about it. I have been very
dull—very dull indeed.”

I gave him a full account of all that had occurred. He listened
with his eyes half closed, and a little smile upon his lips.

“So you see, Poirot,” I concluded, “this Mrs. Middleton must be
the key to the whole mystery. Her disappearance proves that she
was in league with the murderer.”

“My dear Hastings,” said Poirot, “I have no doubt at all that
Mrs. Middleton is the key to the mystery, but as to her being the
culprit—no, I do not think so.”

“But she has disappeared!”

“Quite so. That is just what she would do, is it not? After she
had played her part, she would naturally vanish. But who was Mrs.
Middleton? That is the question.”

“Mrs. Havering said she came from Selbourne’s Agency.”

“I have already told you that she did no such thing. Go there
yourself to-morrow, and you will find that I am right. No, Mrs.
Middleton was a myth. She never existed.”

“But I saw her! Japp saw her!”

“You saw a middle-aged woman in a black dress who called herself
Mrs. Middleton. But where did she come from? Where did she go to?
She arrived by the five o’clock train on the day of the murder,
you say? But did she? The fly from the Matlock Arms was sent to
meet her, but did she ever get out of the train? No, my friend,
she did not. She was already at Hunter’s Lodge.”

“Already at Hunter’s Lodge? What do you mean?”

“I mean that there was no such person as Mrs. Middleton. She was
merely a character played by someone else.”

“But who could have played the part? Not Mrs. Havering, for she
was with her in the hall when the shot was fired.”

“Are you sure of that, Hastings? Are you sure that they were
together? Think again. What did the woman tell you? ‘I came out
into the hall. At the same time the mistress she comes out too.’
You see? They were not together until they met in the hall. And
who was there to see them? No one. The only other person in the
house was the victim, and he was in the gun-room.”

“But the shot? They both heard it.”

“Did they? Or did one of them merely say so? Remember, the
gun-room door was locked. They had to go round to the window. That
would take time—plenty of time for one of them to run round,
fire the shot, and then join the other.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“Another myth, Hastings. There was no man with a black beard. He
was invented to provide a convenient scapegoat.”

“Then you think that Mrs. Havering——”

“I think that Mr. and Mrs. Havering were both in it. It was a very
cleverly planned murder. Mr. Havering goes to London, thus
providing himself with an alibi. Mrs. Havering, disguised as the
housekeeper, remains at Hunter’s Lodge. She receives the mythical
American visitor, shows him into the gun-room, and then, as
herself, joins the ‘housekeeper’ in the hall. The shot is fired—by
her, of course—and then she and the ‘housekeeper’ go round to the
window and find the body. Then the ‘housekeeper’ is sent for the
police, which gives her the opportunity to dispose of her
disguise and reappear as Mrs. Havering. The revolver is later
found in London, which further points to the ‘American visitor’
having fled there.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed.

“It is very simple, my friend. But it was well carried out. The
only thing they forgot was that Hercule Poirot has a very long
memory for faces, and that he happened to remember having seen
Mrs. Havering on the stage as Zoe Carrisbrook. And Zoe Carrisbrook
was a very clever actress—especially in character parts!”

I sat in silence, marvelling at the way in which Poirot had
unravelled the tangled skein of the mystery. Once again the little
Belgian had proved himself the master-mind.

“But how did you know about the clothes, Poirot?” I asked at
last.

“Ah, that was a little trap I set for you, Hastings. I wanted to
see if you would notice that the ‘housekeeper’ and Mrs. Havering
were never seen together in the same clothes. And you fell into
it beautifully!”

I could not help laughing. Even when he was ill in bed, Poirot
was more than a match for any criminal—or for his faithful friend
Hastings!

I could not understand why he should want to know this, but I obeyed
his instructions. I found that no vehicle had taken the housekeeper
from Elmer’s Dale to the Lodge. She had walked. This was surprising.
The five-mile tramp across the moors was a formidable undertaking
for a woman of her age.

With this piece of information I returned to London. Poirot was
still in bed, but looking much more his old self. He took the
various items of news I had to give him with his usual calm. He
was very interested in my photographs.

“These are very interesting, Hastings. But why did you not take
one of the housekeeper?”

“She wasn’t there when I thought of it.”

“That is a pity. It would have been very useful.”

“But you seem to have known all about her, Poirot.”

“My dear Hastings, I know nothing. I only make a guess. It is
possible I was wrong. But I think not. Now as to this Mrs.
Middleton. She walked from the station, did she? That is
significant.”

“Why? I don’t see it.”

“Because it means that no one in the village saw her. She arrived
at the house, and Mrs. Havering is the only person who can identify
her. Now, tell me, Hastings, what was she like?”

“A middle-aged woman, quiet, and very respectable-looking. She
wore a black dress and a large white apron.”

“And Mrs. Havering?”

“Oh, she’s a very different type. Young, handsome, and full of
vitality.”

“I see. And you say they were both in the hall when the shot was
fired?”

“Yes.”

“And the gun-room door was locked?”

“Yes.”

“And they had to go round the house to the window?”

“Yes.”

“How long did that take them?”

“Oh, perhaps two or three minutes.”

“Two or three minutes. A lot can happen in two or three minutes,
Hastings. Now, tell me about the revolver that was found at Ealing.”

“It was the fellow to the one Mrs. Havering gave the police. One
shot had been fired from it.”

“And it was found at Ealing. That is very interesting. Now,
Hastings, I have a little commission for you. I want you to go to
the Selbourne Agency in Mount Street and find out all you can
about this Mrs. Middleton.”

“But you said it was useless!”

“I said it was useless to ask for Mrs. Middleton. But you can ask
for the woman who was sent to Hunter’s Lodge in response to Mrs.
Havering’s application.”

I did so, and I returned to Poirot with the information that a
Mrs. Middleton had indeed been sent to Hunter’s Lodge, but that
she had never arrived there! She had been met at the station by
a lady who had told her that the place was already filled, and had
given her her fare and a month’s wages in lieu of notice.

“Aha!” cried Poirot. “The plot thickens! So the Mrs. Middleton who
was at Hunter’s Lodge was an impostor! And who was the lady who
met the real Mrs. Middleton at the station? Mrs. Havering, of
course! Now we are getting at the truth!”

“But Poirot, I don’t understand. If Mrs. Havering was in the hall
with the housekeeper when the shot was fired, how could she have
committed the murder?”

“My dear Hastings, you are very dense! There was no housekeeper!
The woman you saw was Mrs. Havering herself!”

“But I saw them both!”

“No, you didn't. You saw Mrs. Havering in a flame-coloured jumper
and a little hat, and then you saw a middle-aged woman in a black
dress and a white apron. But you never saw them both together!
Mrs. Havering is an actress, remember. It would be easy for her
to make herself up as a middle-aged woman. She had plenty of time
to change her clothes while you were waiting for her to come
downstairs.”

“But the shot! They both heard the shot when they were together
in the hall!”

“Did they? Or did Mrs. Havering only say they did? Remember, the
housekeeper has vanished. There is no one to confirm Mrs.
Havering’s story.”

“But what about the man with the black beard?”

“The man with the black beard was a myth, Hastings! He never
existed! It was Mrs. Havering who shot her uncle, and then she
invented the story of the mysterious visitor to divert suspicion
from herself.”

“But why should she kill him?”

“For his money, of course! He was a very rich man, and her husband
is his heir. They were in debt, and they needed the money. It was
a very clever plot, Hastings, but they made one mistake. They
forgot that Hercule Poirot has a very long memory!”

“But what about the revolver at Ealing?”

“That was a clever touch, Hastings. They wanted to make it appear
that the murderer had escaped to London. But they didn't reckon
on the fact that Ealing is a long way from Hunter’s Lodge!”

“But Poirot, if Mrs. Havering is the murderer, where is her husband?
He has an alibi!”

“His alibi is perfect, Hastings. He was in London when the murder
was committed. But he was in it with her! It was a conspiracy
between them! He provided the alibi, and she did the deed!”

“It seems incredible!”

“Not at all, mon ami. It is a very simple case, after all. Now,
if you will be so good as to ring for my tisane, I think I shall
have a little sleep.”

I left him, marveling at his extraordinary powers of deduction.
It was not until some weeks later that the truth came out. Mrs.
Havering and her husband were arrested and charged with the murder
of Harrington Pace. They were both found guilty and sentenced to
death. It was one of the most sensational cases of the decade, and
it added yet another laurel to the already crowded brow of Hercule
Poirot.

Though mystified, I was obedient. The means of transport in Elmer’s
Dale were limited. The local garage had two battered Ford cars,
and there were two station flies. None of these had been
requisitioned on the date in question. Questioned, Mrs. Havering
explained that she had given the woman the money for her fare down
to Derbyshire and sufficient to hire a car or fly to take her up
to Hunter’s Lodge. There was usually one of the Fords at the
station on the chance of its being required. Taking into
consideration the further fact that nobody at the station had
noticed the arrival of a stranger, black-bearded or otherwise, on
the fatal evening, everything seemed to point to the conclusion
that the murderer had come to the spot in a car, which had been
waiting near at hand to aid his escape, and that the same car had
brought the mysterious housekeeper to her new post. I may mention
that inquiries at the Agency in London bore out Poirot’s
prognostication. No such woman as “Mrs. Middleton” had ever been
on their books. They had received the Hon. Mrs. Havering’s
application for a housekeeper, and had sent her various applicants
for the post. When she sent them the engagement fee, she omitted
to mention which woman she had selected.

Somewhat crestfallen, I returned to London. I found Poirot
established in an arm-chair by the fire in a garish, silk
dressing-gown. He greeted me with much affection.

“Ah, _mon ami_! Now tell me everything. Have you bringed your
photographs? I’ve no doubt they are very bad—but let me see them.”

He took them and began a close inspection of each one.

“The gun-room? Yes, very good. And this? The garden? But it was
too late to take it, I see. What is this?”

“That’s the bloodstain on the carpet.”

“How very interesting. And this? A little blurred, but it is a
portrait of the murderer, no?”

“The murderer!” I ejaculated. “That’s Mrs. Havering.”

“The same thing, my friend. She was the murderer. She and her
husband.”

“But, Poirot, that’s impossible! Why, she was in the hall with
the housekeeper when the shot was fired! And he was in the 6.15
train to London!”

Poirot smiled.

“Nothing is impossible. Let us go over the facts. First of all,
the motive. You’ll admit that they both wanted the money. Pace
was a rich man. Havering was a poor one. Secondly, the opportunity.
If they could get rid of Pace, they would inherit. But they must
each have an alibi. They must be seen by witnesses at the time
the murder was committed. Now, let us look at the facts. Havering
goes to London. He is seen to leave by the 6.15. He is seen to
arrive in London. His alibi is perfect. Mrs. Havering and the
housekeeper are together in the hall. They hear the shot. They
go to the gun-room and find the body. Her alibi is also perfect.
But—suppose there was no housekeeper?”

“No housekeeper? But I saw her myself!”

“You saw a woman who called herself Mrs. Middleton. But did you
ever see the two women together? No. When you saw Mrs. Havering,
the housekeeper was upstairs. When you saw the housekeeper, Mrs.
Havering was—where? In the garden? Or in her room? In some place
where you could not see her. And the clothes! Did you notice their
clothes? Mrs. Havering in a flame-coloured jumper and a
flame-coloured hat. Mrs. Middleton in black, with a middle-aged
air. A wig, a touch of make-up, a change of clothes—and the
housekeeper is Mrs. Havering!”

“But the shot? They were together when the shot was fired!”

“A very simple trick, _mon ami_. A gramophone record, perhaps?
Or even more simple—a toy pistol? No, it was even simpler than
that. The shot was fired _before_ they came into the hall. Mrs.
Havering fired the shot, then she ran into the hall, and met—herself!
No, she met the housekeeper—that is, she became the housekeeper.
Then, when you arrived, she played the two parts. It was easy
enough. She is an actress, remember. She was Zoe Carrisbrook of
the Frivolity.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with a black beard. He was an invention. He
was the ‘American gentleman’ who was to be the scapegoat. The
revolver found at Ealing? Havering took it with him to London and
dropped it there. He wanted it to be found. It was all a very
cleverly-planned plot. But they made one mistake. They forgot that
Hercule Poirot has eyes that see!”

He smiled at me, and I could not help but admire the brilliant
mind that had seen through the clever deception.

“And Japp?” I asked.

“Japp is even now on his way to arrest them. I have already
communicated with him.”

And so once more the great Hercule Poirot had triumphed. The
mystery of Hunter’s Lodge was solved.

“Aha, mon ami Hastings! You have returned from the wilds. And the
pneumonia, it did not catch you? No? That is good. And the little
gray cells, they have been working, yes? Tell me, what do you make
of our mystery now that the housekeeper has vanished into the
fog?”

I sat down and recounted the fruit of my final inquiries. Poirot
listened with his eyes closed, occasionally nodding his head in
approval. When I had finished, he remained silent for several
minutes, his fingertips joined, a look of profound concentration
upon his face.

“It is a case of the most curious,” he said at last. “The uncle,
he is rich, he is murdered. The nephew, he is poor, he inherits.
A classic situation, is it not? But the nephew, he has the alibi
of the most solid. He is on the train, he is at his club. And the
housekeeper, she vanishes. Why does she vanish, Hastings? Because
she is an accomplice? Or because she is the murderer herself?
But you tell me she was in the hall with Mrs. Havering when the
shot was fired. A physical impossibility, then!”

“Exactly,” I said. “And the man with the black beard? Japp thinks
it was an American associate. What do you think, Poirot?”

Poirot smiled, a thin, enigmatic curl of the lips.

“I think, my friend, that we must look at the facts not as they
seem, but as they must be. Consider the housekeeper. She arrives,
she stays three weeks, she vanishes. No one at the station sees
her arrive. No one sees her leave. She is a phantom, a shadow.
And the wife, the beautiful Zoe Havering, she is the one who
engages her, who tells us what she said, who was with her when the
shot was fired. Does that not suggest something to you?”

“You mean,” I gasped, “that they were in it together? That Mrs.
Middleton was a plant?”

“It suggests,” Poirot said softly, “that perhaps we should ask if
Mrs. Middleton ever existed at all.”

“_Mon ami_,” he said, “I am glad to see you. I have missed you,
yes, I have missed you. You have done your best, and I have
nothing to complain of in your reports. You have told me everything
I wanted to know, and I have arrived at the truth.”

“You mean you know who killed Harrington Pace?”

“I do.”

“Then it was the housekeeper?”

“There was no housekeeper.”

“But I saw her myself!”

“You saw a woman, yes. But she was not a housekeeper. She was
not Mrs. Middleton.”

“Then who was she?”

“She was Zoe Havering.”

I stared at him in amazement.

“But, Poirot, that is impossible! I saw them both together!”

“Did you, Hastings? Think! You saw Mrs. Havering in a
flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured leather hat. You saw
the housekeeper in a black dress, a white apron, and a cap. You
never saw them both at the same time. When you were talking to the
housekeeper, where was Mrs. Havering?”

“She was upstairs.”

“And when you were talking to Mrs. Havering, where was the
housekeeper?”

“She had gone to fetch her mistress.”

“Exactly. It is an old trick, but it nearly always succeeds. A
clever actress like Zoe Carrisbrook would find no difficulty in
sustaining two such parts. A little make-up, a change of voice,
and the thing is done.”

“But the shot? They were both in the hall when the shot was fired!”

“The housekeeper said so. But was she? Remember, there is only
her word for it. And as for the shot—a gramophone record, a
time-fuse—there are a dozen ways in which it could have been
arranged.”

“But the man with the black beard? Mrs. Middleton saw him.”

“Mrs. Middleton said she saw him. And Zoe Havering said she heard
his voice. But did anyone else see or hear him? No. He was a
myth, Hastings, a myth invented to account for the murder.”

“Then you think that Roger Havering——”

“Was the murderer? No, Hastings. He was in London. But he was
the accomplice. It was he who took the revolver to London and
left it where it would be found, to provide an alibi for himself
and to suggest a mysterious murderer from outside. He and his
wife between them planned the whole thing. They were hard up, and
Harrington Pace was rich. With him out of the way, they would
inherit his fortune.”

“But the motive? Why should they kill him now?”

“Because he was going to alter his will. He had found out
something—perhaps about that old cheque of Roger’s—and he was
going to disinherit him. They had to act quickly.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed. “And yet, it all fits in. But
how did you suspect Mrs. Havering?”

“Because of the clothes, Hastings. You described them so
vividly. A flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured leather
hat! No woman would wear such clothes in a house where a murder
had just been committed—unless she wanted to create a vivid
impression, to make it impossible for anyone to mistake her for
the housekeeper. It was a piece of over-acting, and it gave her
away.”

“And the housekeeper’s disappearance?”

“That was the final proof. She had served her purpose, and she
had to vanish. Zoe Havering simply ‘disappeared’ her.”

“What are you going to do?” I asked. “Are you going to tell Japp?”

Poirot smiled.

“I have already told him. He is on his way to Hunter’s Lodge now.
I think he will find that the Haverings have already left, but
he will catch them sooner or later. They have been clever, but
they have not been clever enough for Hercule Poirot.”

And with a little sigh of satisfaction, he returned to his tisane.

“Well, _mon ami_, and how did you like it?”

“Not at all. I’ve never seen a more baffling case.”

“Everything is so simple if one only looks at it the right way.
You see, I have had a great advantage over you, Hastings. I have
not been on the spot. I have been able to look at the facts as a
whole. And what did I see? First, that a man was murdered. Second,
that the murderer was seen by two people. Third, that those two
people were the only people in the house at the time. Fourth, that
the murderer escaped. Fifth, that he was never seen by any one
outside the house. Now, what does that suggest?”

“That he had a car waiting,” I suggested.

“No, no! Think again! What is the most remarkable thing about this
case?”

“The disappearance of the housekeeper?”

“Exactly. Now, why should she disappear? Only because she was
afraid of the police. And why should she be afraid of the police?
Because she was an accomplice. But what was her part? To admit
the murderer. And how could she do that? Only by knowing him.
But if she knew him, she must have seen him before. And if she
had seen him before, she would have known he was not an American
friend of Mr. Pace’s. Therefore, she must have been in the plot.
But if she were in the plot, why should she have been so
extraordinarily foolish as to stay on after the murder? She could
have gone then and there. No, there is something wrong there. Let
us look at it from another point of view. Suppose there was no
murderer?”

“But the man was shot!”

“I know. But suppose there was no _outside_ murderer. Suppose the
murderer was someone in the house. There were only two people in
the house—the wife and the housekeeper. But they were together
when the shot was fired. Therefore, neither of them could have
fired it. But suppose there was only _one_ person in the house?”

“But I saw them both!” I cried.

“Did you? Think, Hastings, think! You saw Mrs. Havering. Did you
see the housekeeper?”

“Well, she opened the door to me.”

“And what was she like?”

“A middle-aged woman in black.”

“Exactly. A middle-aged woman in black. And Mrs. Havering? A
young woman in a flame-coloured jumper. Now, suppose that Mrs.
Havering and the housekeeper were one and the same person?”

“But, Poirot, I saw them both!”

“Did you see them both at the same time? No. One woman opened the
door to you. You asked for the other. She went upstairs and
reappeared as the other. It is an old trick, but a very effective
