one. A little grey hair, a touch of make-up, a change of clothes—it
is easily done. And you, my friend, are so easily deceived!”

“But the shot? They were together when the shot was fired.”

“Were they? The housekeeper said so. But was there any one to
corroborate her? No. Mrs. Havering said so. But was there any one
to corroborate her? No. The only other person in the house was
dead. And the shot? A simple matter of a time-fuse, or even a
string attached to the trigger. Or perhaps there was no shot at
all at that moment. Perhaps the shot you heard was fired by Mrs.
Havering herself after she had run out into the hall.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“A myth, my friend! A creation of Mrs. Havering’s imagination.
She and her husband had planned it all out. He was to go to London
to provide an alibi. She was to stay behind and do the deed.
The 'housekeeper' was a master stroke. It provided a witness who
didn't exist. And the revolver? A stroke of genius! To have it
found in Ealing, where it could be easily traced to them, and yet
where it was impossible for either of them to have placed it.
But they forgot one thing—the 'housekeeper' would have to
disappear. And once she had disappeared, the whole thing fell to
pieces.”

“But why did they do it?”

“Money, my friend, money! The old story. Harrington Pace was a
rich man, and Roger Havering was his heir. They couldn't wait
any longer. It was a cold-blooded, calculated murder.”

“And Japp? Does he know?”

“I have already communicated with him. He is on his way to
Derbyshire now to arrest the Hon. Mrs. Havering. As for the husband,
I think we shall find him in London.”

Poirot leaned back in his chair and smiled.

“A very pretty case, Hastings, very pretty indeed. It is a pity I
was not there to see it for myself. But even from my bed, you see,
the little grey cells were able to solve the mystery.”

“Well, Hastings, my friend, I trust you have been a good boy, and
done exactly as I told you. You’ve brought me your notes? That’s
right.”

He was silent for a few minutes after he had read them through.

“It is as I thought,” he said at last. “A very pretty little case.
But what a pity that you are not more of an artist, Hastings! Your
photographs of the interior were—as I told you—deplorable.”

“I don’t see that that has anything to do with it,” I replied
stiffly. “I suppose you think you have solved the mystery?”

“I have.”

“And the murderer?”

“Is Harrington Pace.”

I stared.

“But Harrington Pace is the man who was murdered!”

“Exactly. That is the point. He is murdered. Therefore he is not
the murderer. And yet he _is_ the murderer. You follow me? No?
I see you do not.”

“You are talking in riddles, Poirot.”

“It is very simple. Who was the last person to see Harrington Pace
alive?”

“Mrs. Havering and the housekeeper.”

“Exactly. And who saw the murderer?”

“The housekeeper. Mrs. Havering only heard his voice.”

“Wait. Let us see. We have a housekeeper who is not a housekeeper.
We have a murderer who is not a murderer. We have a body that is
a body. Is it not so?”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“Listen, then. The housekeeper was not a housekeeper. She was—who
was she, Hastings?”

“I’ve no idea.”

“She was Zoe Havering!”

I stared at him in amazement.

“But Zoe Havering was in the hall with her when the shot was fired!”

“Was she? Who says so? The housekeeper. And who was the
housekeeper? Zoe Havering. You see? There was no housekeeper.
There was only Zoe Havering—playing two parts.”

“But the clothes—the appearance——”

“A very simple disguise. A black silk dress, a touch of grey in
the hair, a quiet, middle-aged manner. You yourself said she was
a good actress. As for the description—you provided it yourself,
Hastings! You saw a middle-aged woman in black. When you saw the
younger woman, she was in a flame-coloured jumper and a
flame-coloured hat. The contrast was so great that it never
occurred to you that they were one and the same person.”

“But the shot? They were both in the hall when the shot was fired.”

“Again—who says so? The housekeeper. There was no one else there.
Zoe Havering—as the housekeeper—goes to the gun-room, fires the
shot, and then runs into the hall, and—as herself—cries out that
she has heard a shot! A few minutes later, she is the housekeeper
again, telling the story to the police.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“There was no man with the black beard. He was a myth—invented
by the 'housekeeper' to provide a murderer.”

“But the revolver found at Ealing?”

“A very clever touch, that. It was intended to lead the police
away from the house. Roger Havering took it to London with him and
left it where it would be found. He, of course, was the accomplice.
He knew all about it. He had to be in London to provide an alibi.
But he knew that his wife was going to murder his uncle.”

“But why? What was the motive?”

“Money, my friend, money! Harrington Pace was a very rich man.
And Roger Havering was his heir. But Harrington Pace was also a
very 'close' man. He wouldn’t part with his money during his
lifetime. And the Haverings were in debt. They couldn't wait.
So they decided to—anticipate—the inheritance.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed.

“It is very simple,” Poirot replied. “The only thing that
puzzled me was the housekeeper. Why should a housekeeper, who had
only been in the house three weeks, and who had ‘splendid
references,’ suddenly disappear? The answer was obvious. Because
she didn't exist! She was a part of the plot. And once I had
realized that, the rest was easy.”

“But how did you know it was Zoe Havering?”

“Because, my friend, you told me! You described her as a very
handsome young woman, with a 'flame-coloured jumper' and a
'flame-coloured hat.' And then you described the housekeeper as a
'middle-aged woman in black.' The contrast was too great,
Hastings—too great! It was the 'flame-colour' that gave her away.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s a most extraordinary case.”

“It is a very pretty little case,” Poirot agreed. “And now, if
you will be so good as to hand me that bottle of tisane... I think
I feel a little better.”

“_Mon ami_ Hastings! But how glad I am to see you. Veritably I have
for you a great affection. And you have enjoyed yourself? You have
run to and fro with the good Japp? You have interrogated and
investigated to your heart’s content?”

“Poirot,” I cried, “the thing’s a dark mystery! It will never be
solved.”

“It is true that we are not likely to cover ourselves with glory
over it.”

“No, indeed. It’s a hard nut to crack.”

“Oh, as far as that goes, I am very good at cracking the nuts! A
veritable squirrel! It is not that which embarrasses me. I know
well enough who killed Mr. Harrington Pace.”

“You know? How did you find out?”

“By sitting here and thinking, _mon ami_. I have not yet been out
of the house. It is a very simple case, although the circumstances
rendered it a little difficult to prove. For example, did it not
strike you as a very singular thing that a man should be shot by
an American who spoke like himself? One would expect his
associates to be of his own nationality, certainly, but why should
he be murdered by one of them? And then there was the mystery of
the housekeeper. Why should she run away? She had no reason to
fear the police, had she?”

“Evidently she had, or she wouldn't have gone.”

“But she had no reason, Hastings. She had a perfect alibi! She
was in the hall with Mrs. Havering when the shot was fired.”

“Then why——”

“Because she did not exist!”

I stared at him.

“She did not exist? But I saw her myself!”

“You saw a middle-aged woman in black, with a touch of white at
her throat and wrists, and a cap on her head. Her hair was grey,
was it not? And she wore glasses?”

“Yes.”

“And you only saw her in the dimly-lighted hall? And for a very
few minutes?”

“That is true.”

“And it was the same with the inspector? He only saw her for a
few minutes in the hall?”

“Yes.”

“Then it is quite simple. There was no Mrs. Middleton. There was
only—Mrs. Havering!”

“Mrs. Havering! But I saw her too! She came down the stairs in a
flame-coloured jumper!”

“After you had been waiting for some minutes, is it not so?
Sufficiently long for a quick-change artist! Zoe Havering was an
actress, remember. It was a most clever and daring idea. She plays
the two parts, the housekeeper and the mistress. No wonder they
were never seen together!”

“But the shot? We both heard the shot when they were together in
the hall!”

“A very simple trick, Hastings. A time-fuse—or even a
slow-burning candle. It is an old device, but often effective.
And while the 'housekeeper' and the mistress are 'together' in the
hall, the revolver is fired in the gun-room by this means. Mrs.
Havering then sends the 'housekeeper' for the police, and, once
round the corner, Mrs. Middleton disappears, and Mrs. Havering
returns to the house, to be found there by the police when they
arrive. A few minutes would be enough for the change.”

“And the man with the black beard?”

“Was Mr. Havering, of course. He arrives by the 6.15, but gets out
at the first station, and returns to Hunter’s Lodge by car. He
enters the gun-room, and is seen to do so by the 'housekeeper'
(his wife). He then changes his clothes, and gets back to the
station in time to catch the train to London. The revolver he
throws out of the window as the train passes Haven Green. A very
neatly-planned crime, Hastings!”

“But why should they want to kill the poor old man?”

“Money, my friend, money! Havering was his uncle's heir, and he
was in debt. A very common motive, alas!”

“It seems incredible!” I murmured.

“Not at all. The only thing that was a little difficult was the
housekeeper’s disappearance. But even that was simple enough.
She just—vanished!”

“But what are you going to do, Poirot? You must tell Japp!”

“I have already done so, Hastings. But I fear it will be difficult
to prove. Still, I have done my part. The rest is with the police.”

I sat in silence, marvelling at the brilliant mind of my little
friend. Once again he had triumphed, even from a bed of sickness!

“And now, Hastings,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye, “if
you will be so good as to hand me that bottle of medicine—the one
with the red label—I think I will take a little more of it. It
has a most excellent effect upon the brain!”

I did as he requested, and as I watched him sipping the noxious
mixture, I could not help feeling a pang of regret that such a
brilliant career should be so nearly at an end. But Poirot only
smiled.

“Do not distress yourself, _mon ami_,” he said. “I have still many
years of usefulness before me. And who knows? Perhaps some day I
shall even find a case that is worthy of my powers!”

And with that he settled himself back among his pillows, a look
of supreme contentment upon his face.

“My friend, it was simplicity itself. The solution lay in the very
heart of the facts you provided. You see, but you do not observe.
You told me that Mr. Havering was in London, verified by the train
times. You told me the housekeeper and Mrs. Havering heard the shot
together. Thus, they both had alibis. But then, we have the
disappearance of the housekeeper. Why does a 'nice, quiet woman'
vanish? Because she does not exist, Hastings!”

“By the use of my little grey cells, my friend. They are not
affected by _la grippe_. You should try to use yours, Hastings.
Now, tell me, who killed this poor American?”

“The man with the black beard,” I said promptly.

“And where is this man with the black beard?”

“That we don’t know. He must have been an enemy of Mr. Pace’s.”

“A very convenient enemy! He arrives, he kills, he vanishes—and
no one sees him! Not a soul! The station-master, the porters, the
people in the village—no one has seen this mysterious stranger.”

“He might have come in a car.”

“Exactly. He might have come in a car. But did he?”

“Well, someone must have killed the man.”

“I quite agree. Someone did kill him. But who?”

“If it wasn’t the man with the black beard, it must have been——”

“Who, Hastings?”

“Not—not Havering?”

“Havering was in the 6.15 train, and that was confirmed. He was
not in Derbyshire at nine o’clock.”

“Then it must have been the housekeeper—Mrs. Middleton?”

“A middle-aged woman, I think you said? Was it she who shot him
from behind with a heavy revolver?”

“It doesn’t seem likely.”

“It is more than unlikely—it is impossible. And yet she vanishes.
Why does she vanish?”

“Because she was an accomplice.”

“An accomplice of whom?”

“Of the man with the black beard.”

“But we have already seen that there was no man with a black beard!”

“Then what is the explanation?”

Poirot leaned back and closed his eyes.

“It is all so very simple,” he murmured. “So very simple. There
is only one person who could have killed Harrington Pace. It was
a person who was in the house at the time, a person who had a
motive, a person who could have disposed of the revolver in
London.”

“You mean—Mrs. Havering?”

“Exactly. Mrs. Havering.”

“But the housekeeper was with her!”

“Was she? Was she, Hastings? That is the point. Who saw the
housekeeper? You? No. Japp? No. Only the Haverings and each other.
And why did the housekeeper vanish? Because she never existed!”

“But I saw her myself!” I cried. “She opened the door to me.”

Poirot shook his head.

“You saw a middle-aged woman in black. You did not see Mrs.
Middleton. You saw Mrs. Havering, Hastings!”

“Mrs. Havering? But she was a young woman—a girl!”

“A young woman who had been an actress, remember. A few touches
of make-up, a middle-aged wig, a black dress—and there is your
Mrs. Middleton! She opens the door to you, she tells you her
story, then she goes upstairs, changes her clothes, and comes down
as the charming Mrs. Havering!”

“But the shot? We both heard the shot when she was in the hall!”

“Did you? Are you sure? Or did you only hear what you expected to
hear? A shot can be fired by a simple mechanical device. A clock,
a string—it is easily arranged. And the revolver in London?
Havering took it with him and dropped it over the railings at
Ealing. He had his alibi, and his wife had hers—provided by the
mysterious Mrs. Middleton. It was a clever plot, Hastings, very
clever. But they made one mistake. They should not have sent for
Hercule Poirot!”

I sat in silence, amazed by the simplicity of it all.

“And what are you going to do?” I asked at last.

“I have already told Japp. He is on his way to arrest them now.”

Poirot sighed and picked up his cup of tisane.

“It is a pity,” he murmured. “She was a very handsome woman. But
murder, Hastings—murder is not to be permitted. Not even by the
most charming of women!”

“By my little grey cells, Hastings! I have used them, as I always
do, and they have not failed me. The solution was as clear as
daylight, once one looked at it from the right point of view. It
is a simple matter, after all.”

“But who was it? Who was the black-bearded man?”

“There was no black-bearded man, Hastings! That was the first point
to realize. It was a most ingenious and well-thought-out plan. It
was a masterly stroke of genius, that! The cleverness of it lay
in its simplicity. Let us examine the facts. Harrington Pace is
found dead in the gun-room. A man with a black beard was seen to
enter the house by the housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton. Mrs. Havering
and the housekeeper both hear the shot, and find the gun-room door
locked on the inside. They go round to the window, and find the
body. The murderer has disappeared. Now, what do we know about
this Mrs. Middleton? We know that she was engaged by Mrs. Havering,
but that the Agency had never heard of her. We know that she
arrived at Hunter’s Lodge in a mysterious manner, and that she
vanished equally mysteriously. We know that she and her mistress
were together when the shot was fired. Therefore, neither of them
could have committed the murder. Is not that so?”

“Yes,” I agreed.

“But suppose, Hastings, that there was no Mrs. Middleton?”

“No Mrs. Middleton? But I saw her myself!”

“You saw a middle-aged woman in black, with a quiet, respectable
manner. Did you see her and Mrs. Havering together?”

“No,” I admitted, “now I come to think of it, I didn’t.”

“Exactly! The housekeeper was Mrs. Havering herself! A little
disguise, a touch of make-up, a change of voice—and the thing was
done! It was a stroke of genius, as I said. She had already
arranged with her husband that he should go to London, and that
she should stay behind. She knew that he would be away, and that
she would be alone in the house with her uncle. It was the perfect
opportunity.”

“But the shot? We both heard it!”

“A simple matter of a time-fuse, or some such device. Or perhaps
she fired it herself, before she came out into the hall. The
important thing was to create an alibi for herself, and she did it
by inventing the mysterious Mrs. Middleton.”

“But the black-bearded man? Who was he?”

“He was also an invention, Hastings! A myth! There was no such
person. Mrs. Havering simply told the story of his arrival, and
the housekeeper (who was herself) confirmed it. It was a very
cleverly-laid plan, and it nearly succeeded.”

“But how did you find out, Poirot?”

“By the description you gave me of the clothes they wore, Hastings!
You mentioned that Mrs. Havering was wearing a flame-coloured
jumper and a flame-coloured hat. Now, a woman who had just
undergone such a terrible experience would hardly be thinking of
her clothes, would she? She would be in a state of collapse. But
Mrs. Havering was perfectly calm and collected. She had even had
the presence of mind to change her clothes! That was the first
clue. And then there was the matter of the housekeeper’s arrival.
No one had seen her. That was very significant. And finally, there
was the fact that the Agency had never heard of her. It all pointed
to one conclusion.”

“But what about the revolver? It was found in Ealing.”

“That was the husband’s part in the business. He took it with him
to London, and disposed of it there. He wanted to make it appear
that the murderer had fled to London. It was all part of the plan.”

“And the motive?”

“Money, of course! Harrington Pace was a very wealthy man, and
Roger Havering was his heir. They were in desperate need of money,
and they saw a way to get it. It was a cold-blooded and
premeditated murder.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed.

“It is the truth, Hastings! And now, if you will be so good as to
hand me my tisane, I think I will try to get a little sleep. This
influenza is very exhausting.”

I did as he requested, and as I left the room, I couldn't help
marvelling at the extraordinary powers of my little friend. Once
again, he had triumphed where others had failed. The mystery of
Hunter’s Lodge was solved.

“By my little grey cells, Hastings. I sit here and I think. And
I have the advantage that I am not blinded by the personages
themselves. I see only the facts. For instance, the housekeeper.
Why does she disappear? Because she is a myth. She does not exist.
She is a part of the comedy. We have two women at Hunter’s Lodge,
Mrs. Havering and Mrs. Middleton. But has anyone else seen them
both together? No. Only when the shot was fired, which was to
establish an alibi. But who fired the shot? Not the man with the
black beard—he is another myth. No, the shot was fired by a
mechanical device—a simple matter of a string and a trigger. The
two women were one and the same—Mrs. Havering herself!”

“Your illuminating answers to my wires supplied me with the truth.
See here, Hastings, let us examine the facts methodically and in
order. Mr. Harrington Pace is a man with a considerable fortune
which at his death will doubtless pass to his nephew. Point No. 1.
His nephew is known to be desperately hard up. Point No. 2. His
nephew is also known to be—shall we say a man of rather loose
moral fibre? Point No. 3.”

“But Roger Havering is proved to have journeyed straight up to
London.”

“Precisely. He has what you call a cast-iron alibi. But wait. Let
us look at the case from a different angle. We have a visitor,
an American with a black beard. He is seen only by the
housekeeper. He is never seen again. We have a housekeeper who is
likewise never seen again. Is it not a little remarkable? Two
people, both of whom vanish into thin air! Is it possible, my
friend, that they were one and the same person? That the
mysterious American and the mysterious housekeeper were both
portrayed by the same actor?”

“But Poirot,” I exclaimed, “the housekeeper was a woman!”

“Was she? You saw her, Hastings. Japp saw her. Did either of you
really look at her? A middle-aged woman in a black dress, a
widow’s cap, a touch of white at the throat and wrists—what is
easier to impersonate? A man of Roger Havering’s build, with a
fairly high-pitched voice, could play the part to perfection. He
arrives at Hunter’s Lodge in the character of the new
housekeeper, having already, through his wife, provided himself
with the necessary credentials from a reputable agency.”

“But the shot!” I cried. “Mrs. Havering and the housekeeper were
together in the hall when the shot was fired!”

Poirot smiled, that small, feline smile that usually preceded his
most devastating revelations. “Were they, Hastings? Or did Mrs.
Havering merely *say* they were? Remember, there were no other
witnesses. The only person who could confirm the housekeeper’s
presence was the mistress of the house—his accomplice.”

“Granted. But who saw him arrive in London? Nobody! It was 10.30
before he appeared at his club. He might have reached town by the
10.30. It is true that he was seen to leave by the 6.15 from Elmer’s
Dale. But what was to prevent him from getting out at the first
station and returning to Hunter’s Lodge in a car? He would then
have had time to commit the murder and get back to London by the
later train.”

“But the housekeeper?”

“Ah, yes, the housekeeper. She is the crux of the whole thing.
What did you tell me of her? She was a middle-aged woman, was she
not? And what did you tell me of Mrs. Havering? That she was an
actress. Don’t you see, Hastings? There was no housekeeper. Mrs.
Havering _was_ the housekeeper!”

“But, Poirot, I saw them both!”

“Did you see them together?”

“Why, no, I didn’t. I see what you mean. Mrs. Havering could have
doubled the parts.”

“Precisely. It would be a simple matter for an actress of her
ability. A wig, a little make-up, a change of voice—and the deed
is done! She and her husband planned it between them. He provided
the alibi, she provided the witness. They knew that a housekeeper
would be expected, so they created one. The 'Mrs. Middleton' who
was seen by you was Mrs. Havering in disguise.”

“But the black-bearded man?”

“A myth, my friend. A creature of their imagination. There was no
black-bearded man. It was Mrs. Havering herself who shot her uncle,
after her husband had left for London. Then she assumed the
disguise of the housekeeper, and waited for the police to arrive.
The revolver was later disposed of in London by Roger Havering.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed.

“It is the only explanation that fits all the facts. And now, if
you will excuse me, I think I will have another cup of that
excellent tisane.”

And Poirot, with a smile of satisfaction, settled back into his
pillows.

“He did indeed. But we have No. 4. His wife. She remains on the
spot. She is a woman of great intelligence. She has been on the
stage. Point No. 5. This woman, of whom we have no previous
record, is chosen as housekeeper. Point No. 6. This woman, after
the murder, vanishes into thin air. Point No. 7. Why? Because she
never existed! Mrs. Middleton was Mrs. Havering in a clever
disguise!”

“Poirot!” I gasped. “But they were both seen together by the
constable who came from Elmer’s Dale!”

“No, no, Hastings. That is where you are wrong. They were seen
together by no one but each other. It was Mrs. Middleton who
described the murderer; it was Mrs. Havering who confirmed her
story. When the police arrived, they saw Mrs. Havering. They never
saw Mrs. Middleton. She was ‘resting’ or ‘out on an errand.’ A
very little makeup, a touch of grey in the hair, a padded waistline,
and the change from the flame-coloured jumper to the black
housekeeper’s dress is easily made.”

“But the shot? They both heard it!”

“Exactly. Mrs. Havering, as the housekeeper, goes to the gun-room.
She and the uncle are alone. She shoots him. Then she runs into
the hall, and, as herself, meets the ‘housekeeper’—that is, she
simply cries out as though she were speaking to someone. The
revolver? She has it in her pocket. Later she walks to the village
and drops it where it will be found in London, to provide a clue
to the American ‘friend.’ Or, better still, she gives it to her
husband when he leaves for London at 6.15.”

“But, Poirot, he left before the murder!”

“Did he? Or did he? We have only the word of the two women. What
if the murder was committed earlier? What if the 6.15 train
carried not only Roger Havering but also the weapon? Or what if
the ‘visitor’ was indeed Roger Havering himself, returning in
secret? No, the simplest explanation is usually the best. The
revolver found in London was a plant. The black-bearded man was
a myth.”

“But Japp? Japp will never believe this!”

“Japp is already beginning to suspect. But there is a difficulty.
Evidence! We have no evidence. We have only my theory. And the
Haverings are clever. They have covered their tracks well.”

“Then they will get away with it?”

Poirot’s eyes flashed.

“Perhaps. But they have to deal with Hercule Poirot! I may not
have the evidence to hang them, but I have the wit to see through
them. And now, _mon ami_, let us have some more of that excellent
tisane. It is good for the chest, and it warms the heart!”

“Exactly. He is also proved to have arrived there. But did he? He
travelled in a first-class carriage. It would be quite easy for
him to have got out of the train at the first station it stopped
at, and to have caught a return train to Elmer’s Dale. But it
would have been much simpler for him to have had an accomplice.”

“An accomplice? Mrs. Middleton?”

“_Précisément_! We will come to that in a moment. But first let us
consider the mysterious visitor. Who was he? An American, with a
black beard. Now, who was he? Did he really exist at all? I think
not. The only people who saw him were the housekeeper and Mrs.
Havering. Mrs. Havering is a very clever woman, and a very
beautiful one. She is also a very good actress. She was once Zoe
Carrisbrook, don’t forget that. But she is not a very good
housekeeper. She does not know how to engage a housekeeper. She
did not even tell the Agency which of the women they sent she had
engaged. But the Agency did send some women. And Mrs. Havering
paid the engagement fee. Now, why did she not tell them? Simply
because she did not engage any of them! She wanted a housekeeper,
but she wanted a particular kind of housekeeper. She wanted a woman
who would do exactly as she was told. She wanted a woman who would
be a witness to a murder! And that woman had to be someone she
could trust. Who better than herself? For she was Mrs. Middleton!
She could not be in two places at once, you will say. But could
she not? What was to prevent her from being the housekeeper in the
morning and Mrs. Havering in the afternoon? A change of dress, a
wig, a little makeup—and the thing was done! She could even have
been both at the same time, if she was careful. And she was very
careful. She never appeared as Mrs. Havering when she was Mrs.
Middleton, and vice versa. And when the murder was committed, she
was both of them! She was the housekeeper who showed the visitor
into the gun-room, and she was the mistress who heard the shot and
ran to the door with the housekeeper!”

I stared at him in amazement.

“But—the visitor? Who was the visitor?”

“Precisely. He has an alibi. But who else have we? There is Mrs.
Havering—and the housekeeper. Each of these women is the other’s
alibi. If one of them killed him, the other must have been an
accomplice. Now, let us consider the housekeeper. She is
represented to us as a middle-aged, respectable woman. She is
suddenly engaged by Mrs. Havering. No one else has seen her. She
vanishes. She is a myth—a Mrs. Harris! Where did she come from?
Where did she go? She never existed. She was Zoe Havering in a
wig and a touch of make-up!”

“But, Poirot,” I cried, “they were both seen together in the hall
by the dead man’s nephew!”

“No, no! Think, Hastings. The nephew was in London. It was the
dead man’s _uncle_ who saw them—no, he was in the gun-room. It
was the _nephew’s wife_ and the _housekeeper_ who were together.
Wait! I see your confusion. Let us be precise. Who saw the
housekeeper? Only three people. Mr. Pace—who is dead. Roger
Havering—who arrived when she had already disappeared. And Zoe
Havering—who _was_ the housekeeper!”

“But Japp saw her!” I protested. “He spoke to her!”

Poirot shook his head sadly. “No, Hastings. Japp saw a woman in
black who called herself the housekeeper. But he saw her _after_
the murder. He saw her when Zoe Havering had already had time to
change her clothes. The woman he saw was indeed Zoe Havering,
playing a part. But the woman who opened the door to the 'American'
visitor, the woman who screamed in the hall—that woman was also
Zoe Havering. There was never any other woman in the house.”

“But the visitor? The man with the black beard?”

“A very simple disguise for Roger Havering! He did not go to London
on the 6.15. He went to the station, yes—he was seen there. But he
did not get on the train. He hid, waited for nightfall, put on a
false beard and a light overcoat, and returned to the house. His
wife let him in. He went to the gun-room, shot his uncle, handed
the pistol to his wife, and then—this is the clever part—he
literally _ran_ to London! Not on his feet, no. He had a car
stashed nearby. He drove like the wind to a suburban station—Ealing,
to be exact—tossed the weapon over a fence, and caught a local
train into the city. He arrived at his club a little late, perhaps,
but with a perfect alibi. While he was racing south, his wife was
playing two parts at Hunter's Lodge: the grieving niece and the
terrified housekeeper.”

“_Précisément_—and therefore, as Mr. Havering left Elmer’s Dale at
6.15, and since Mr. Pace cannot have been killed before he left,
or the doctor would have spotted the time of the crime as being
given wrongly when he examined the body, we conclude quite rightly,
that Mr. Havering did not shoot his uncle. But there is a Mrs.
Havering, Hastings.”

“Impossible! The housekeeper was with her when the shot was fired.”

“Ah, yes, the housekeeper. But she has disappeared.”

“She will be found.”

“I think not. There is something peculiarly elusive about that
housekeeper, don’t you think so, Hastings? It struck me at once.”

“She played her part, I suppose, and then got out in the nick of
time.”

“And what was her part?”

“Well, presumably to admit her confederate, the black-bearded man.”

“Ah, yes, the black-bearded man! That reminds me of a little story.
It was about a certain young actor who was very clever at
make-up. He could play a variety of parts. He could be a young man,
or an old man, or a middle-aged man with a black beard. He could
be anything he chose.”

“But you are not suggesting that Zoe Havering is a man, Poirot?”

“No, no, Hastings. That would be a little too much even for my
imagination. But there is another actress in our story. You your-
self reminded me of her. ‘The girl who used to act at the
Frivolity—Zoe Carrisbrook.’ A very clever young woman, I should
imagine.”

“You mean she——?”

“Wait a moment, Hastings. Let us look at it from another point of
view. There is a man called Harrington Pace, a rich man, a man
without any near relations except his nephew. Suppose that nephew
to be a man of some resource and with a wife who is an actress.
Suppose they want money, and want it badly. What would be the
simplest way of getting it?”

“By killing the uncle, I suppose.”

“Exactly. But then there is the question of the alibi. The nephew
must be in London when the murder is committed. But who is to
commit the murder? The wife? But she also must have an alibi.
She must be seen by some reliable witness at the time the shot
is fired.”

“The housekeeper!” I cried. “But she was the confederate!”

“Was she? Was there ever such a person as the housekeeper?”

“But I saw her myself!”

“Did you, Hastings? Are you sure?”

“Of course I did. She opened the door to me.”

“And what was she like?”

“A middle-aged woman, Poirot. Quite ordinary.”

“And when did you see Mrs. Havering?”

“A few minutes later.”

“And what was she wearing?”

“A flame-coloured jumper and a little hat of flame-coloured leather.”

“And what was the housekeeper wearing?”

“Black, Poirot. Quite ordinary black.”

“And you did not see them together?”

“No—o. Mrs. Havering was upstairs when I arrived.”

“And the housekeeper went to fetch her?”

“Yes.”

“And then Mrs. Havering came down?”

“Yes.”

“And what happened to the housekeeper?”

“She—she went back to the kitchen, I suppose.”

“Did you see her again?”

“No.”

“And Japp? Did he see them together?”

“No. He saw the housekeeper first, and then Mrs. Havering.”

“Exactly. Don’t you see, Hastings? There was no housekeeper. There
was only Zoe Havering! A quick change of costume, a little
make-up—it was easily done for a clever actress. She is the
housekeeper who admits the black-bearded man—who is, of course,
her husband!”

“But Roger Havering was in London!”

“Was he? Are you sure of that, Hastings? He was seen to leave by
the 6.15 train. But was he seen to arrive in London? No. He could
easily have got out at the first station, jumped into a waiting
car, driven back to Hunter’s Lodge, committed the murder, and
then driven to some station near London where he could catch a
local train and arrive at his club at the time he said. The
revolver found at Ealing? A very clever touch that! It was
intended to lead the police to think that the murderer had
escaped to London.”

“But the housekeeper’s box? It was full of clothes.”

“Zoe Havering’s old clothes, no doubt. She would have plenty of
them. A few minutes’ work would suffice to pack a box and leave
it behind.”

“It seems incredible,” I murmured. “And yet—it would explain
everything.”

“Of course it would. It is the only explanation that fits all the
facts. And now, Hastings, if you will be so good as to ring the
bell, I think I could enjoy a little more of that excellent tisane
of yours. After all, I have not died this time!”

“There again, Hastings, the black-bearded man was a very elusive
creature. No one but Mrs. Middleton ever saw him. Mrs. Havering
only heard voices. And why did the housekeeper never go to the
Agency in London? Because she was never there. She was a woman
with a past, no doubt. But what was her past? And how was she
recommended to Mrs. Havering? Why, Mrs. Havering herself says she
engaged her on the spot from the Agency. But when I inquired at
the Agency I found that Mrs. Havering had omitted to mention which
woman she had selected. Now what does that suggest?”

I stared at him.

“You mean that Mrs. Havering herself——”

“Just so. Zoe Havering is a clever woman, and an actress to boot.
She was Zoe Carrisbrook, you remember? What more easy than for her
to play the part of the housekeeper as well as her own? She had
only to change her clothes and put on a wig. And that was why she
was so careful to be out of the room when the housekeeper was
supposed to be there, and vice versa. It was she who admitted the
black-bearded man, and it was she who shot her uncle while the
housekeeper was supposed to be in the kitchen.”

“But the housekeeper was with her when the shot was fired!” I
exclaimed. “You are forgetting that.”

“Not at all. There was no housekeeper. There was only Zoe Havering.
She fired the shot, and then ran into the hall, pretending to be
herself, and said that the housekeeper was with her. It was a
daring game, but she played it well.”

“But the black-bearded man? Who was he?”

“There was no black-bearded man. He was a myth, created by Zoe
Havering to divert suspicion. She knew that her husband would be
suspected, and she wanted to provide him with an alibi. And she
succeeded.”

“But how did she get the revolver to London?”

“That was easy. She just posted it to herself, and then went to
London and picked it up. She is a very clever woman, Hastings,
very clever indeed.”

I was silent for a few moments, taking it all in. Then I said:

“But what about the motive? Why did she kill him?”

“For the money, of course. She knew that her husband would inherit
his uncle’s fortune, and she wanted it for herself. She is a
woman who will stop at nothing to get what she wants.”

“And what is to be done now?”

“Nothing. We have no proof. It is only my theory, but I am sure
it is the right one. Zoe Havering has committed the perfect crime,
and she will go scot-free.”

I looked at Poirot in amazement. He seemed almost to admire the
woman’s cleverness.

“But justice must be done!” I cried.

“Justice is not always done in this world, Hastings. Sometimes
the guilty escape, and the innocent suffer. It is the way of the
world.”

And with that he turned back to his book, as if the matter were
closed.

I could not help feeling a sense of disappointment. It seemed so
unfair that such a cold-blooded murderess should go unpunished.
But I knew that Poirot was right. We had no proof, and without
proof we could do nothing.

The case of the Hunter’s Lodge mystery would remain forever
unsolved, a testament to the cunning and daring of one woman.

“But who is the black-bearded man? Why, _mon ami_, he was simply
the other revolver! The murderer, having shot his victim, had only
to make a bolt for it through the window. Now, Hastings, consider
for a moment the question of those two revolvers. Why were there
two? To make it look as though the murderer had brought his own
weapon? But then, why was the other revolver found at Ealing?
Does that not strike you as being a very remarkable fact?”

“I must say it does,” I admitted.

“Now, consider the question of the housekeeper. She was seen only
by Mrs. Havering and—by nobody else! The boy from the garage did
not see her. The station officials did not see her. No one in the
village saw her. She arrives, and is seen by Mrs. Havering. She
is there for three weeks, and then she vanishes. And all the time
she is seen by—whom? By Mrs. Havering!”

“But Japp saw her!” I cried.

“Did he? Think, Hastings, think!”

“Why, of course—no, by Jove, you’re right! Japp only saw her for
a moment in the dimly-lighted hall. And I—I only saw her in the
same way! She wore a cap and a large apron, and she had a muffled
way of speaking.”

“Exactly. Mrs. Havering is a clever woman. She is also a very
good actress. She has been on the stage, remember. She plays the
part of the housekeeper and her own part alternately. It is
extremely simple. The black-bearded man is a myth. There was no
black-bearded man. When the shot was fired, Mrs. Havering was alone
in the gun-room. She then rushes out, and, as the housekeeper,
meets herself—no, that is not possible—she rushes out, and
declares that she and the housekeeper have heard the shot. Then,
as the housekeeper, she goes for the police, while as herself she
remains to keep watch by the body. All she had to do was to change
her clothes—and you will remember she was wearing a flame-coloured
jumper when you saw her. A few moments would suffice for that.”

“But the revolver at Ealing?”

“Ah, that was Roger Havering’s part. He took the revolver with
him to London, and dropped it at Ealing. A very clever touch, that.
It was to provide an alibi for the weapon, as it were. He had his
own alibi, and he wanted one for the revolver too!”

“Then you think—?”

“I do not think—I know! It was a very cleverly-planned murder.
But they made one mistake. They provided themselves with an
imaginary witness. And imaginary witnesses are always a mistake.
They are too perfect. Mrs. Middleton was too perfect a housekeeper.”

“And what are you going to do?”

“I? I shall do nothing. I have no evidence. But I shall send a
little note to Mrs. Havering, just to let her know that Hercule
Poirot is not quite so simple as he looks!”

“And the murderer?”

“The murderer, my friend, is Roger Havering. He it was who
planned the whole thing, and his wife who carried it out. A
very pretty pair! But they will not go unpunished. No, they will
not go unpunished.”

Poirot’s voice was very grave.

“There is such a thing as—justice, Hastings. And though they have
escaped the law, they will not escape—that!”

He was silent for a moment, and then he added, with a return to
his old manner:

“And now, _mon ami_, let us forget the Haverings, and their little
misdeeds. It is time for my tisane. Will you be so good as to
prepare it for me?”

I rose to obey. As I did so, I caught sight of the little paragraph
in _Society Gossip_.

“‘Hercule Poirot—and believe me, girls, he’s some Hercules!’” I
read aloud.

Poirot smiled.

“It is true,” he said. “I am a very great man. But all the same,
it is a good thing that I am not a criminal. I should be very
troublesome to the police!”

“The black-bearded man? Did any one but the housekeeper see him?
Did any one but the housekeeper hear him?”

“Well, Mrs. Havering—she heard the voices, and the shot.”

“The voices—yes. But what did she hear him say? Nothing. She
confessed to you that she didn’t see him. And the housekeeper?
What did she see? A man with a black beard. A man who might have
been—anybody. And what did she hear? An American accent. But,
Hastings, does it not strike you as being a very remarkable thing
that an American should have a black beard? Americans are almost
without exception clean-shaven. Now, if the man had been an
Englishman, or a Frenchman—but an American!”

“It was probably a disguise.”

“_Précisément_. But why a disguise that would at once attract
attention? A clean-shaven man would have passed unnoticed.”

I looked at him, but did not speak.

“Now, another thing. Where did the murderer get the weapon? From
the wall of the gun-room. That means he must have been familiar
with the house. He must have known that the revolvers were there,
and that they were loaded.”

“That is true.”

“Now, we come to the most important point of all. The housekeeper’s
disappearance. If she were an accomplice, why did she not disappear
at once? Why did she wait until the next day? She must have known
that her description would be given to the police, and that her
capture was only a matter of time.”

“I suppose she thought she would be safe for a bit.”

“On the contrary, she was in the greatest danger. Every moment she
remained she was risking discovery.”

“Then why did she stay?”

“Because, Hastings, she _could not_ go. She had to wait for—for
what, do you think?”

“I have no idea.”

“She had to wait for the arrival of—Mrs. Havering!”

I stared at him in amazement.

“But Mrs. Havering was there all the time.”

“Was she? Are you sure? Think, Hastings, think. You saw her for the
first time when you arrived at Hunter’s Lodge. She was wearing a
flame-coloured jumper and a flame-coloured hat. She was a very
handsome and striking-looking woman. But the housekeeper? What was
she like? A middle-aged woman in black. Now, suppose—just suppose
for a moment—that there was no housekeeper?”

“No housekeeper? But I saw her myself!”

“You saw a middle-aged woman in black. But did you see her face?
Was she not always in a dim light? And Mrs. Havering? You saw her
in the hall, you say. Was she not also in a dim light? And her
face? Was it not partially hidden by her hat?”

“But they were both there together! They were in the hall together
when the shot was fired.”

“Were they? Who says so? The housekeeper—and Mrs. Havering. But
did any one else see them? No. Mrs. Middleton was a myth, Hastings.
She never existed. Mrs. Havering played the two parts. It was she
who, disguised as the housekeeper, admitted the non-existent
American. It was she who, in the character of the housekeeper,
afterwards told the story of the murder. It was she who, later,
as Mrs. Havering, confirmed that story.”

“But the shot? Who fired the shot?”

“Mrs. Havering, of course. She had previously moved the revolvers.
She fired the shot, and then, after a suitable interval, she
appeared as the mistress of the house.”

“But the man? The man with the black beard?”

“There was no man. Mrs. Havering simply invented him.”

“And the housekeeper’s disappearance?”

“Mrs. Havering simply ceased to play the part. She was no longer
the housekeeper. She was just—Mrs. Havering.”

“But what about the parcel that was found at Ealing?”

“Ah, that was Roger Havering’s part in the business. He took the
revolver to London with him and dropped it where it was sure to be
found. It was a very clever move, that. It diverted suspicion
from the house.”

“Then they were both in it?”

“Of course. It was a very neatly-planned murder. But they made one
mistake. They forgot that Hercule Poirot is not easily deceived.”

I was silent for a moment, then I said:

“It’s a wonderful theory, Poirot. But can you prove it?”

“I think so. There is the matter of the clothes, you see. Mrs.
Havering’s flame-coloured jumper and hat—very distinctive, you
observe. And the housekeeper’s black dress. They were both in the
house. If my theory is correct, they will be found there still.
I have already communicated my suspicions to Japp, and I have no
doubt that by now he has made a search of the premises.”

The door opened and Japp himself entered. He looked somewhat
disconsolate.

“Well,” said Poirot, “what news?”

“You were right, Monsieur Poirot. We found the black dress and the
wig in a cupboard in Mrs. Havering’s room. But I’m afraid we’re too
late. They’ve both cleared out.”

Poirot nodded.

“I expected as much. They are clever, those two. But they will be
caught, Japp. They will be caught.”

“I hope so,” said Japp fervently. “It’s a cold-blooded business.”

Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells—they do not fail one!”

I could not help but admire his extraordinary perspicacity. It was
indeed a remarkable case, and one that added yet another laurel to
the fame of Hercule Poirot.

But there was one thing that still puzzled me.

“Poirot,” I said, “how did you know that the housekeeper was a
myth?”

“My dear Hastings, it was simple. You told me yourself that she
was a middle-aged woman in black. Now, what is the first thing a
woman does when she wants to disguise herself? She puts on black
clothes and a wig. It is a classic disguise. And then there was
the matter of the American accent. As I told you, Americans do not
have black beards. It was a slip—a very small slip, but enough for
Hercule Poirot!”

I could not help but laugh.

“You are indeed a wonderful man, Poirot!”

“_Mais oui_,” he said, with a twinkle in his eye. “I am indeed!”

“Ah! The black-bearded man! And who was he, I wonder? Did any one
see him? No. He was a myth—a figment of the imagination! It is
very easy to invent a black-bearded man. You have only to say that
he was there. No one can prove he wasn’t.”

“But the housekeeper saw him!”

“And who was the housekeeper? A woman who had never been heard of
at the Agency. A woman who was never seen by any one but Mrs.
Havering. A woman who, if you come to think of it, bore a very
close resemblance to Mrs. Havering—in height and build.”

“Poirot!” I gasped. “You mean that there was no housekeeper?”

“Exactly. It was a most ingenious idea. Mrs. Havering, an actress
of some talent, plays two parts. As the housekeeper, she admits
the mythical man with the black beard. As herself, she is with
the housekeeper when the shot is fired. But there is no shot—at
that moment. The shot was fired before, by Mrs. Havering herself,
after her husband had left for London. Then she waits for the
opportune moment, she and the housekeeper together—that is to say,
Mrs. Havering alone—create the necessary disturbance, she
discharges the pistol, and the trick is done. The ‘housekeeper’
is seen by no one but herself. She then ‘sends’ the housekeeper
for the police. The housekeeper, of course, never returns. She
simply ‘vanishes’—into Mrs. Havering!”

“But the revolver found at Ealing?”

“A very clever touch, that. Mr. Havering, who, of course, is his
wife’s confederate, takes the revolver with him to London and
disposes of it there. He is a man of limited intelligence, or he
would not have left it where it was so easily found.”

“And what of the motive?” I asked.

“Money, my friend, money. The oldest motive in the world. With
Mr. Pace dead, the Haverings inherit everything. They were
desperate, and they took a desperate chance.”

“But can you prove all this?”

“I? No. I am a poor sick man, in my bed. But Japp—he is another
matter. He will find the proofs, now that I have shown him where
to look.”

And indeed, it was Japp’s discovery of a flame-coloured jumper,
hidden away in a box of ‘Mrs. Middleton’s’ clothes, that finally
sealed the fate of the Haverings.

As Poirot had said, it was a very simple case after all.

“Oh, no, that was not her part! Her part was what you have just
mentioned, to provide an alibi for Mrs. Havering at the moment the
shot was fired. And no one will ever find her, _mon ami_, because
she does not exist! ‘There’s no sech person,’ as your so great
Shakespeare says.”

“It was Dickens,” I murmured, unable to suppress a smile. “But what
do you mean, Poirot?”

“I mean that ‘Mrs. Middleton’ was Zoe Havering, and Zoe Havering
was ‘Mrs. Middleton’! Figure to yourself, she was an actress!
I suspect she had a double part to play that evening. She was
seen by the visitor in her own character, then she hurried away
and changed into the clothes of the housekeeper. When she had
discharged the revolver and killed her uncle, she and her husband
between them concocted the story of the bearded man.”

“But, Poirot, I saw them both together! I saw Mrs. Havering and
the housekeeper!”

“Did you, Hastings? Did you see them both at the same time? Think.”

I reflected. No, I had not. I had seen the housekeeper first, and
then she had gone upstairs and Mrs. Havering had come down.

“But the voice?” I objected. “And the appearance?”

“A clever actress can change her voice and her appearance,
_mon ami_. And remember, you had never seen either of them before.
The housekeeper was a ‘middle-aged woman in black’—a very easy
disguise to assume. And as for the beard—well, that was a stroke
of genius! It diverted attention from the real murderer and
suggested a mysterious stranger.”

“But the revolver found at Ealing?”

“A very simple matter. Roger Havering took it with him to London
and dropped it where it was sure to be found. It was all part of
the plan to provide an alibi for himself and his wife.”

“And what about the Agency? Mrs. Havering said she engaged the
housekeeper there.”

“She lied, Hastings! She never engaged a housekeeper at all. She
merely told the Agency that she had done so, to prevent them from
sending any more applicants to the house. It was all very
cleverly thought out.”

“Then you think Roger Havering was in it too?”

“Of course! He and his wife together planned the whole thing.
He provided the revolver and the alibi for himself, while she
carried out the actual murder and provided the alibi for herself
with the help of the mythical Mrs. Middleton.”

“But what are you going to do, Poirot? Are you going to tell Japp?”

Poirot shook his head.

“What proof have we, Hastings? None! It is all a matter of
deduction. We can prove nothing. The Haverings are clever—very
clever. They have covered their tracks well. No, I shall do
nothing. But they will not enjoy their ill-gotten gains, of that
I am sure. The memory of that night at Hunter’s Lodge will
haunt them to the end of their lives.”

I sat in silence, marvelling at the ingenuity of the crime and the
still greater ingenuity of my friend who had solved it from his
sick-bed.

“And to think,” I said at last, “that I was there on the spot and
saw nothing!”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye, “you saw
everything! But you did not observe! That is the difference. You
looked at the housekeeper, but you did not see Zoe Havering. You
looked at the gun-room, but you did not see the truth. It is the
little grey cells, Hastings! The little grey cells! They alone
can see the truth.”

He leaned back in his chair and closed his eyes.

“And now, _mon ami_,” he murmured, “I think I will have another
cup of that excellent tisane you prepared for me. It is truly
beneficent.”

“I mean that Mrs. Havering and Mrs. Middleton were one and the
same person. Think of it, Hastings. A little clever make-up, a
change of voice, a wig—and the thing is done. To the servants at
Newmarket, Mrs. Havering was well known. To a housekeeper newly
engaged, and who had never seen her mistress, the part was easy.
Mrs. Havering, then, as Mrs. Middleton, greets her husband’s uncle
at the door, shows him into the gun-room, and then, as Mrs.
Havering, she comes into the hall to find her ‘housekeeper’
disturbed by the sound of voices. A few minutes later, she fires
the shot, through the window, after first locking the gun-room
door from the inside, and then, as Mrs. Havering, she joins the
‘housekeeper’ in the hall. The ‘housekeeper’ is then sent for the
police, and Mrs. Havering is left alone to dispose of the wig and
other properties, and to wait for her husband’s return. The
revolver is posted to a fictitious address in London, and the
trick is done.”

“But the black-bearded man?” I asked. “Where does he come in?”

“He does not come in at all, Hastings! He was a myth, invented to
account for the crime.”

“And the motive?”

“The motive is simple—money. With Mr. Pace dead, the Haverings
would inherit his fortune. They were, as I have said, in desperate
need of it.”

“It’s a most ingenious theory, Poirot,” I said, “but have you any
proof?”

“Is it not obvious? What did you tell me of the housekeeper?
‘A quiet, middle-aged woman.’ And of Mrs. Havering? ‘A very
handsome young woman.’ And yet, _mon ami_, when you saw Mrs.
Havering for the first time, she was wearing a flame-coloured
jumper and a little hat of flame-coloured leather. Now, why should
she wear a hat in her own house? It was to hide her hair, of
course! And she would be quite a different-looking woman in a
prim, black dress and a transformation and a little makeup.
Havering was already in London. He had brought the revolver with
him and dropped it where it was sure to be found—thus drawing
attention to the fact that it was the one used in the murder.
The black-bearded man was a myth—a myth which Zoe Havering, in her
character of Mrs. Middleton, had already prepared the ground for.
She herself admitted him, she herself (in the character of the
housekeeper) told the master that a gentleman wished to see him.
Then, as Mrs. Havering, she met the housekeeper in the hall. A
simple matter of a voice, a slamming door, and a shot fired by
a woman who was a very good actress! It was she who killed
Harrington Pace.”

“But the voice? The housekeeper’s voice?”

“You yourself heard her, Hastings. Was there anything remarkable
about it? No. And why? Because it was the voice of Zoe Havering!”

“I mean that the housekeeper and Mrs. Havering were one and the
same person. It was a very clever piece of work. Mrs. Havering
was an actress, remember. That is why I was so interested in the
clothes she wore. There was a flame-coloured jumper, was there
not? That would be very easy to change for the black of the
housekeeper. And the wig! And the middle-aged appearance! All
very easy for a clever woman like Zoe Havering. Then she meets
her husband, they go into the gun-room—I should think he was with
her—they make a noise as of quarrelling—he goes out—she fires the
shot—and then they both run out together, or she runs out and
meets the housekeeper who is—herself!”

“But Poirot, that is impossible! The housekeeper was with her!”

“No, no, Hastings. That was what you were told. But who told you?
Mrs. Havering and the housekeeper. But there was no housekeeper!
Mrs. Havering only said there was. She was the housekeeper herself.”

“But the man with the black beard?”

“Another piece of play-acting. There was no man with a black beard.
There was only Mr. Havering who, before he left for London,
arranged for the gun-room window to be open, and then he goes
off to the station. After he has gone, his wife—in her character
of housekeeper—admits the ‘American gentleman,’ and then she
changes her clothes, and as Mrs. Havering she and her uncle go
to the gun-room. Then the quarrel, the shot—and then she is the
housekeeper again for a few minutes while she goes for the police,
and then she is Mrs. Havering again! And all the time there is
no one to say she is not telling the truth!”

“But the revolver found at Ealing?”

“Ah, that was Roger Havering’s part. He took it up to London with
him and dropped it where it would be found. A very neat touch,
that!”

“Then they both did it?”

“Yes. It was a very clever conspiracy. They will both be very
rich now. But they will not enjoy their riches, Hastings. I,
Hercule Poirot, say so!”

“But can we prove it?”

“I fear not. We have no evidence. But I have a little plan. I
shall write a letter to Mrs. Havering. I shall tell her that I
know all. And I shall see what she says.”

“She will say nothing.”

“We shall see.”

Poirot’s plan was carried out. But no answer ever came to his
letter. Zoe Havering and her husband had disappeared. They were
never seen again.

“You see, Hastings,” said Poirot, as he sat by the fire, “I was
right. They knew that I, Hercule Poirot, was on their track. And
so they fled. It is a great thing to be a great detective!”

I looked at him, and I could not help smiling.

“Yes, Poirot,” I said, “you are certainly a very great detective.”

And Poirot, with a satisfied sigh, turned back to his tisane.

“Did you ever see the two women together, Hastings? No, you did
not. The housekeeper was not there when you were with her
mistress, and her mistress was not there when you were with the
housekeeper. Mrs. Havering is a clever actress, _mon ami_. She
dressed the part and played it with consummate skill. She was
Mrs. Middleton when you arrived, and then, after she had sent
you to wait in the hall, she slipped upstairs, changed her
clothes, and came down as Mrs. Havering.”

“But the voice!” I protested. “The housekeeper’s voice was quite
different.”

“_Naturellement_. Mrs. Havering has been on the stage, remember.
A simple matter for her to disguise her voice. And then, she
would only have to speak a few words to you.”

“But the black-bearded man! He was seen to enter the house.”

“By whom? By the housekeeper—that is, by Mrs. Havering. No one
else saw him. He was a myth, Hastings—a myth!”

“Then who shot Mr. Pace?”

“Roger Havering shot him, of course. He never went to London at
all.”

“But the 6.15 train? He was seen to leave by it!”

“No, no, Hastings. He was seen to enter the car that was to take
him to the station. That is all. He could easily have slipped
out of the car again, and hidden himself in the garden until
the time came for him to do his work. Then, after the murder,
he could have made his way to London by a later train, or
even by car.”

“But the revolver found at Ealing?”

“A very clever touch, that. It was intended to make it appear
that the murderer had fled to London. Roger Havering dropped it
there himself, no doubt.”

“And what about the Agency? Mrs. Havering said she had engaged
the housekeeper from there.”

“She lied, of course. She never engaged a housekeeper at all.
It was all a part of her plan to provide herself with an alibi.”

“It’s incredible!” I exclaimed.

“It is very simple, when you come to think of it. The two of them
planned it together. It was a cold-blooded, heartless murder.”

“And they will get away with it?”

“I fear so, Hastings. We have no proof—no proof at all. It is
very galling, but what would you? We must accept the facts.”

“I can’t believe it,” I said. “It seems so—so impossible.”

“Nothing is impossible, _mon ami_, to the mind that is trained to
observe and to reason. And now, if you will be so good as to
hand me that bottle of medicine—the one with the red label—I think
it is time for my dose.”

I did as he requested, and then sat for a long time in silence,
thinking over the extraordinary story he had told me. It was
hard to realize that those two young people, who had seemed so
pleasant and so full of life, could be guilty of such a
dreadful crime. But I knew Poirot, and I knew that he was
seldom wrong. And as I looked at him, sitting there in his
gaudy dressing-gown, I felt a renewed sense of admiration for
his extraordinary powers. He might be ill, he might be
eccentric, but he was still the greatest detective of his
time.

The mystery of Hunter’s Lodge was solved—but at what a cost!
The guilty would go free, and the innocent would never know the
truth. It was a sobering thought, and one that remained with
me for many a long day.

“I mean that Zoe Havering was an actress before her marriage, that
you and Japp only saw the housekeeper in a dark hall, a dim
middle-aged figure in black with a faint subdued voice, and finally
that neither you nor Japp, nor the local police whom the housekeeper
fetched, ever saw Mrs. Middleton and her mistress at one and the
same time. It was child’s play for that clever and daring woman.
On the pretext of summoning her mistress, she runs upstairs, slips
on a bright jumper and a hat with black curls attached which she
jams down over the grey transformation. A few deft touches, and
the make-up is removed, a slight dusting of rouge, and the brilliant
Zoe Havering comes down with her clear ringing voice. Nobody looks
particularly at the housekeeper. Why should they? There is nothing
to connect her with the crime. She, too, has an alibi.”

“But the revolver that was found at Ealing? Mrs. Havering could
not have placed it there?”

“No, but her husband could. He took it up to London with him. He
and his wife had planned the thing out. A clever woman and a bold
one, and a man who is a weak tool in her hands. Together they
executed this most ingenious crime.”

“Then it was Mrs. Havering who shot her uncle?”

“Certainly. After her husband had left for the station, she
assumed her character of the mysterious housekeeper, and admitted
her confederate, the black-bearded man. Only there was no such
person. She herself, in that character, entered the gun-room, and
shot her uncle. Then she and the housekeeper together—that is to
say, she alone—raised the alarm. It was simple, and it was
effective.”

“But the description of the man?”

“A creation of their own brains, Hastings. They knew that an
American with a black beard would be a likely person to be
suspected. They had probably even provided for some such person
appearing on the scene if necessary.”

“And what are you going to do, Poirot?”

“I have already done it, my friend. I have sent a little note to
the lady, and I think it will have the desired effect. If she is
as clever as I think her, she will see that the game is up. If
not—well, I have told Japp what I think. It is for him to act.”

I was silent. Poirot’s logic was always so pitilessly clear.
Presently I spoke.

“It seems a pity that such a clever woman should have thrown her
life away.”

“She will not have thrown it away, Hastings. She will have used it
to the best of her ability. And now, if you will be so good, I
think I could enjoy another cup of that excellent tisane you
prepared for me.”

I rose and went to the mantelpiece. As I did so, my eye fell upon
the row of medicine bottles.

“By the way, Poirot,” I said, “there is one thing that puzzles me.
Why did you ask for a description of the clothes they wore? What
had that to do with it?”

Poirot smiled.

“Everything, my friend. It was the one thing that gave me the clue.
You see, if Mrs. Middleton and Mrs. Havering were one and the same
person, it was essential that they should not wear the same clothes.
But a change of dress takes time. Now, if the housekeeper was
wearing a black dress, and Mrs. Havering a flame-coloured jumper,
the change could be made in a few seconds. A jumper is easily
slipped on over a black dress. That was why I was so anxious to
know what they were wearing. When you told me that Mrs. Havering
was wearing a flame-coloured jumper, I knew I was on the right
track. It was the one thing that could not be hidden.”

“I see,” I said slowly. “It was very clever of you, Poirot.”

“It was simple, Hastings, very simple. But then, as I have always
told you, it is the simple things that are the most difficult to
see.”

I handed him his cup of tisane, and he drank it with every
appearance of enjoyment.

“And now, my friend,” he said, as he set down the cup, “I think I
will sleep. I am still a little tired, you understand. But
to-morrow—to-morrow I shall be myself again, the great Hercule
Poirot!”

And with a little sigh of satisfaction, he closed his eyes.

I stood for a moment looking down at him. He was a strange little
man, but there was no doubt about his genius. I felt a sudden wave
of affection for him. He might be vain, he might be eccentric, but
he was the best friend I had in the world.

I turned away and walked softly out of the room. Outside, the
afternoon sun was shining, and I felt a sudden desire for fresh
air. I would go for a walk in the park, and think over all that
had happened. It had been a strange case, but thanks to Poirot,
it was solved. And as I walked, I couldn't help wondering what the
future held for Roger and Zoe Havering. Would they be able to
escape the consequences of their crime, or would justice finally
overtake them? Only time would tell.

But one thing was certain: as long as Hercule Poirot was on the
case, there was no escape for the guilty. His “little grey cells”
were always at work, and no matter how clever the criminal, they
were no match for the greatest detective in the world.

“No, but her husband could! It was he who took it up to London with
him and dropped it between the railings as he walked home from the
District Station. A very clever move that. It seemed to give the
lie to any suspicion of his being the murderer. It was his part,
just as it was his part to find the American gentleman whose beard
and overcoat were already in the house—bought, no doubt, some weeks
before. It was an admirable scheme! Zoe Havering kills the old man,
whilst Roger Havering is safely on his way to London. Then she
becomes the housekeeper, and waits for the American gentleman to
arrive. She lets him into the gun-room, and after a few minutes’
interval she fires the shot. Then, as the housekeeper, she runs
into the hall, where her mistress is supposedly sitting. A few
seconds later she is Zoe Havering, and the housekeeper has vanished.”

“But the American gentleman?”

“There was no American gentleman. Mrs. Havering—as the
housekeeper—merely told her story. No one else saw him. He was
a myth, Hastings, a myth! It was a very clever and very daring
crime.”

“And what are you going to do about it?”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders.

“Nothing. We have no proof. We can only wait. But I do not think,
Hastings, that they will enjoy their ill-gotten gains. There is
a little thing called conscience, and it is sometimes a very active
thing.”

I was silent. Poirot’s logic was always so cold and so unerring.

“But what about the description of the clothes, Poirot?” I asked.
“Why did you want that?”

Poirot smiled.

“Because I wanted to see if you had any eye for such things,
Hastings! You had not. You described the flame-coloured jumper,
the little hat of flame-coloured leather, and the black-curled
wig—but you never mentioned that Mrs. Havering was wearing the
very same shoes as the housekeeper!”

I sighed.

“I’m afraid I’m a bit of a failure as a detective, Poirot.”

“_Mais non, mais non, mon ami_! You are very useful to me. You see
everything with the eyes of the ordinary man, and that is a very
great help to me sometimes.”

And with this doubtful compliment I had perforce to be content.

“No, Hastings, that was her husband’s contribution. When he
returned to London, he brought with him the missing revolver, and
he it was who left it in the parcel on Haven Green. A clever
touch, that, as it pointed to someone else who might have a grudge
against Harrington Pace and lived in that direction.”

“The housekeeper was only seen in the dim light?” I queried.

“Exactly. And the black-bearded man? Why did no one see him
except the housekeeper? Simply because he didn’t exist. No one
saw him at the station. No one saw him on the road. He was just
a convenient invention to provide a motive for the murder. The
shot that was fired? Only a blank cartridge, Hastings, fired by
Mrs. Havering herself to bring the housekeeper on the scene—or
rather, to make it appear that the housekeeper and Mrs. Havering
were together. The real shot was fired earlier, after Roger
Havering had left for London, and before the housekeeper had
supposedly admitted the visitor. Harrington Pace was dead before
nine o’clock. But Mrs. Havering had to make it appear that he was
killed by a stranger.”

I sat in silence for a moment, my mind racing.

“But the motive, Poirot? Why should she kill him? Roger Havering
was his heir.”

“_Mon cher_, Harrington Pace was a rich man, but he was also a
miser. He would not give his nephew a penny during his lifetime.
And the Haverings were in desperate straits. It was a cold-blooded,
premeditated crime. They needed the money, and they took the
shortest way to get it.”

“It’s incredible,” I said. “And we can prove nothing?”

“_Mais non_, _mon cher_, it was her husband. When he arrived in
London, he went to Haven Green and hid the weapon as he had arranged
with his wife. Then he proceeded to his club, all according to
plan. It was a very clever little plot, and they would have won
hands down but for one thing.”

“And that was?”

“Me, Hercule Poirot! I, who can see through a brick wall, if the
brick wall is only a woman’s make-up!”

“And the black-bearded man?”

“A myth! There was no black-bearded man! Only a voice, which
Mrs. Middleton, that excellent and respectable housekeeper,
asserted was American. And the shots were fired by Zoe Havering
herself!”

“You think so?”

“I am sure of it. Zoe Havering was the one who had the opportunity.
She was the one who could move about the house without suspicion.
She was the one who had the motive. And, above all, she was the
one who had the talent for such a daring and cold-blooded piece
of acting.”

“But, Poirot, how can you prove all this?”

Poirot smiled, a slow, enigmatic smile.

“I cannot prove it, Hastings. That is the tragedy of it. There is
no evidence. The housekeeper has vanished. The revolver has been
found, but it cannot be traced to the Haverings. The alibi is
perfect. No, we can do nothing. But there is one thing that gives
me satisfaction.”

“What is that?”

“That Zoe Havering knows that I know. She will never feel quite
safe again. She will always be wondering when the blow will fall.
And for a woman like that, the uncertainty is a worse punishment
than the gallows.”

“I suppose you’re right,” I said, though I felt a certain amount
of disappointment at such a conclusion to the case.

“And now, Hastings, if you will be so good as to bring me that
bottle of green medicine—the third from the left—I think I will
take another dose. It is really most beneficial.”

And with a sigh of content, Poirot settled himself down among his
pillows.


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


The case of the murder at Hunter’s Lodge was never solved. The
police were unable to find any trace of the mysterious
black-bearded man, and the housekeeper, Mrs. Middleton, was never
seen again. Roger Havering inherited his uncle’s fortune, and he
and his wife continued to live their gay and butterfly existence.
But sometimes, when I see Zoe Havering’s name in the paper, I
wonder if Poirot was right, and if she ever feels a shadow of
fear. And then I remember the look in Poirot’s eyes as he spoke,
and I am sure that he was right. For Hercule Poirot is never
wrong.

“No, but her husband could. He took it up with him in his
travelling-bag. A very simple and effective piece of work,
Hastings. And now you see why the housekeeper has vanished. She
never existed. The two of them, husband and wife, have planned
this thing between them. It was Zoe Havering who shot her uncle.
She was alone with him in the gun-room. She was the ‘black-bearded
American.’ A few quick touches, a false beard, a light overcoat,
and she was ready for her part. She had the revolver which her
husband had given her before he left. She shot her uncle, then
locked the door from the inside, and escaped through the window,
throwing her disguise into some convenient hiding-place. Then she
ran round the house, entered by the back door, and as the
housekeeper she came into the hall to meet herself—that is to say,
she came into the hall to find her mistress. A few moments later
she is upstairs, the housekeeper has vanished, and Mrs. Havering
comes down to meet the police.”

“It’s incredible!” I gasped. “And yet, Poirot, it fits! It fits
every fact of the case. But we have no proof.”

Poirot sighed.

“That is the trouble. We have no proof. We have only my ‘little
grey cells.’ And they are not, I fear, enough to convict a
murderer.”

“No, that was Roger Havering’s job—but it was a mistake on their
part. It put me on the right track. A man who has committed a
murder with a revolver which he found on the spot would fling it
away at once, he would not carry it up to London with him. No, the
motive was clear, the criminals wished to focus the interest of
the police on a spot far removed from Derbyshire they were anxious
to get the police away as soon as possible from the vicinity of
Hunter’s Lodge. Of course the revolver found at Ealing was not the
one with which Mr. Pace was shot. Roger Havering discharged one
shot from it, brought it up to London, went straight to his club
to establish his alibi, then went quickly out to Ealing by the
district, a matter of about twenty minutes only, placed the parcel
where it was found and so back to town. That charming creature,
his wife, quietly shoots Mr. Pace after dinner—you remember he was
shot from behind? Another significant point, that!—reloads the
revolver and puts it back in its place, and then starts off with
her desperate little comedy.”

“It’s incredible,” I murmured, fascinated, “and yet——”

“Wait a bit, Hastings, I have not yet finished! Let us look at the
story of the housekeeper. She has disappeared, as we know, but how?
Not by car or fly—the only ways of getting away from that isolated
spot. No, she must have been hidden in the house. And where? I ask
you that, Hastings! Where? Why, she was not hidden at all! She
simply walked out of the house as Mrs. Havering!”

“Mrs. Havering! But the housekeeper was middle-aged and she——”

“My dear friend, a touch of grey hair, a few lines on the face—it
is easy for an actress! Mrs. Havering had only to change her dress,
put on the housekeeper’s clothes, and there she was! And when the
police were searching for Mrs. Middleton, she was sitting calmly
in the drawing-room as Mrs. Havering. It was a stroke of genius,
that!”

“Then you think that they were both in it?”

“I am sure of it. They both had everything to gain by Mr. Pace’s
death. He was a rich man and Roger Havering was his heir. But they
will never be caught, Hastings. They are too clever for that.
There is no evidence against them—nothing but my own deductions.
And what are they worth? Nothing in a court of law!”

Poirot sighed and took a sip of his tisane.

“It is a pity,” he murmured. “I should have liked to have had the
hanging of that beautiful and wicked woman.”

“And what about the black-bearded man?” I asked.

“Oh, he was just a myth, an invention of the two of them to put
the police on the wrong scent. There never was any such person!”

I sat in silence for a few moments, marvelling at the
extraordinary cleverness of the pair.

“It’s a wonderful story, Poirot,” I said at last. “But tell me,
how did you know?”

Poirot smiled.

“My friend, it was the clothes! You told me that Mrs. Havering
was wearing a flame-coloured jumper and a hat of flame-coloured
leather. Now, no woman who had just seen her uncle murdered would
dream of wearing such gay and festive attire! It was a mistake,
a great mistake on her part. She should have worn black—or at
least something quiet and subdued. But her vanity was too much
for her—she wanted to look her best! And that was her undoing.”

He paused, then added with a twinkle in his eye:

“And then there were the photographs, Hastings! You will remember
that I told you not to waste your time taking them? They were, as
I suspected, quite useless—but they served their purpose in
convincing you that I was a very difficult person to please!”

I laughed.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said. “I don’t know how you
do it.”

“It is the little grey cells, my friend,” Poirot replied, tapping
his forehead. “The little grey cells! They never fail me!”

“And yet, Hastings, it is true! And how well she played her part,
did she not? That little flame-coloured jumper, she was sure that
everyone would remember it. And they did! You yourself were much
impressed with it, and so was the good Japp. Oh, she is a clever
woman! But she has over-reached herself this time. We must tell the
good Japp at once. He must look for her at Newmarket and then we
shall see if she is as clever as she thinks herself.”

“You mean, Poirot, that Roger Havering and Zoe Havering were in it
together?”

“Precisely. He provided the alibi and the distraction in London;
she performed the deed and the character of the witness at home.
The 'black-bearded American' was a phantom, a voice heard through
a door, and a description given by a woman who was, in fact, the
killer herself.”

“And yet, Hastings, it is true. I have been able to make certain.”

“How?”

“By means of your description of the clothes. Mrs. Middleton wore
a black woollen shawl, and she was slightly bent. Zoe Havering
wears a flame-coloured jumper, and is slender and boyish. When
the housekeeper was seen by the police, her face was in shadow.
The dresser she had prepared was as simple as possible. The two
women were never seen together. Why? Because they were one and
the same. Zoe Havering was her own housekeeper. When the 'housekeeper'
went to fetch the police, she simply walked a distance, changed her
attire in the darkness of the moors, and eventually returned or
made sure she was seen as the mistress. The 'man with the black beard'
was a myth, a creation to explain the shot that Zoe herself fired
using her husband's revolver. She then cleaned the weapon, or
rather, Roger took the actual murder weapon to London to dispose of
it, while leaving a duplicate—which you found—to be 'discovered' by
the police to further the illusion of a mysterious intruder."

"But Poirot, the housekeeper disappeared later!"

"Exactly. After the police had been and the 'danger' of immediate
suspicion had passed, Zoe simply stopped playing the role. She
claimed the housekeeper had vanished. Since no one had really
vetted Mrs. Middleton's background—Zoe having faked the Agency
correspondence—there was no one to prove she ever existed as a
separate entity. It was a bold gamble, Hastings, played by a woman
with the nerves of an actress and the heart of a criminal."

“_And yet it is the truth!_ But we shall never be able to prove
it. Japp is at Elmer’s Dale now, searching for the housekeeper,
