but he will never find her. The Haverings are too clever for us.
They have played their part well, and it will be a lesson to me
not to be too sure of my little grey cells next time. But wait!
The murderer has not yet outwitted Hercule Poirot!”

And, reaching out his hand, Poirot picked up a small and
inconspicuous object which lay on the table. It was a single,
brightly coloured, flame-coloured silk thread.

“From the jumper, Hastings! I saw it when I looked through your
negatives—the ones you thought were underexposed. It was caught
on the rough wood of the window-frame. A small thing, but enough.
And here is a second clue.”

He held up a tiny piece of black hair.

“From the wig of the ‘housekeeper,’ my friend! I found it when I
visited Hunter’s Lodge myself this morning, while you were still
asleep. I did not need to wait for your return to London to know
where the truth lay.”

“But it is not incredible at all! It is a very simple and
straightforward case. There is just one more thing I should like
to see before we go. If we are lucky, we may yet find a trace of
the elusive Mrs. Middleton.”

I looked at him.

“What do you mean?”

“Well, you know, we have her box. It must be at the police station
at Elmer’s Dale. I think it would be as well if we were to examine
it. You remember I asked you for a description of the clothes worn
by the two women?”

“Yes, but what on earth has that got to do with it?”

“A great deal, my dear Hastings! You said that Mrs. Havering wore
a flame-coloured jumper. Now, what did the housekeeper wear?”

“A black dress, of course.”

“Yes, but what sort of a black dress?”

“I don’t know. Just a plain black dress.”

“Exactly! A plain black dress. Now, in Mrs. Middleton’s box there
was only one black dress. It was a very good one, too, was it not?”

“I don’t know. I didn’t notice.”

“But I did! And it was a very expensive one. Now, does a
middle-aged housekeeper, a woman in Mrs. Middleton’s position,
possess expensive black dresses? I think not. No, that dress was
Mrs. Havering’s. It was a very clever and very daring woman who
planned that murder, Hastings. She had courage and she had
resource.”

“And what are you going to do about it?”

“Nothing, my friend. We have no proof. We can prove nothing. Let
us hope that Justice will find its own way in the end. And now,
let us have a little dinner together at the Ritz, and forget all
about this very unpleasant business.”

I could only agree. Poirot was always right. In this case, as in
so many others, he had seen through the surface of things to the
truth which lay beneath. It was a triumph of the little grey cells.

“After all,” I said, as we sat at our table, “it was a very near
thing for you, Poirot. If you hadn’t been ill, you might never
have solved it.”

Poirot smiled.

“Perhaps, Hastings, perhaps. But as I said before, it is possible
that I shall not die this time!”

“And yet it is true. _Bien sur_, my friend, it is true. But to
bring that precious pair to justice, that is another matter. Well,
Japp must do what he can—I have written him fully—but I very much
fear, Hastings, that we shall be obliged to leave them to Fate, or
_le bon Dieu_, whichever you prefer.”

“The wicked flourish like a green bay tree,” I reminded him.

“But at a price, Hastings, always at a price, _croyez-moi!_”

Poirot’s forebodings were confirmed. Japp, though convinced of the
truth of his theory, was unable to get together the necessary
evidence to ensure a conviction.

It was some three months later that I read in the morning paper of the
tragic death of Mr. and Mrs. Roger Havering in an aeroplane accident
on the way to Paris. I showed the item to Poirot. He nodded gravely.
“It is the justice of the good God, Hastings. They have paid the price
of which I spoke. And now, if you please, my tisane—it is getting
cold, and I must not neglect the health of the great Hercule Poirot
for even a single moment!”

I heard no more of the case until some six months later, when a small paragraph in the morning paper caught my eye. It recorded the death of Mr. and Mrs. Roger Havering in a tragic motor accident in the South of France; their car had plunged over a cliff, leaving no survivors. I showed the snippet to Poirot. He looked at it for a long time in silence, his eyes dark with a sudden gravity. “Perhaps it is better so,” he said at last, folding the paper with his usual precision. “The law of man is a clumsy instrument, Hastings, but the hand of Fate—ah, that is a different matter! It strikes when least expected. And now, _mon ami_, bring me my hat and my cane. The influenza, it is departed, and the world—the world of the wicked—it awaits the return of Hercule Poirot!”

It was about a month later that my eye was caught by a headline in the morning paper. The Hon. Roger Havering and his wife had both been killed in an aeroplane accident while crossing to Paris. I showed the paragraph to Poirot. He took the paper from me and read it in silence. “The price, Hastings,” he said at last, as he laid it aside. “The price of which I spoke. It has been paid. They have gone to a higher tribunal than any of this world. It is, as I said, the justice of _le bon Dieu_.”

It was some six months later that a small paragraph in the papers caught my eye. An aeroplane, crossing to Paris, had crashed in mid-channel, and among the names of the victims were those of Mr. and Mrs. Roger Havering. I showed it to Poirot. He nodded his head gravely. “The justice of the law may be evaded, Hastings, but there is a higher justice that finds its own way. They have gone to answer for their crime. And for me—well, I have still my little paragraph in _Society Gossip_ to console me for the fact that, for once, the great Hercule Poirot did not bring his criminals to the gallows.”

It was barely three weeks later that we read in the morning paper of the tragic aeroplane accident which had occurred on the way to Paris. The Hon. Roger Havering and his wife had both been killed instantly. I showed the paragraph to Poirot. He nodded gravely. “You see, Hastings? I told you that they would pay the price. _Le bon Dieu_ has a better memory for justice than the twelve men of a jury. The ‘housekeeper’ has vanished for the last time. And now, _mon ami_, be so good as to bring me my clothes brush. There is a speck of dust upon my sleeve that is causing me a veritably criminal amount of suffering!”

Mr. Pace’s huge fortune passed into the hands of his murderers.
Nevertheless, Nemesis did overtake them, and when I read in the
paper that the Hon. Roger and Mrs. Havering were amongst those
killed in the crashing of the Air Mail to Paris I knew that Justice
was satisfied.
